data.text: The complaint was filed by the victim's aunt, who had been told by the victim what was happening in her home. Lorena Martínez, the prosecutor for Domestic Violence and Gender Violence in Tartagal, represented the Public Prosecutor's Office in the debate hearing in which a man was sentenced by Chamber II of the Court of Justice of that district to eight years of effective imprisonment for being the perpetrator of the crime of sexual abuse with double carnal access qualified by the relationship and by the pre-existing cohabitation and minority. The facts judged were denounced on January 31, 2024 by a woman, who claimed that her eleven-year-old niece with developmental delay, arrived at her house and told her that her father was sexually abusing her. Prosecutor Martínez initiated a penal investigation, gathering the necessary evidence that allowed the accused to be convicted of the sexual abuse of his daughter. In the sentence, Chamber II of the Tartagal Court of Justice ordered the extraction of genetic material from the convicted individual by the Molecular Biology Service of the Technical Department of the Fiscal Investigation Corps (CIF) and its subsequent registration in the Genetic Data Bank, after assigning the Unique Genetic Identification Data (DUIG), in compliance with the provisions of National Law No. 26,879 and Provincial Law No. 7775, and in this regard, the Office of Hearing Management (OGA) was notified to proceed with the corresponding proceedings.

At least 10 dead in a clash between two criminal gangs in Lagos, Nigeria, 10 Feb (EFE). At least 10 people died on Sunday in clashes between members of two criminal gangs in southern Nigeria, in the state of Rivers, confirmed EFE on Monday the Police, although witnesses estimated at least 18 the fatalities. There was a clash between two groups in the locality of Obelle, in the Emuoha zone, yesterday morning. Ten people have been confirmed dead as a result of the violence, detailed to EFE by phone the Police spokesperson in Rivers, Grace IringeKoko. The majority of the victims are members of the gangs but some innocent civilians were also killed, she added, pointing out that calm has returned to the area after the deployment of security forces. However, a resident of the affected locality who witnessed the events, called Chika Chukwu, estimated 18 dead and highlighted that the majority were innocent people. Members of the group, numbering about 25, stormed the community early in the morning and began shooting, a neighbor told EFE. According to Chukwu, it was a retaliatory act for an attack registered the previous week in which members of the rival gang killed several people. Now, everyone lives in fear. Some people have fled out of fear that the gang will commit new attacks, he lamented. This type of criminal group, often composed of young people and known in the country as sects, is common in Nigeria, especially in the Niger Delta region in the southern part of the country, but has extended its activities to other African countries and even to Europe, especially in France and Italy. Although they first appeared in the 1950s on the campuses of some universities as student fraternities, many of these sects are currently made up of all kinds of people and have become armed groups, often used by politicians and other prominent figures to achieve their objectives through violent methods. These gangs, which are illegal in the country, commit various types of crimes, ranging from human trafficking to narcotics trafficking, passing through prostitution or cybercrimes.

Last Saturday, February 8th, the Diocese of Segorbe-Castellón held a Vigil of Prayer and Reflection in observance of the 11th World Day of Prayer and Reflection against Human Trafficking, organized by the Secretariat for Migrations and Human Mobility together with Diocesan Caritas. This Day of Prayer, celebrated throughout the Church, coincides with the liturgical memory of Saint Josephine Bakhita, a woman who was enslaved, liberated, and found Jesus Christ, dedicating her life to the fight against human trafficking. The Vigil, held at the Co-Cathedral of Santa María in Castellón, was presided over by D. Juan Crisóstomo Nangagahigo, Director of the Secretariat. During the celebration, reflection was given to the urgent need to eradicate human trafficking, a complex phenomenon affecting millions of people worldwide, especially women and children, subjected to sexual exploitation, labor exploitation, and other forms of slavery. Under the banner of Ambassadors of Hope Together Against Human Trafficking, the vigil invited all attendees to be active agents in the fight for human dignity, in harmony with Pope Francis's call. The event was part of this Jubilee Year of Pilgrims of Hope, whose social project for 2025 focuses primarily on raising awareness and taking action against human trafficking. The vigil featured the participation of faithful from the entire Diocese, who united their voices and prayers in a show of solidarity with the victims of human trafficking. Throughout the celebration, the importance of prayer, reflection, and personal and community commitment in the fight against this grave reality was emphasized. This year, the Jubilee 2025 social project will continue to focus on raising awareness about human trafficking, with the goal of mobilizing the entire Christian community to eradicate this modern form of slavery and promote a more just and humane world. The next event, a video forum on the documentary "Irioweniasi. The Thread of the Moon," will take place next Wednesday, February 12th at 7:00 p.m. in the Santa María salons, Castellón. Share

The trial scheduled for Monday in the First Section of the Provincial Court of Ciudad Real against two young men accused of sexually abusing, deceiving, and using a 13-year-old girl to create child pornography did not take place as the parties reached an agreement. It was agreed that the young men R.J.A.H. and A.V.S. would be sentenced to 11 years and 9 months and 6 years and 6 months in prison respectively. In addition, they would be held liable for a civil responsibility of 5,000 euros each. The prosecutor in his accusatory writ had requested 19 years in prison for R.J.A.H. for two counts of sexual assault, one count of deception, and a third count of using a minor to create child pornography. On the other hand, for A.V.S., the prosecution had requested 16 years in prison for a count of sexual assault and another count of using a minor to create child pornography. Justice has been served. We are very satisfied. Manuel Ángel Terriza, the prosecutor's attorney, has assured that justice has been served by acknowledging the accused's responsibility, both criminally and civilly. We are very satisfied. He explained that the accused have reached an agreement with the Public Ministry and the private prosecution, in which they have acknowledged the facts, in exchange for a reduction in the sentence and an agreement regarding civil liability. A.V.S. claims that if he had known the minor's age, he would not have maintained that sexual relationship. My client has acknowledged the facts because he could not do otherwise, among other things, because he never denied them. What he denied was knowing the minor's age. He has always said that if he had known, he would never have maintained that sexual relationship, explained the attorney Rodrigo González, who represented A.V.S.'s interests. After the hearing, the defense attorney assured that his client has accepted a plea agreement in the entirety of the facts without going into the individualization of each behavior. Regarding the reduction of the sentence compared to the previous requests by the prosecution, González explained that this is a very specific matter with a series of very specific facets that are not always going to be given, and that the Penal Code provides very severe penalties for pedophilia. Let no one draw conclusions here that do not correspond to the general cases. And it is that, he explained, circumstances have been given so that the prosecution has offered a sentence significantly lower than the one requested in writing, and the parties, valuing all the circumstances, have considered that we had to accept that agreement, starting from the basis that my client did not have an exact knowledge of the minor's age, which is why the sentence is reduced. He exposed that the Penal Code severely punishes having sexual relations with minors under 16 years old. A different matter is that it foresees some circumstances that may mitigate some penalties, such as the acknowledgment of the facts or the possible unawareness of the minor's age, as occurred in this case. He also pointed out other circumstances recognized by the jurisprudence, such as the maturity of the individuals or the age gap, adding that in the case of his client, the ages were 13 and 18 years. Given all these circumstances foreseen by the jurisprudence and because civil liability has been indemnified, according to the lawyer's explanation, this is why it was possible to reach an agreement where the reduction of the penalties is so significant. In this regard, he has repeatedly and emphasized that maintaining sexual relationships with minors can lead to very severe penalties, where the circumstances of the case will not be recognized. He contacted the 13-year-old girl through Instagram. The facts date back to 2023, as stated in the prosecution's accusation, when R.J.A.H., 21 years old, contacted the minor through the social network Instagram, posing as another young woman to gain the victim's trust, who at the time of the events was 13 years old. After gaining her trust, the young man confessed to the victim that he was a boy. Subsequently, both agreed to meet at a tourist apartment in Daimiel to engage in sexual relations on two occasions. During one of them, a friend of the main accused, A.V.S., appeared at the apartment, also engaging in sexual relations with the 13-year-old minor. Meanwhile, R.J.A.H. He realizado grabaciones de videos con su teléfono móvil de las relaciones sexuales para, posteriormente, enviarlas a través de una aplicación de mensajería instantánea en la que se observa a la víctima manteniendo relaciones sexuales.

Approximately 4,000 migrants have been detained in the United Kingdom since July 2024 as part of the fight against illegal immigration, with arrests made in nail salons, car washes, and restaurants. These arrests represent a 38% increase from the previous year, with 609 detainees alone in January 2025. British authorities warn of false promises that fuel perilous journeys and labor exploitation, while Interior Minister Yvette Cooper highlights the application of the law against these practices to record levels. Moreover, a new law is being processed to combat human trafficking, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for those who facilitate illegal crossings of the English Channel.

In a shocking incident that has shaken the community of Añatuya, a case of repeated sexual abuse has been reported against a 13-year-old girl, who recently gave birth at the local hospital. The minor, from Icaño, was allegedly subjected to humiliation by her cousin's boyfriend, who, according to the victim's account, would lock her in a room and repeatedly sexually abuse her. The situation came to light when the girl was admitted to the hospital in labor. There, despite the insistence of healthcare professionals, the minor revealed the abuse she had suffered, identifying her aunt and her boyfriend as the perpetrators of the crimes. District Attorney Alejandra Sobrero has ordered a thorough investigation, and it is expected that in the coming hours, both implicated parties will be detained and charged with the crime of repeated sexual abuse with carnal access. In the coming days, the minor will be assisted by psychologists in Cámara Gesell, with the goal of providing the necessary support and gathering more details about the reported incidents. Additionally, testimonial statements will be taken from relatives, neighbors, and medical staff who attended to the victim. This aberrant case has caused great commotion in the community of Añatuya, which demands justice and clarification of the facts.

After social media echoed about the alleged abuse by a university official at the Autonomous University of Chiapas (Unach) in Ocozocoautla, the State Commission for Human Rights in Chiapas (CEDH) issued precautionary measures in favor of the students. The Commission initiated an ex officio investigation into public complaints of alleged human rights violations committed by Héctor N, director of the Chemistry School at the university's main campus in Ocozocoautla. The accusations include sexual abuse, harassment, and violence against students and their families, according to testimonies published on social media by the Dignidad Universitaria collective and psychologist Gina Esquinca Rincón, daughter of a university academic. Measures and Institutional Response The ECHR issued precautionary measures to protect the physical, emotional, and psychological integrity of the university community, considering that the presence of the administrator could pose a risk. In a statement, the organization emphasized its commitment to eradicating violence in educational spaces and announced that it would monitor the case. In turn, Unach suspended Hector N from his duties. The institution noted that administrative actions were applied in response to the alleged violation of rights, without specifying if the process includes definitive sanctions. Testimony The case gained public relevance after the open letter from Gina Esquinca Rincón, the academic's daughter, addressed to the rector of Unach, Oswaldo Chacón Rojas. In the document, the psychologist denounced having suffered child sexual abuse, physical, and psychological violence at the hands of her father over 23 years. She also revealed that there are other victims. According to testimonies gathered by student organizations, complaints of sexual harassment against them date back two decades, without the university or authorities taking decisive action. Activists and former victims demand that the State Attorney General's Office (FGE) open an investigation file to determine responsibilities.

This Sunday, personnel from the Migrant Division who were conducting prevention tasks as part of the Green Spaces operation on Juan B. Justo Street and Alberdi Avenue in the area of the 25 de Mayo Plaza in Resistencia, detained an 18-year-old young man who had an outstanding arrest warrant. At the time of checking his data through the Biometric Management System (SiGeBi), they detected that the citizen had a request for apprehension and detention in a case for Suspected Sexual Abuse from December 2023 at the request of the Family and Gender Violence Division of the General San Martin locality. In this way, he was detained and placed at the disposal of the N General San Martin Prosecution Office.

The trial against Néstor Pinta, former Sports Director of Patagones, has begun. The recognized rower and teacher is accused of cooperating in the perpetration of gravely outrageous sexual abuse crimes committed by his father, who took his own life after the allegations became public. The case, which will be extended until the 12th, will be handled by the Criminal Court N° 3 of Bahía Blanca, and the possible sentence could range from 4 to 10 years in prison. The incidents occurred between 2015 and 2016, and Pinta is accused of having covered up for his father Aldo, who committed the abuses against a 15-year-old girl who practiced the sport at the Patagones Municipal School. The complainant victim spoke of situations that were repeated like a ritual. The students would go to the Pinta family's house, drink mate with pastries, and train at the gym.

The possibility that Brayan Campo, the confessed child killer of girl Sofia Delgado, could be released on bail has generated indignation and concern in Candelaria, Valle del Cauca. The municipality's mayor alerted about a request from the Attorney General's Office to declare the nullity of the trial, which could delay the process and result in a possible expiration of terms. Delays in the trial and fear of impunity Sofia Delgado, 12 years old, disappeared on September 29, 2024, in the corregimiento of Villagorgona, and her body was found on October 17 in a rural area of the municipality. Brayan Campo, 32 years old, confessed to the crime and revealed the exact location of the corpse. Despite the contundency of the evidence, the trial against him faces constant delays. Sofía Delgado Zúñiga Through a statement, the mayor of Candelaria, Gessica Vallejo Valencia, expressed her concern before the request of the Prosecutor's Office to annul the process and return it to the hearing phase. This could generate unnecessary delays in a case that has already been postponed three times, warned the mayor. Last January 27, the mayor sent requests to the Council of the Judiciary of the Cauca Valley, the Colombian Institute of Family Welfare (ICBF), and the Governor of the Valley, asking for strict monitoring of the judicial process. She insisted that no more delays should be allowed that could favor the accused. Background of Brayan Campo and the horror of the crime Campo, who already had a record for sexual abuse against a minor in 2014, deceived Sofia when she went to his store to buy a shampoo for pets. According to the investigation, the man convinced her to enter with the promise of a collar for her dog, and once inside, he brutally struck her with a shovel until causing her death. Days before the femicide, Campo had attempted to kidnap another girl, but she managed to escape. The community of Candelaria fears that her possible release would represent a latent threat to other minors. Community rejection and call for justice The case has generated a strong rejection in society and has highlighted failures in the judicial system. The governor of the Valley, Dilian Francisca Toro, demanded speed in the process and joined the outcry for justice. We cannot allow the killer of an innocent girl to request the annulment of the process. This man must receive the maximum penalty to prevent him from attacking the life of any minor in the country again, she emphasized. From the Candelaria Municipal Government, there has been a reiteration of the commitment to accompany the Delgado Zúñiga family and ensure justice is served. The community, on the other hand, demands that legal maneuvers that would allow impunity be avoided and that the trial against Brayan Campo proceed firmly until his definitive conviction.

San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chis. Clinical Psychologist Gina Gabriela Esquinca Rincón, 46 years old, reported her 46-year-old father Héctor Armando Esquinca Avilés, director of the School of Chemical Sciences at the Autonomous University of Chiapas (Unach), for exercising physical and psychological violence when she was a child, but also for sexually abusing her. In a letter she posted on her Facebook page, Gina Gabriela asserts that she is fully in possession of her mental faculties when making the accusation. I am fully in possession of my mental faculties. I am a psychologist and was a victim of child sexual abuse, physical, and psychological violence perpetrated by my father Héctor Armando Esquinca Avilés, she accuses. Her family members closest to her are aware of the physical and sexual violence Héctor Armando exercised against her daughter. My brothers, grandmother, uncles, friends know, everyone knows and has always known, including my mother. You offered me with a sexual intention, when I was 17 years old, to your brother Raúl, who always behaved honorably, and although he kept silent, he accused you with my brother Emilio years later.Esquinca Avilés has a PhD in Genetics and Molecular Biology and a PhD in Biotechnology and Bioengineering. He was a teacher at Miguel Hidalgo College in Tapachula and at the School of Agricultural Sciences located in the municipality of Huehuetán, and currently he is the director of the School of Chemical Sciences, located in the municipality of Ocozocoautla. Upon learning of the case, the Unach reacted mildly by stating that they have knowledge of public accusations against some officials of this institution and establish that actions will be taken against the university official accused. Immediate affirmative actions will be taken to protect the members of the university community. The State Commission for Human Rights (CEDH) announced that it has initiated investigations to join a complaint after the public denunciation, which was made against Esquinca Avilés, and issued precautionary measures in favor of the university community and the institution's personnel. Read also: 7 clandestine graves found in Baja California Sur, number of skeletons or belongings unknown Feminists demand Unach and the Women's Prosecutor's Office investigate Esquinca Avilés for sexual abuse and harassment Feminist organizations have rallied behind Gina Gabriela and requested that Unach comply with Article 3 of 3, which prohibits individuals who have been denounced for family violence, sexual crimes, and non-payment of alimony from holding public positions and being public officials. The feminist organizations are asking the Women's Prosecutor's Office to open an investigation file on the reported incidents and for Unach to acknowledge that it is a supportive institution, to set precedents in this and other cases of sexual violence. Journalist Fátima Monterrosa revealed that at the Hidalgo College in Tapachula, Esquinca Avilés, where he taught chemistry and biology classes, he sexually harassed the female students. What I am about to recount, I lived through. Nobody told me. He was a teacher who harassed high school students, asked them to lift their skirts to see their legs, tried to touch them, threw chalk on the floor and bent down to see the women's underwear, and was violent with the men, to the point of throwing the chalk and the ruler directly at their heads when they didn't answer his chemistry questions. He would fail all the students who didn't obey him, and then bribe them. He would ask for money or buy whiskey bottles in exchange for passing the course. He failed me when I protested, but I managed to pass the course through extraordinary means. I thought the guy was no longer teaching, that he had retired, but now I find out about all the atrocities he committed throughout his academic history. I hope the authorities don't protect him. My support and solidarity with Gina Esquinca, Monterrosa wrote on social media. The Chiapas Prosecutor's Office has made no announcement regarding the accusation made against the university official.

Pedro Sánchez on machista violence If there is a silence that needs to be broken today, it is that of men The President of the Government defends the Spanish model as the best in the world during the ceremony for the 20th anniversary of the comprehensive law If there is a silence that needs to be broken today, it is that of men. With this phrase, pronounced during the multitudinous act to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the comprehensive law against gender violence, the President of the Government, Pedro Sánchez, has highlighted what he considers one of the most urgent and necessary issues to achieve the objective with which the norm was drafted and approved during the presidency of the also socialist José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero to end violence against women. Sánchez, responsible for closing an act to which dozens of women and men who worked to push forward that norm have attended, has recalled how the law was drafted with three objectives that seemed unattainable back then. One, understanding that that violence was a structural violence rooted in machismo, two, taking it out of the private sphere, so that shame would change sides, and three, involving everyone on the same front against violence. By everyone, the president referred to everyone who works against violence at some point, from the police, doctors, social services, and the justice system. Training in equality would be beneficial for some legal operators, he also said, after the recent controversies caused by Judge Carretero's interrogation of Elisa Mouilaá, or the decision of another judge to deny, just last week, protection measures to Catalina, measures she requested, and that the police requested, before the woman was murdered this Sunday. Catalina was murdered in her home in Benalmádena allegedly by her ex-partner, by that man against whom she requested measures from the justice system, and the justice system did not protect her. Neither her nor her four remaining children, three of whom are minors, have been left orphaned. They were the symbol on Monday of the 1,295 women who have been murdered by their partners or ex-partners since records have been kept, dating back to 2003, and of the 474 minors whose fathers or stepfathers killed their mothers, 474, since official data have been collected, starting in 2013. Because before there were many others, and many others, and not just minors. Perhaps one of the most well-known and who never formed part of the statistics is Raquel Orantes, the daughter of Ana Orantes, the woman whom journalist Sandra Sabatés, the host of the event at the Reina Sofia Museum, has named to recount how she put the body, put the voice so that that dark, invisible, hidden issue of machismo violence in that moment, in 1997, became a social, and political issue. Raquel, her daughter, who is present here today, has said that she is aware of the gratitude of thousands of women from all over the world towards her mother for her act of bravery of speaking in front of a television camera at that time. Women who are brave when they should be free. And she remembered how, institutionally, she and her siblings were alone, like the children of women who were murdered are, within the fight against violence, the great forgotten ones. We were not even victims, we became so afterwards, with the creation of that integral law. Some minister still remembers that he said it was an isolated incident. There are already almost 1,300 isolated incidents. That which Raquel Orantes remembered, that lack of understanding of violence by a political representative, and their denial of it as structural violence, could have been, almost 25 years ago, understandable in a Spain where they still talked about passionate crimes and said they were family matters. Now, she has also added that there are still those who want to return that violence to the domestic sphere. Sánchez has also alluded to this. The unanimity with the law was a resounding message to all of Spain, that we were together and united for this, and it was heard in Spain and around the world, the first integral law against gender violence made history, for the good, and a month later with its entry into force we began to write it. Unfortunately, such a broad consensus does not seem possible today, the negationism of the far right counts on powerful tribunals of power and they dedicate themselves to inflicting more pain on the victims when they speak, for example, of false denunciations. Bullets that spread through the internet and reach the mobile phones of our children, voices that feed their professional and personal success with a fragile and toxic idea of masculinity, voices that lead many men to base themselves on the old idea of women's subjugation. But we feminists are many more. Now, the President has said, and also pointed out Minister of Equality, Ana Redondo, work on the renewal of the State Pact 400 new measures aimed at protecting minors, combating economic, digital violence, the trafficking of women and girls, forced marriages. We will work to make that renewal of the pact come to fruition, because it is just and indispensable, and a priority. 20 years ago, Spain took a giant step to eradicate this violence. For those who survived and for those who suffer it today, let us fight for this cause until our last breath. The 016 phone line answers calls from victims of macho violence, their families, and their surroundings 24 hours a day, every day of the year, in 53 different languages. The number is not registered on the phone bill, but you have to delete the call from the device. You can also report through the email [email protected] or via WhatsApp at the number 600 000 016. Minors can contact the Fundación ANAR's phone number at 900 20 20 10. In case of an emergency, you can call 112 or the National Police's phone numbers (091) and the Civil Guard (062). If you're unable to call, you can use the ALERTCOPS app, which sends a panic alert to the police with geolocation. 30 Years in Prison for Raping His Two Granddaughters in Jaén Courts The testimonies of the 10- and 12-year-old girls are of the utmost credibility and are backed by evidence Sections Services Highlights Edition Courts The testimonies of the 10- and 12-year-old girls are of the utmost credibility and are backed by evidence Sexual aggressions of such magnitude, both in terms of quantity and frequency, and some of which were especially violent, making them absolutely incomprehensible and reprehensible in minors of such young age. This is how the Third Section of the Provincial Court of Jaén views the facts judged on January 24, in which a man was accused of raping his two granddaughters over four years, when they were 10 and 12 years old. The grandfather, in prison since the complaint, has been sentenced to 30 years in prison. It all started when the mother's father returned from Chile and moved in with them. Between the workload of their parents and health problems, the grandfather took care of the grandchildren, two girls and a boy (4 years old). He would use the naps to get into bed with them and perform touchings, and even raped them on multiple occasions, according to what they reported. It happened almost every day, since she was very young, one of the younger girls claimed. Related News In the verdict, which this newspaper has had access to, it is stated that there is no doubt about the continuity of the criminal behavior and the exploitation of the already convicted man to find opportunities to be alone with the girls and rape them thousands of times, as one of the younger girls indicated. The testimony described by the victims, as indicated in the verdict, confirms the facts by making an expressive account of the multiple sexual aggressions they suffered, as well as the testimony of the witnesses, who were the parents and teachers of their school, where everything came to light when one of the girls spoke up. In the same way, after the incident was reported and a complaint was filed, the minors underwent a medical examination, and the forensic report confirmed the sexual assaults. The Márgenes y Vínculos Foundation, which interviewed the girls, emphasized that their testimonies are credible, on a scale where this consideration is the maximum in terms of credibility. The 65-year-old man has also been convicted of possession of child pornography. Despite the small number of files, it is undeniable that he has been proven to possess it, and its explicit content, they say, cannot be explained to have any other purpose than the sexual, for his own pleasure and satisfaction of his unbridled instincts. In conclusion, he is sentenced to 30 years in prison for two counts of sexual assault on a minor under 16, with the prohibition of approaching the girls within 300 meters when he leaves prison for the next 10 years. He been condemned for a crime of domestic violence and another for possession of child pornography. On the other hand, he was acquitted of the two continued crimes of threats, the two continued crimes of psychological injuries, and the minor crime of injuries, the victims being indemnified with 50,000 euros each.

The Minister of National Security is accompanied by Governor Gustavo Sáenz at 11:00 am in the border town, where the inauguration of the Safe Site for Victims of Human Trafficking is scheduled to take place in the migration sector. Intendant Baltasar Lara Gros is also participating. The official ceremony will take place at 11:00 am, where the ribbon-cutting will be held and the presentation of the Protocol of Action for the use of the safe space for the protection of human trafficking victims will be made. Equipment will be handed over, and then the authorities will visit the works at the 28 de Julio Post. Subsequently, national and provincial authorities will hold a press conference.

A 28-year-old woman was detained on suspicion of sexual abuse of a minor under 14 in Talcahuano, Biobío Region. According to Carabineros, the woman was being sought on an active arrest warrant issued by the Guarantee Court for the crime of sexual abuse. She was apprehended on Sunday in Caleta Tumbes by officers from the Second Police Station in Talcahuano. The investigation will be kept confidential due to the type of crime and the age of the victim. Meanwhile, the woman remains at the disposal of the justice system for detention control and subsequent formalization hearing.

I REMAIN DETAINED IN THE COURT He was sentenced to 16 years in prison in Ushuaia for sexual abuse The sentence was in line with what the Prosecution had requested, the grounds will be known next Friday A 38-year-old citizen was sentenced to 16 years in prison in Ushuaia on Friday after being found guilty of two counts of sexual abuse. The trial was held last week and the court determined the penal responsibility of the defendant for a repeated and aggravated sexual abuse with carnal access, and a simple abuse. Additionally, he was declared penalmente responsible for a sexual abuse with carnal access aggravated by the relationship, when the accused was 17 years old. In arguments, the Prosecution had requested the same sentence that the judges of the Tribunal imposed. On the other hand, the defense had requested his acquittal. Businessman Marcelo Claure sparked controversy on social media by commenting that he considers offering a $1 million reward for the capture of former President Evo Morales, who is currently facing a crime involving a minor. In this context, Claure shared on his social media a photograph, whose location and date are not specified, showing a "wanted" poster with Morales' face and a composition that shows him behind bars. Then, the businessman wrote, "What do you think if I offer a $1 million reward? I'll think about it. The LuchoXBolivia (Luis Arce) government will grab him or their knees will tremble." The post received thousands of reactions and dozens of comments. Some of his followers supported the proposal, while others suggested that the money could be used for people in need. The responses poured in for Claure. Among them were those who congratulated the bravery and courage of the businessman, those who attacked the administration of President Luis Arce for not executing the arrest order against Morales, investigated for a presumed case of human trafficking, and those who marked a strong defense for the former president. Morales is being investigated for allegedly having a relationship with a minor while in office, with whom he would have had a child. In the context of these human trafficking investigations with aggravating circumstances, on January 17, Judge Nelson Rocabado of the Fifth Instructional Court of Anticorruption and Violence against Women in Tarija, declared Morales in rebellion, after he failed to appear for questioning. A search and arrest warrant is also outstanding against Morales, who has not been apprehended to date. EVO RESPONDS Morales' response was not long in coming. In this occasion, the former president spoke through the microphones of radio Kawsachun Coca, from his Sunday program Evo pueblo, in the Trópico de Cochabamba. Seriously, first they want to kill me, poison me, detain me, and send me to the United States. Now, whoever detains Evo, a million dollars. It's in your hands, Ramiro, joked the former president with the radio host of Kawsachun Coca. Morales compared Claure's offer with the one made by the United States, the country that offered up to 25 million dollars to detain or deliver information that would lead to the capture of the President of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro. From five million to Maduro, they went up to 20 million. I'm starting with a million dollars. These people are crazy or foolish, I don't understand. That's how I think they failed their businesses with lithium, they have to attack. We are defenders of natural resources, concluded the former president.

Ángela (nombre ficticio), who was a victim of human trafficking in Thailand, was forced to engage in online scams after her return. Upon her return, she received hospitality training at a local school in Lusaka, Zambia, sponsored by Catholic leaders working to end human trafficking in the country. (GSR photo by Ajiambo) In February 2021, Ángela came across a job posting on Facebook for a teaching position in Thailand that offered a good salary. The company was seeking an English teacher who also spoke Mandarin. Having proficiency in both languages, she applied for the job. Upon arriving in the country, she discovered that it was not a teaching position, but rather, she was forced to contact people online to scam them or involve them in online scams. Ángela, cuyo nombre real pidió que no fuese revelado, explicó a Global Sisters Report que fue trasladada a Tailandia desde Zambia por una banda criminal que le quitó los documentos de viaje y le exigió que reclutara a más gente o pagara un cuantioso rescate para liberarla. Si te niegas a trabajar, te torturaremos o te electrocutaremos, le decían sus torturadores, según recuerda, quienes la obligaron a participar en uno de los tipos de estafa de mayor crecimiento en el mundo, conocida como la "estafa del cerdo", en la que los estafadores engañan a las personas para que inviertan en plataformas de criptomoneda tras generar confianza a través de relaciones digitales. Sorprendentemente, algunos estafadores, como la misma Ángela, son víctimas de las redes de trata de seres humanos, cuyos operadores suelen engañarlos con promesas de trabajos reales y luego los obligan, mediante amenazas de violencia, a participar en estafas. According to a URL from the United Nations Office for Human Rights, hundreds of thousands of people trafficked into the Southeast Asian region, particularly in countries such as Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia, and the Philippines, among others, after being lured by job advertisements on the internet that promised well-paying jobs. The report states that traffickers confiscate the travel documents of the victims upon their arrival, who are then imprisoned, tortured, sexually abused, and forced to work in online scams.Angela and her three companions escaped from their workplace, near the border between Thailand and Laos, after enduring a year of mistreatment. The four hid in a garbage truck and, once outside, turned themselves in to the police, who detained them for two weeks for being in the country illegally. They then deported Angela to Zambia. My only wish was to go there and get a job that could change my life and that of my brothers. But when I got there, my life got worse because I did things to people that I regret to this day. I robbed innocent people and I will never be able to forgive myself, she said between tears. Upon returning to Zambia, Angela suffered severe mental health problems, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The members of her church introduced her to the nuns who run a hrefURLKum ZambiaURL(Takuza), an organization that aims to end human trafficking in Zambia. Takuza is made up of 45 nuns from various congregations who dedicate themselves to identifying those affected by human trafficking. The sisters also work to raise awareness and provide support to victims of human trafficking. The organization collaborates with the police and the advisory units of Zambia, whose advisors help victims of human trafficking to recover from trauma. Human trafficking is a global issue, and as Yakuza, we address all issues related to human trafficking, said Sister Kayula Lesa, member of the Charity Sisters As an organization, we continuously seek out people who have been victims of human trafficking or are at risk and need our help. We provide guidance and psychological support to the victims, offering them the opportunity to express themselves, heal, rebuild their trust, and lead a better life, she noted. Sister Kayula Lesa, member of the Charity Sisters, speaks with survivors of human trafficking on March 12 in Lusaka, Zambia. The nuns have been raising awareness about human trafficking and also helping the victims. (Foto GSR URL Aijambo) Takuza relies on the support of the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation, which also finances Global Sisters Report. Lesa observed that Angela had suffered severe acts of violence, sexual exploitation, and psychological abuse during her captivity in Thailand. In addition to PTSD, anxiety, and depression, she also felt shame. We have advisors working with Angela and other survivors to help them overcome their traumas and manage their mental health, Lesa explains, adding We also focus on reintegrating survivors into their families and training them to start small businesses. Angela is one of the thousands of survivors of trafficking who receive support from nuns in this southern African country with over 20.7 million inhabitants. Among the forms of human trafficking are forced labor, sexual exploitation, forced criminal activities, forced marriage, illegal adoption, slavery, organ removal, and baby trafficking. Landlocked Zambia is vulnerable to modern slavery as a country of origin, transit, and destination, particularly for women and children, according to the 2023 edition of the U.S. Department of State's Trafficking in Persons report. The majority of cases occur along the nation's borders and involve the trafficking of women and children from poor rural areas to urban areas or neighboring countries such as Namibia, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique. Sister Patience Shinondo, a member of the Sisters of Charity, works with other stakeholders in the fight against human trafficking in Zambia. (Foto GSR URL Ajiambo) The report also revealed that these women and children, victims of human trafficking, are subjected to sexual exploitation, domestic servitude, forced begging or forced labor in various destinations, as smuggling routes between the Horn of Africa and Southern Africa often pass through Zambia. Meanwhile, the US Department of State report acknowledges that despite Zambia not fully complying with the minimum standards for the elimination of human trafficking, the country is committed to combating exploitation and human trafficking. According to the report, authorities initiated 42 investigations into human trafficking and continued eight in 2022, compared to the 12 investigations in 2021. Additionally, 79 victims of human trafficking were identified in 2022, compared to 42 in 2021. Our efforts in the fight against human exploitation and trafficking have over time succeeded in reducing the cases of human trafficking in the country, and we have been able to return the future to many victims, declared Lesa, director of Takuza, who added that her organization had intensified awareness campaigns throughout Zambia to reach the largest number of human trafficking victims and also to train communities, especially young people, on how to recognize human trafficking and its objectives.As sisters, we have been organizing monthly workshops in schools and churches to raise awareness and help young people affected by human trafficking, Lesa stated, and pointed out that the economic and educational opportunities that her organization has provided to victims and young people in recent years would further reduce the risk of trafficking due to poverty. Sister Patience Shinondo and Father Philip Meraba, both from Takuza, are advocating for addressing the issue of illegal immigration by urging the Government to strengthen the borders. According to Shinondo, Zambia is facing the problem of human trafficking, with most of its victims being brought into the country to work in the mining sector. Zambia is the world's second-largest producer of cobalt after its neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. Once the Government discovers these illegal immigrants, they are detained and end up in prisons without the means to return to their countries of origin, Meraba, a member of the Society of African Missionaries, asserts. Meraba visits detainees in prisons and helps them to be deported to their countries. Shinondo, a member of the Sisters of Charity, stated that she is working to obtain more resources to assist more victims of human trafficking. In that sense, they plan to offer them training in trades such as tailoring, restoration, and mechanics to help them rebuild their lives. Regarding those incarcerated for human trafficking, he mentioned that they are released on bail and provided with plane tickets to return to their countries of origin. We have successfully facilitated the return of five undocumented immigrants to their homes since we launched this project last year, he reported. Currently, Ángela has high hopes that the therapy sessions she attends at Yakuza will help her fully recover and move forward. I have returned to the country, but I still don't have a job. My problems persist, but I have hopes that things will improve. Although it's difficult to forget what I went through, I feel somewhat happy thanks to the continued support I receive from my therapist and the nuns, she said. Note: This article was originally in English on August 22, 2024.

Prosecutor Natalia Montanía charged a 15-year-old Brazilian boy with allegedly sexually abusing a 13-year-old girl at a residence in the Paraná Country Club in Hernandarias city. The alleged perpetrator supposedly filmed the sexual act and later shared it on social media. The case involves the alleged commission of punishable acts of child sexual abuse, as defined in Article 135 of the Penal Code, and the violation of Law No. 2861, which prohibits the commercialization and distribution of pornographic material, utilizing the image or representation of minors or incapacitated individuals, in accordance with Article 29, paragraph 1, of the Penal Code. According to the complaint filed by the victim's mother on February 4, 2025, the incident occurred on November 15, 2024, at the end of a birthday party at the aforementioned condominium. On that occasion, the teenager allegedly invited the girl to get into a truck he was driving. After a brief investigation, they arrived at a residence where they allegedly had sexual relations. The complaint states that the incident was recorded and later disseminated on social media. The victim confirmed what happened during a psychological evaluation at the Public Ministry's Victim Support Center, where she stated she felt fear and shame. The minor only revealed what had happened to her mother after images of the incident began circulating on social media, mainly among students in the gated neighborhood. This led to the formalization of the complaint and the start of the investigation, which concluded with the accusation of the teenager. As a provisional measure, Prosecutor Montanía requested the temporary internment of the accused in an adequate home, in accordance with Article 427 of the Penal Procedure Code and Law N 2861, to prevent the risk of flight. She also requested the designation of a social worker from the Judiciary to evaluate the minor's family environment. In addition, the prosecutor's office requested the Juvenile Court to grant a six-month period to deepen the investigation and formulate the corresponding accusation.

The Argentine Minister of Security, Patricia Bullrich, will arrive at the border with Bolivia on Monday to sign the contract for the start of construction of the fence as part of the Güemes Plan, which aims to combat federal crimes such as narco-trafficking, human trafficking, and contraband, with a primary focus on the departments of Orán and Aguas Blancas, according to local media. The event will take place at the Migraciones offices in Puerto Chalanas, Aguas Blancas, Orán department, in Salta, at 11:00 hours, where the Minister also intends to inaugurate the work. At the event, the Minister will also inaugurate the so-called Safe Site for Victims of Trafficking at Migraciones, whose objective is to provide comprehensive protection and assistance to victims of trafficking, within the framework of the security and human rights policies promoted by the Argentine government. Additionally, equipment will be handed over to the National Gendarmerie and a tour of the works at the 28th of July Post, located on the border with Bolivia, will be conducted. Bullrich had stated in an interview with Argentine radio Mitre that we are in order. Now we have Aguas Blancas, the Triple Frontier (between Brazil, Paraguay, and the province of Misiones) under control for a long time, now we are going to go to the area with Brazil, and he added that the main focus is set on the border zone between the Argentine city of Bernardo de Irigoyen, in the northeastern extremity of Misiones, and the Brazilian towns of Dionisio Cerqueira and Barracao. The Almerian Church reminds us that human trafficking is a scourge. I echo and disseminate this, considering it praiseworthy and plausible, that the Diocese of Almería, under the episcopacy of Bishop Antonio Gómez Montes, joined in prayer last Saturday, February 8, in the parish of Santa Teresa of Jesus in the Almerian capital, under the pastoral rectorship of Canon and Parish Priest Rvdo. Francisco Ruiz Fornieles, on the occasion of the March against Human Trafficking. The Catholic and Apostolic Church of Rome has celebrated around the world the Day of Prayer and Reflection against Human Trafficking. In the framework of the Jubilee Year, the proposed motto has been Ambassadors of Hope together against human trafficking. As always, the date coincides with the Liturgical Memory of Saint Josefina Bakhita, a Sudanese woman and religious figure, a woman who was enslaved, who after her liberation, found Jesus Christ and consecrated herself to Him. With the aim of healing the wound that is human trafficking, Cáritas Diocesana de Almería, Adoratrices, Hermanos de la Cruz Blanca, Oblatas del Santísimo Redentor, and the Secretariat for Migrations attended this special gathering. The vigil and social project were also joined by the brotherhoods with canonical headquarters in that parish, such as the Hermandad de la Caridad and the Hermandad de Pasión, represented by their Major Sisters, María del Mar Botella Gil and María Carmen Pantoja Arias, respectively, along with members of the Government Board and their brother and sister confreres. José Cárdenas Aragón, a member of the Association of Hermandades and Cofradías in the city of Almería, also attended, representing his Government Board as a Vocal for Hermandades de Gloria. It is worth highlighting that this year, the Human Trafficking Day has a special relevance due to the fact that the social project to live the Jubilee 2025 has as its center the work of the Church in this reality. This project insists on the social commitment that must be born in people, fruit of the Jubilee and of their personal and community experience. Human trafficking, sexual and labor exploitation are the slavery of the 21st century and one of the objectives of the social project for this jubilar year is to make this reality visible. In addition, other keys of the project go through reflection and prayer, commitment and economic contributions. It is for this reason that the presence of the Brotherhoods and Confraternities in this social project is of vital importance for the entire diocesan and confraternal community. Charity and assistance works are deeply linked to the very reason for being and essence of the reality of the brotherhoods, as one of the main pillars of popular Catholicism. Charity is the most outspoken manifestation of openness, availability, service, and love towards one's neighbor, since as Christians, and in our case as confreres, the love of God leads us to love our neighbor. In the words of Pope Francis, it is a crime against humanity and he calls for facing it and caring for its victims. We need to eliminate the causes of this complex phenomenon as well as adequately assist people who fall into the snares of trafficking. (Words of Pope Francis to the members of the Grupo Santa Marta and RENATE, October-November 2016). Peace and Good Rafael Leopoldo AGUILERA MARTÍNEZ

Chihuahua. According to intelligence sources consulted by REFORMA, the Aragua Train cell in Chihuahua focuses on human trafficking through job scams, extortion under the "gota a gota" scheme, and other crimes. The group's expansion has been facilitated by the migratory flow, using the state as a transit and settlement point for its criminal structure. The Aragua Train was born in 2009 in Venezuela and has managed to operate in at least eight countries, including the United States. Its incursion into Mexico has been progressive, with a strong presence in Mexico City, Chiapas, Tabasco, Tamaulipas, and Baja California, detailed by REFORMA. Security authorities in Chihuahua have warned about the risk posed by the expansion of this organization and are working on strategies to contain its growth in the state. The diversification of their crimes and their ability to infiltrate vulnerable communities have raised alarms among law enforcement agencies. In the United States, the criminal organization has been the target of various operations, such as the detention of a hundred of its members in Denver and other arrests in New York. Under the administration of Joe Biden and now of Donald Trump, efforts to dismantle their criminal networks on U.S. territory have been intensified. Patricia Andrade, director of the Raíces Venezolanas Foundation in Miami, stated that many Venezuelan migrants reject the presence of the Tren de Aragua and support the arrests. We migrants who came to work are paying for a very small percentage that has generated this crisis, she declared.

Courtesy of IPS The gang violence in Haiti continues to have a devastating impact on the population, highlighted a new report by the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), as figures and data emerge on the latest attack by criminal groups on a residential area of this capital. Several of these groups attempted to take control of the Kenscoff commune by force, a hillside area south of Port-au-Prince where part of Haiti's elite resides, while in the low-lying areas, the poorest sectors live in slums that are mostly under the control of gangs. According to the authorities, at least 40 people died in the clashes between gang members and police forces, and several homes were set on fire in the commune, but a complete official death toll has not been published. But Marie Yolène Gilles, of the civil rights organization Fondasyon Je Klere, said Wednesday that, according to resident testimonies, around 150 people were killed in the attacks, an undetermined number are still missing, and at least a hundred houses were set on fire. The violence of gangs that have controlled many areas of the capital for several years and have spread to the north and south of Haiti, 27,800 square kilometers and 11.5 million inhabitants, has exacerbated the country's structural crisis of poverty, hunger, and its consequences in this Caribbean nation. The new Binuh report highlights that at least 5,626 people died and over 2,213 were injured in the last year due to the actions of armed gangs. These figures show a marked increase of more than 1,000 deaths compared to 2023. The attack on the Kenskoff commune shows that the belligerence of criminal groups remains in place despite the country having already received around 900 personnel from the Multinational Mission in Support of Security, mostly from Kenya (around 700), as well as from the Bahamas, Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Jamaica. In the last quarter of 2024, there was an alarming increase in deadly attacks related to gangs, resulting in at least 1732 fatalities and 411 injured, due to armed group violence, self-defense units, and law enforcement operations, according to the Binuh report. The report highlights three large-scale massacres resulting in over 300 deaths, with the most severe attack occurring in the Wharf Jérémie neighborhood of Port-au-Prince. Between December 6 and 11, at least 207 people were killed by a gang led by Monel Felix, known as Micanor, who accused the victims, mainly elderly women, of practicing voodoo (a religion and magical practices of African origin) and being responsible for the death of his son. The armed gang executed people in their homes and at a local place of worship before burning or dismembering the bodies to conceal evidence. There was no reported intervention by law enforcement during the five-day attack. Similar atrocities took place in Pont Sondé and Petite Rivière de l'Artibonite, a department to the north of the capital, where coordinated offensives by gangs left at least 170 people dead in early December. The killings sparked reprisals by self-defense groups, intensifying the violence even further, underscoring the unrelenting brutality affecting the nation. Haiti's security forces have also been implicated in severe human rights violations. The report documents over 250 police-led executions in 2024, with two children among the victims. Many people were executed after being detained, while others, including street vendors and motorbike drivers, were shot for failing to provide identification. Miragoâne's prosecutor was cited for six extrajudicial executions, bringing the total number of killings by prosecutors in 2024 to 42. Despite calls for accountability, investigations into police abuses are largely stalled. Binuh noted that no agent has undergone background checks since June 2023, reflecting a profound lack of oversight. Haití has experienced a 150% increase in kidnappings, and gangs are increasingly targeting children. The report highlighted widespread sexual violence, with at least 94 documented cases of rape and sexual exploitation in the last quarter of 2024 alone. Child trafficking and forced recruitment by armed groups continue to rise. Despite the magnitude of the crisis, Haiti's judicial system remains paralyzed. Over one million people have been forcibly displaced, forced to flee their homes to escape violence.

Four Suspects Arrested for Killing a Dog Four men were apprehended by agents from the Comisaría 115 in the Arroyo Porã neighborhood, in the Cambyretá district, after being identified as the alleged perpetrators of a dog's death. The incident was recorded on closed-circuit images, where one of them is seen shooting at the animal. The detained individuals were identified as Diosnel Duré Vigo (37), Severo de Jesús Medina (61), Jorge Ríos González (48), and Fernando Maidana Villalba (26), all without prior criminal records. During the procedure, carried out on the public street of the San Antonio de Arroyo Porã neighborhood, a motorcycle was confiscated from Duré Vigo. According to the police report, the security cameras of the complainant, Julia Mabel Paredes Giménez (36), captured three of the suspects walking in front of her residence, while another was riding a motorcycle. In the images, one of them can be seen making a movement with his right hand, after which the dog, which was inside the dwelling, fell to the ground with a visible wound behind the ear, causing instant death. The authorities transported the animal to a veterinary clinic for inspection. The case was reported to the Public Ministry and the detained individuals were informed of their rights in accordance with the National Constitution and the Penal Code. The incident is being investigated as a supposed case of zoocidio, in accordance with Law N 4.840 on Animal Protection and Welfare. Minister Patricia Bullrich will today inaugurate a space for victims of human trafficking in Aguas Blancas, visit security department facilities and bring cutting-edge technology acquired from the US government for border control. It is also expected that the head of the Security portfolio will place the first column of the 200-meter fence in the Migration area, which caused a strong controversy with the Bolivian government. The placement of this foundational column on November 11 will carry strong symbolism about the new border security policy driven by the government of Javier Milei. The event will be headed by Bullrich, alongside Governor Gustavo Sáenz, and Orán Mayor Baltasar Lara Gros. The event will begin at 11 am at the Migration Office in Aguas Blancas. The day's agenda will include the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the modular housing office destined for victims of human trafficking, followed by the presentation of the protocol for using this secure space. The implementation of this infrastructure aims to provide a safe and suitable environment for victims, who will be able to receive the necessary attention in a protected location. In addition to the inauguration of the safe site, the day's activities will include a tour featuring several strategic activities. From Migrations, the authorities will move to the Aguas Blancas Gendarmerie Base, where they will present an advanced security technology facilitated by U.S. National Security authorities. This involves person recognition equipment that will improve border control and the detection of illicit activities. The event will feature the presence of authorities from the United States Department of Homeland Security, who will deliver advanced equipment for facial recognition, as part of an international collaboration that strengthens the fight against organized crime. The arrival of cutting-edge technology, such as the BITMAP system, will mark a before and after in the region's capabilities for control and prevention of crimes, strengthening the tools available to security forces in their fight against human trafficking and narcotics trafficking.

Last Saturday, Peruvian and US authorities announced the capture of 23 members of the Venezuelan transnational gang known as Tren de Aragua. The operation, which took place on Friday night, also allowed for the rescue of 84 victims of human trafficking for sexual exploitation in various locations in Lima. General Aldo Dávila, head of the human trafficking police, provided details at a press conference. Among the detained, he confirmed, were 12 Venezuelans and 11 Peruvians. Additionally, among the rescued victims, there were three minors, two of Venezuelan nationality and one Peruvian. Capture of Tren de Aragua The operation was carried out in three districts on the outskirts of Lima: Santa Anita, San Martín de Porres, and Puente Piedra. According to a statement from the U.S. embassy, the operation was coordinated near midnight with the participation of over 300 Peruvian police and prosecutors, along with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. In eight strategic locations, suspects were arrested and victims of exploitation were released. U.S. Ambassador to Peru Stephanie SyptakRamnath highlighted the operation as an example of international cooperation to improve security for both countries and the region. Continued fight against organized crime The Peruvian general also revealed that the Peruvian police have been working since 2022 with logistical and technological support from the United States to dismantle the Tren de Aragua, a criminal organization that has expanded its operations to several countries in Latin America. This gang, which emerged in Venezuela over a decade ago, has been linked to kidnappings, extortions, and other crimes, capitalizing on the country of origin's migration crisis. In recent years, Peruvian police have apprehended several high-ranking members of the Tren de Aragua, including Héctor Prieto, known as Mamut, leader of the Alayón dynasty. Despite being incarcerated, Prieto continued to direct illicit activities from prison until his recent transfer to a high-security prison in the Andes, a measure to reduce his influence. This operation not only highlights international cooperation in the fight against organized crime but also underscores the ongoing challenges faced by authorities in the region to maintain public security. From the perspective of enforced disappearance, the UN warns that security-oriented policies (implemented by Mexico and the United States) and massive deportations are increasing disappearances among the migrant population. The focus on detection and detention creates environments that facilitate disappearances, said Alan García Campos, coordinator of the Legal and Analysis Unit of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights of the United Nations. He noted that the UN's Committee on Enforced Disappearance, during its visit to Mexico, formulated specific recommendations to adopt a differentiated approach regarding migration and deportations. THE SITUATION IN MEXICO WITH DEPORTATIONS Mexico is characterized by being a country that expels migrants, it is a country of reception, and in this, a huge effort is required so that migration does not constitute a risk factor, that subjects people to conditions of disappearance, and other types of violations of human rights, forced labor, assassinations, human trafficking, expressed Alan García.THERE ARE NUMBERS OF DISAPPEARED PERSONS IN THEIR MIGRATORY PROCESS IN MEXICO The UN Mexico Human Rights Commissioner stated that unfortunately, an element that afflicts the Mexican state is that in the existing records, the complexity and potential doubts that may exist, do not have all the information broken down, disaggregated, as to be able to characterize with a certain estimate, the universe of migrant people, in the context of the mobility that are disappeared. That is, there are no numbers or database of how many disappear in their migration process. Despite this, Alan García warns that there is no doubt that there are facts that have shaken the country's conscience, around the context of mobility, in some cases forced disappearances of a temporary or short duration (express kidnappings). Caso Cazador: 10 Detained in Raids Against the WolvesOn the early morning of February 7, 2025, the State Attorney General's Office and the National Police carried out a massive operation called Caso Cazador, resulting in the capture of 10 members of the criminal group Los Lobos. This operation involved 18 simultaneous raids in the provinces of Pichincha, Guayas, Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, and Tungurahua. The Caso Cazador focuses on the investigation of organized crime, involving leaders of Los Lobos, who are accused of crimes such as sicariato, kidnapping, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and possession and carrying of firearms. During the raids, authorities seized computers, cell phones, cash, and other elements that will serve as evidence in the judicial process. Among those detained are two individuals identified as alias Kun and Cuco, considered mid-level targets. In addition, it was discovered that four of the detained individuals were directing criminal activities from a detention center. This criminal group is also linked to a terrorist bombing attack in Esmeraldas and the kidnapping of two citizens in the same city. The Prosecution and Police have highlighted the importance of this operation to dismantle one of the most dangerous criminal organizations in the country. The Wolves, along with Los Choneros, are considered transnational terrorist groups with significant reach in Ecuador's criminal pyramid. The authorities have urged citizens to collaborate with any information that may help identify other members of this criminal network. The Prosecution will continue with the investigations to ensure that all those responsible are brought to justice. Sources: Teleamazonas, Primicias, El Universo, La Hora.

The Autonomous University of Guerrero (UAGro) reported that with purposes unrelated to seeking justice, individuals with political motivations have re-posted a six-year-old journalistic note that accused a former employee of the institution of human trafficking against women. This weekend, they issued a statement in which they reiterate, as they did six years ago, their categorical disassociation from this illicit act, and that they are not responsible for the illegal actions of a former employee, who at no time represented the values and principles that govern our institution. Lorenzo N was detained on January 18, 2019, after ministerial police managed to rescue five women, three of whom were minors, victims of the crime of human trafficking, in Chilpancingo. Community Sexual Violence The Devastating Impact on Education of Young Mothers in Guatemala Data from the Sexual and Reproductive Health Observatory (Osar) indicates that 90% of girls between 10 and 14 years old who became mothers in 2024 were outside the educational system. Ana Lucía Ola 10 February 2025 0010h Nine out of ten girls who became mothers in 2024 were outside the educational system. (Prensa Libre Photo Archive) In 2024, there were 2,146 pregnancies in girls between 10 and 14 years old, 62 fewer than those registered in 2023, a decrease of only 2.8%. The data shared by the Sexual and Reproductive Health Observatory (Osar) shows that since 2020, each year has closed with more than 2,000 cases. For Mirna Montenegro, director of Osar, the report made by the Ministry of Health on these pregnancies has a data that catches the attention, and it is that nine out of every 10 girls would be outside the educational system, 935 to be exact, while 135 are in primary school and 43 in basic school. She points out that the registry shows that girls have between three and four years of schooling, and in that passage through school, they should be provided with sexual education that contributes to their empowerment, self-esteem, and reducing abuses. Pregnancies in minors between 10 and 14 years old are the result of a sexual violation, as established by the Penal Code, and must be reported to the authorities, but it is not always achieved, which is why the number of girls who become mothers may be higher. Montenegro recalls that in one of the first cases that the Osar accompanied, the director of a school in Jutiapa summoned the mother of a 12-year-old pregnant student, telling her: Your daughter is no longer a girl, take her out of school because she's pregnant and let her study at night. A rotten apple can spoil the rest. Another case occurred in the capital. It was August, and a judge ruled that a 13-year-old girl with seven months of pregnancy and her mother attend a parents' school. When asked by the Osar's lawyer if it wouldn't be better for the girl to finish the school cycle since she was in the sixth grade, the judge responded: No, she's pregnant, she needs to learn to be a mother. Montenegro indicates that in the comprehensive care route for pregnant girls, it is established that the Ministry of Education (Mineduc) must have programs for girls in this condition to return to the educational center. We don't even have information on how many were in school in 2024. The issue may seem unimportant, but it is a right of girls that is not being fulfilled, he adds. For Otto Rivera, executive secretary of the Institutional Coordinator for the Promotion of Children's Rights (Ciprodeni), it is lamentable that 90 percent of pregnant minors are not in school. This data, he emphasizes, is a reflection of the low primary school coverage, primarily among girls and adolescents in the country, as it truncates their life project. Additionally, it reveals the absence of a true integral protection system and guarantees of rights for this group of the population, and that it has not been a priority for the State. Faced with a pregnancy, socially the minors are assigned the status of mother, even if they are 11 or 12 years old, as reported by the director of Osar. That stigma fuels the complications that these girls face in their community. With forced maternity weighing on them, they leave school, reducing their opportunities for labor insertion and leaving them with only one scenario: dedicating themselves to household chores, which maintains the circle of poverty. The alternative work many have is as domestic workers. The report on pregnancies in minors between 10 and 14 years old indicates that 34.3% of cases occurred in Alta Verapaz, Quiché, and Huehuetenango, the three departments with the highest incidence of poverty in the country, at 90.3%, 86.4%, and 81.2%, respectively, according to the National Institute of Statistics (INE). It is a vicious circle. No study, no training for formal or remunerated work, more poverty, more violence, there is malnutrition, there is neonatal death, a greater number of pregnancies, there is suicide, says Montenegro. It is also observed that there is an effect on the physical health of the pregnant minors. According to the Vidas Robadas campaign report by Osar, victims may suffer from preeclampsia, anemia, uterine tract infection, childbirth complications, intrauterine growth problems, premature birth, and low birth weight. The risk of maternal mortality doubles in women under 15 compared to adult women, as indicated by Osar. Additionally, the impact on mental health is significant, as being a victim of sexual violence and forced into motherhood can lead to depression, fear, sadness, anger, guilt, anxiety about the future, and shame.Births From January to December 2024, the birth registration for mothers between 15 and 19 years old was 54,615. Meanwhile, the number of children born to mothers between 10 and 14 years old was 1,953. Alta Verapaz (7,128), Huehuetenango (6,677), and Quiché (4,917) continue to be among the departments with the highest cases. These are data collected from the National Registry of Persons (Renap). Abordaje Montenegro mentions that there is a route established in the country for the care of pregnancy in girls and adolescents, but it is not being met. The right to health is developed with deficiencies, and education lacks adequate sex education for prevention and programs for minors to return to school. The Ministry of Education (Mineduc), according to the portfolio, proposes to minors the option to continue their education through the school subsystem, with accompanying curriculum adjustments and guides for flexible distance learning schedules, included in the different extracurricular education programs. Additionally, there is follow-up on the continuity of studies to ensure their permanence and promotion in school, to guarantee their right to education. According to the ministry, starting from 2025, a new program to prevent violence will be in operation, which includes sexual violence and all forms of abuse to prevent incidents such as sexual abuse and pregnancies in girls. Prevention includes the provision of information and the creation of mechanisms to report risks of abuse, either against oneself or against other students. Pregnancies in girls continue, with Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango, Quiche, San Marcos, Solola, and Guatemala presenting the highest numbers. Additionally, work is being done in collaboration with the Ministry of Health to strengthen the capacities of teachers, parents, and administrative staff, who will have access to information to act preventively and, when necessary, attend to existing cases. On the other hand, the Ministry of Social Development has the Vida program, which consists of a conditional transfer to which minors who have been forced into early motherhood, as a result of sexual abuse, are entitled. Osar indicates that this only covers 6 percent of the approximately 120 cases reported per year. Although they have a judge's order for the child's affiliation to last one to two years, if they are integrated. In Alta Verapaz, in 2024, only 19 girls were registered, he adds, but the data is a consolidated figure up to that date. Meanwhile, only 4 percent of the cases (violations) reach trial, and the time it takes for the trial to take place ranges from 4 to 5 years. The process is slow and discourages victims. Rivera mentions that for changes to occur in this matter, the country needs a true system of protection for childhood and adolescence, in addition, the laws must be based on the human rights approach and social protection. A better investment is also needed in this segment of the population, and spaces for participatory and safe protagonism should be opened.

Two weeks after reporting repeated episodes of physical, psychological, and sexual violence, a 27-year-old woman from Puerto Iguazú continues to receive no protection measures from the Justice system. The complainant, an influencer in the city of the Cataracts, expressed her concern since her aggressor, Maximiliano O. (32), an agent of the Argentine Federal Police, remains at liberty. On January 25, the young woman filed a complaint at the Iguazú Women's Police Station, detailing episodes of abuse that included physical aggression, threats, and sexual abuse. Despite having requested a panic button, the Justice system has not enabled it, leaving the victim without effective security measures. Lack of judicial action The young woman expressed her frustration at not being summoned to testify or receiving concrete responses from the authorities. Although an attempt was initially made to activate a panic button, technical failures prevented its functioning, and there was no subsequent follow-up. A never-ending ordeal The cycle of violence began four months ago, with physical and psychological aggression in Misiones and Entre Ríos. The young woman reported suffering sexual abuse, constant threats, and emotional manipulation. Additionally, the accused already has previous complaints filed against him for gender-based violence. Alarming statistics According to the Provincial Registry of Domestic Violence, in 2023, 29,741 complaints of gender-based violence were registered in Misiones, a 15.6% increase from the previous year. 79.3% of the victims were women, highlighting the urgent need to strengthen protection and attention for complainants. The victim insists on her plea for justice I still don't have an anti-anxiety button, and he's still free. A cry that reflects the lack of responses in cases of gender-based violence, which, despite complaints, continue without concrete actions from the judicial system.

The United States Embassy in Peru reported on the detention of nearly two dozen suspected members of the Tren de Aragua, in a mega operation carried out in Lima. Peruvian authorities provided details on the mega operation in which the capture of these 23 suspected remnants of the Hijos de Dios gang, a faction of the transnational criminal organization Tren de Aragua, was achieved. These detentions were carried out by the Directorate Against Human Trafficking and Illicit Migration of the Peruvian Police, which worked in conjunction with agents from the United States Embassy in Lima.
