The prosecution requested the dismissal of Intendant Espinoza for the abuse reported by Melody Rakauskas Sostuvo that there is no evidence and that the woman had a pattern of behavior of obtaining money from married men The head of the communal La Matanza can go to oral trial The prosecutor Mónica Cuñarro proposed the dismissal of the Intendant of La Matanza, Fernando Espinoza, in the case in which he is being processed for the sexual abuse of the young woman Melody Rakauskas, understanding that there is no evidence to support the accusation and that the supposed victim usually related to married men to record them and ask for money Espinoza is being processed for these facts, a framework that was confirmed by a ruling of the Chamber of Crime Rakauskas requested as a private prosecutor that the instruction be closed because it is complete and that the case against the Matanzan communal leader be taken to oral trial Prosecutor Cuñarro stated that Rakauskas had a pattern of behavior that made his account of the accusation against the Peronist leader implausible. When Espinoza was given a hearing, he proposed his dismissal and, when consulted by the prosecution, Prosecutor Cuñarro said there was no evidence. Now, the judge in charge of the case, Fernando Caunedo, who is a substitute, must decide whether to proceed to trial despite this. Without a public prosecutor, that is, without a public accuser, but with a private accuser, the oral trial can still take place. However, Espinoza has filed a motion in the National Chamber of Appeals to dismiss the case, to revoke his indictment, and to close the case. Cuñarro sent the ruling to General Prosecutor Mauricio Viera, for review, so that in any case it is he who will accuse or allow the case to proceed to trial with the private accuser. In her 79-page opinion, she recalled that before this ruling, two other prosecutors had already advocated for Espinoza's dismissal. The prosecutor questioned the validity of the supposed victim's account, arguing that there are contradictions and her refusal to undergo a psychiatric evaluation and provide her cellphones to undergo an examination. The prosecutor said that in this case, the supposed victim's account is not accompanied by a 911 report, medical attention, or the testimony of witnesses, police complaints, or cameras. In addition, she said that it is not in dispute that Espinoza went to Melody's house that night, but pointed out that the evidence gathered does not allow verifying that there was a simple sexual abuse by Espinoza against the plaintiff. Melody said it's the victim's right not to undergo forensic examinations or not to provide their electronic devices for examination, but she noted that the Public Ministry cannot be forced to fill in the gaps of that decision with statements based on faith. In this sense, the prosecutor evaluated that Melody's account is significantly disputed because there are no elements to support her claims. On the contrary, she wrote that there is a pattern of behavior in the accuser consisting of relating to married men, creating or exploiting compromising situations and then recording them and demanding some kind of benefit. She argued that the woman filed the complaint without instigating action and, from there, initiated a negotiation with the accused and after a year and a half, she dropped it without effect. In the messages they exchanged, she said that the initiative for that negotiation was Melody's, since it was she who demanded a meeting with Espinoza. The prosecutor insisted that the woman's refusal to provide her messages is to conceal others that would harm her version of events. She even stated that there are manipulated messages. The third element highlighted by prosecutor Cuñarro is the girl's refusal to undergo an examination, because she claimed it would put her version of the events into crisis. And she dismissed the need for Espinoza to tolerate an accusation based on mere indications that are not exhibited in quantity, univocally, and gravely. Among the evidence valued by prosecutor Cuñarro are reports from the Foreign Ministry about an episode that occurred in March of last year at the airport in New Delhi. There, Melody said she was detained by Indian agents, who drugged her with a canteen containing a suspicious liquid to kill her, and linked what happened to this case, when she was taken to a hospital, where the doctors advised her psychiatric hospitalization. The diplomats informed the justice that far from trying to kill her, it was Melody who took psychiatric medications to attempt to commit suicide, according to what she confided to her mother, who was subjected to a stomach lavage and repatriated on a return flight, with a medical indication to undergo psychiatric hospitalization. In her particular accusation, Melody states that she suffered situations of violence over the past few years. Espinoza is being processed for the crimes of simple sexual abuse and disobedience for failing to comply with a perimeter restriction on approaching the victim. The accusation asserts that there was an abuse of power by Espinoza over Rakauskas in his capacity as an employer. According to the victim, she would have met with Espinoza on three occasions for work-related purposes within her department. In one of those encounters, in May 2021, Espinoza would have begun to make advances towards her, then forced and groped her, despite the woman's resistance. The witnesses who confirmed the indictment of the mayor valued the victim's testimony and evidence that coincided with her statements. They mentioned that Melody went to the municipality for a job opportunity and that the case began in 2021 after a message that Espinoza allegedly sent to the complainant. Regarding the offense of disobedience, the judges considered that the indictment should also be confirmed. According to the file, on July 1, 2021, Espinoza allegedly violated the existing provision from June 4 of that year that prohibited him from approaching the complainant or contacting her in any way. That day, the defendant allegedly contacted her through an ex-partner to retract the complaint and also spoke to her by phone. They also allegedly sent a blank document to submit to the court to withdraw the judicial complaint.

Human Trafficking is not only a grave crime, but also a rejection of the dignity that God has given to every human being, said the president of the Migration Committee of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops. Citing Pope Francis, Bishop Mark J. Seitz of El Paso, Texas, said that human trafficking is a wound in living flesh on the body of Christ and on the body of all humanity, demanding a continuous and united response. The bishop made these comments in a statement on February 6, published by the USCCB before the World Day of Prayer and Reflection against Human Trafficking, which takes place on February 8, the feast day of St. Josephine Bakhita, the first Sudanese saint of the Church. As a child, she was kidnapped by Arab slave traders. A Muslim owner called her Bakhita, which means fortunate; other owners were an Arab chief and a Turkish general. She endured years of cruelty, even torture, before being sold to an Italian consul who planned to set her free. He took her to Italy, where she worked as a nanny for another family. In 1889, Bakhita obtained her freedom in court. She was baptized as Josephine, entered the Canossian Sisters, and served her order in Italy for over 50 years as a cook, seamstress, and porter. Since her canonization by Pope John Paul II in 2000, she has become the patron saint of survivors of human trafficking. Bishop Seitz encouraged Catholics and all people of good will to unite in prayer and action to combat human trafficking, often described as modern-day slavery, while urging elected officials to address the issue constructively by strengthening existing protections and expanding services for survivors of human trafficking, including those made possible by the historic Trafficking Victims Protection Act. The law was first enacted in 2000 and has been reauthorized several times since then, most recently on February 13, 2024, when the U.S. House of Representatives voted 414-11 to reauthorize the law for another five years, something that U.S. bishops and other Catholic organizations had been advocating for many years, according to Bishop Seitz. The law classifies human trafficking as a federal crime with severe penalties. His proposals include the protection of immigration for foreign victims of human trafficking and the possibility of obtaining permanent resident status for non-immigrants, raising public awareness and helping to identify signs of trafficking, and coordinating anti-trafficking efforts between the government and other organizations. Unfortunately, many of the proposals currently being debated would weaken or eliminate decades of bipartisan progress on this issue, said Mons. Seitz in his February 6 statement. We must reject policies that give more opportunities to bad actors to exploit the vulnerable, either within or outside the borders of our country. The Catholic Church in the United States has long been at the forefront of the fight against human trafficking, and American bishops remain steadfast alongside our Holy Father in his constant efforts to shed light on this global injustice, he said, adding that the Pope often reminds the faithful that we must mobilize our resources to combat trafficking and accompany those who have been exploited in this way. This requires an ongoing effort of collective vigilance, Bishop Seitz said. For if we close our eyes and ears, if we become complacent, we will have to answer for it in the Final Judgment. Guided by Catholic teaching and the Vatican's Pastoral Guidelines on Human Trafficking, the USCCB remains committed to raising awareness about trafficking and amplifying efforts to prevent it. The Catholics are called to face this problem with courage and compassion, to initiate difficult conversations and to confront the harsh reality of human trafficking and exploitation, the bishop added. We ask for the intercession of Saint Josephine Bakhita as we pray for the end of human trafficking and for the healing, protection, and safety of all victims and survivors alike, especially children and those in our society who are afraid to seek help because they are marginalized. Bishop Seitz said that the life of Saint Josephine Bakhita is a reminder that the fight against human trafficking is not just a social issue, but a spiritual mission. As a survivor of human trafficking, Saint Josephine Bakhita's transformation from captive to religious is a powerful testament to hope, healing, and unbreakable resistance, he added.

The girl said that her aunt's partner was abusing her, with the complicity of her family (Google Maps) A complaint of child sexual abuse was known last weekend when a 13-year-old girl entered a hospital in Santiago del Estero pregnant and about to give birth. After giving birth, the girl herself reported that her aunt's partner was abusing her and that her family was complicit in what was happening. The case was known last Saturday. According to police sources, on that day a minor of an age entered the Colonia Dora Hospital and, after being examined by a doctor, was referred to the Añatuya Zonal Hospital, where it was discovered that she was in labor. She gave birth moments later; the baby, weighing 2,900 kilograms, was born at term and in good health. Police sources told Infobae that, after the birth, authorities interviewed the girl's aunt, who lives with her since she was 2 years old. According to her account, she was unaware that her niece was pregnant. In the meantime, the girl provided more details that her aunt forced her to be locked up with her partner, a man identified as R.C., who abused her. She said that this happened three times a week. The prosecutor in charge of the case, Alejandra Sobreso, ordered the case to be investigated as repeated sexual abuse with carnal access. She also ordered a police report, interviews with the obstetrician and the girl's aunt, a medical report, and a pre-psychological interview. According to El Liberal, the accused are a 62-year-old municipal employee and his 26-year-old partner, who upon learning of the accusations sent a message to a relative denying the facts. The Police arrived at their home in the Las Trincheras neighborhood and both were taken to the Icaño locality police station. Previous incident A similar episode occurred in January of last year in the city of Saladillo, when it was revealed that a 13-year-old girl gave birth to a baby at the Alejandro Posadas zonal hospital. Due to the incident, the prosecutor's office was investigating the mother and her partner. A similar case occurred in January in Saladillo. The doctors who treated the minor confirmed that she was admitted to the hospital with severe abdominal pain. Initially, they believed it was a stomach problem, but after conducting the necessary tests, they discovered that she was 35 weeks pregnant. Immediately, the professionals notified the Saladillo Youth and Adolescence Agency to intervene. Several local media outlets reported that, after learning the news, the neighbors mobilized to the family's residence, located on Pereyra Street between Almafuerte and Sarmiento, to demand justice, but everything ended in a violent confrontation with the Police. Although they claim that several abuse complaints had been filed that incriminated the mother and her partner, the authorities denied this version. It is essential to note that prior to this incident, there were no formal complaints filed by neighbors or the education system, or the health system that had alerted authorities about this situation, which prevented the prior intervention of the corresponding bodies, the Municipality stated in a press release. In an interview with TN, Alejandro Armendáriz, the interim mayor of the Buenos Aires city, described the family situation as very delicate. The mother of F. (the girl who had the baby, whose identity is being protected) is living with a young man who would be the stepfather, and it is in that environment that what is suspected to have happened, he revealed. The case is under the jurisdiction of prosecutor Roberto Javier Berlingeri, of the Functional Instruction Unit (UFI) N2 of Saladillo, who has the mother of the minor and the stepfather as the main suspects for alleged sexual abuse.

California Governor Gavin Newsom and his supporter Demi Lovato sign separate progressive bills that provide legal and financial protection for children who influence the internet. The enacted bill was SB764, which establishes legal and financial protection for children in monetized online content, requiring parents to set aside a percentage of the child's earnings in a trust. Another bill, AB 1880, expanded the Coogan Law, which protects child performers, including actors, to include online child content creators. The law requires employers to deposit at least 15% of their income into a trust until the child reaches adulthood, including legal guardians acting as employers. Children cannot give their consent on their own and not all parents are aware of the dangers of exposing their children to the internet at such an early age. Although I strongly agree with the implementation of these laws, I believe they should have been put in place much earlier. Beyond that, the 15% requirement is not sufficient compensation for child actors and influencers, ideally it should be at least 50% in general. By assigning such a small percentage of value to child labor, the State allows for the exploitation of children by employers and families. As a result, we have seen the effects of child abuse throughout the country due to the fact that the laws were not put in place earlier. For example, in 2019, the family YouTube channel, Fantastic Adventures, made headlines for accusations of child abuse. The mother was accused of neglect and physical abuse of her adopted children who starred in the channel. Each of the channel's sponsored videos would accumulate around $20,000, according to NBC News. Another recent and current example of child abuse related to social media is the YouTube channel 8 Passengers Ruby Franke, the mother and creator of the parenting advice channel, and her partner Jodi Hildebrandt, were sentenced to up to 30 years in prison for torturing and abusing Franke's children. Graphic details reveal that Franke's 9-year-old son was forced to perform manual labor, and that her other child was often tied up and restrained. It appears that Hildebrandt was involved in making one of the children repeatedly jump into a cactus, according to CBS News. YouTube does not have policies against these family productions and has no control over what happens behind the scenes. Although the policies adopted in California are good steps towards protecting children from potential abuse, there are still many things that could be improved. I previously mentioned that I believe children should receive at least 50% of their earnings. I think it's a fair amount because it's the child who does the work, not the father, but we still have to consider the things that parents provide, such as gasoline to drive or special clothing or accessories for filming. This leads us to wonder if children should or should not work on the internet. What ages do we consider acceptable as a society for children to produce content with the help of a tutor. In general, I think there should be more protection across the country for children who suffer abuse in the online entertainment industry. There should also be more rules and laws to prevent children from being exposed online from such an early age. One way to prevent this could be for social workers to make regular visits to families that regularly post content of their children. It may seem invasive, but it's a plausible solution. Another possible solution could be the periodic psychological evaluation of parents and children separately to help maintain communication and promote the overall health of the family while creating content.

Paloma Gallardo and Josué Salvatierra, murdered in Florencio Varela Paloma Gallardo (16) did not suffer sexual violence before being murdered, as her parents claimed since the discovery of her body in a vacant lot in Florencio Varela. This information was confirmed on Tuesday with the additional results of the autopsy performed on the victims' bodies, according to sources on the case who spoke to Infobae. The examination also revealed another shocking detail: the couple had been hit on the head for half an hour. I want it to be clear what happened. My daughter was raped and Josué defended her. That's why they were killed, said Omar Gallardo, Paloma's father, at the funeral where they bid farewell to their remains. He later insisted on this theory on multiple occasions, which by then contradicted the preliminary examination by forensic experts, who also did not detect any signs of abuse. In several interviews, the man provided graphic details about what he saw on his daughter's body when he identified her in the vacant lot, including alleged bruises and bites in erogenous and genital areas. These claims were discredited by the expanded autopsy report. Omar Gallardo, Paloma's father, sang a religious song at his daughter's funeral. Despite the conclusiveness of the results, from this part of the complaint, Infobae was informed that they will continue to claim that there was an unconsummated sexual abuse against Paloma. In addition, the complementary autopsy confirmed the double skull fracture as the cause of death. It also added an estimate that accounts for the macabre nature of the fact, that the blows, with a blunt object, would have lasted for more than 30 minutes. The case was left without a prosecutor. This Tuesday, in addition, Judge Adrián Villagra of Guarantees Chamber N8 in Quilmes, accepted the request made by prosecutor Hernán Bustos Rivas, head of UFI N5 in Florencio Varela, to step aside from the investigation into the double murder of Paloma and Josué Salvatierra (14). The posters with which they searched for Josué and Paloma while they were missing The prosecutor argued alleged threats and grievances from the lawyer Carlos Dieguez, who represents the parents of the boy. Before being consulted by Infobae, the lawyer denied the accusations of the prosecutor, although he acknowledged having met him, in his office, on February 6 last year. According to what the former prosecutor of the case communicated to Judge Villagra in a resolution that this medium had access to, the situation to which the lawyer was exposed represents a moral violence that prevents him from proceeding with the prosecution of the case with the necessary spiritual balance. The Quilmes District Attorney's Office will designate a new UFI (Unidad Fiscal Investigadora, or Investigating Fiscal Unit) on Wednesday to continue the investigation. The clarification of the case has advanced very little so far. Fiscal Bustos Rivas, in a period of ten days, was unable to identify suspects with a significant link to the evidence collected at the crime scene. There were raids in the Bosques area, but all with negative results. The latest images of Josué and Paloma alive, just meters from the vacant lot where they were killed. At all times, the Public Prosecution Office maintained as its main hypothesis the robbery followed by homicide. However, this version did not satisfy any of the two plaintiff parties. The Salvatierra family, through their lawyer, stated that the children would have been killed because they saw something related to the operations of the narcomenudeo (a type of small-scale narco-trafficking) that operates in the abandoned land where the bodies were found. We have another hypothesis different from the police version, not the one of robbery. Who kills two people in broad daylight to steal a backpack and two cellphones? What resistance could a 14-year-old boy and a 16-year-old girl have put up? The lawyer for Josué's parents posed more questions than certainties. Another point he objected to was the crime scene. For this part of the indictment, the children did not die in the same place where their bodies were found, but in the vicinity of that wasteland. This hypothesis, added to the fact that the meadow was set on fire, is framed within the alternative line of investigation that postulates that before the double crime, something more than a simple robbery occurred.

The Northern Center Prosecutor's Office opened an investigation after the former partner of Deputy Jorge Durán (RN) filed a complaint for sexual abuse against him. According to police information, the accusation was formalized on the early hours of Tuesday, leading the Sexual Crimes Brigade of the PDI to conduct procedures at the parliamentarian's residence in Colina. The complainant was taken to the Medical Forensic Service (SML) for forensic examinations. Durán, on the other hand, filed a complaint for extortion against the woman, stating to Carabineros that she had requested payment for managing his social media accounts and that if he did not comply, she would denounce him. According to BioBioChile, the parliamentarian stated in a statement that the relationship was consensual and that they had a meeting at his residence with other people present. Government Reaction The Minister of Women and Gender Equality, Luz Vidal, classified the complaint as serious and stated that the ministry is providing support for the complainant through the National Women and Gender Equality Service (SernamEG). Additionally, she mentioned the Antonia Law, which establishes measures to prevent the re-victimization of those reporting sexual crimes, as reported by La Tercera. From Renovación Nacional (RN), the party issued a statement pointing out that this is a complaint that must be investigated by the Public Ministry and that the background information was sent to the Supreme Court of the community. According to sources from the political party, the suspension of the deputy's membership is being evaluated while the investigation is underway. About Deputy Durán, 44 years old, he has been a councilor of Cerro Navia and has been a deputy since 2017. According to ExAnte, during the pandemic, he supported withdrawals of pension funds, which generated tensions within his political sector. The Prosecution maintains the details of the investigation under reserve, while the Sexual Crimes Brigade of the PDI continues with the proceedings.

data.text: Eight people have been charged in connection with the trafficking of women from Venezuela and other countries for their sexual exploitation in central Tennessee, federal prosecutors and law enforcement announced on Tuesday. The defendants are accused of luring dozens of victims to the US with promises of a better life before saddling the women with scandalous debts that far exceeded the cost of their travel. Coerced by the debts, the women were forced to have sex with strangers for the benefit of the defendants, said US Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee, Rob McGuire. It is alleged that the illegal sex trade operation was active from at least July 2022 to March 2024, according to prosecutors. The eight defendants were in federal custody on Tuesday morning, McGuire said. Two of the defendants were accused of using their ties to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua to intimidate women, according to the indictment. The federal indictment does not specify if those two defendants were members of the gang or used the specter of affiliation with Tren de Aragua as a tactic of fear, although the TBI previously identified one as a confirmed member. We will do everything necessary to try to save the lives of the victims we help, said McGuire. He said he could not comment if any of the undocumented victims in the U.S. could face deportation, but said it is an interest of our office that any survivor of sex trafficking has the ability to make their perpetrator answer to the court. The formal accusation of several individuals was made public on Tuesday, and officials from the prosecutor's office, the FBI, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the National Security Investigations met in federal court in downtown Nashville to make the announcement that afternoon. The accused are Yilibeth Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero Yuribetzi Del Valle Gomez Machuca Wilmarys Del Valle Manzano Soloranzo Endrik Alexander Morales Rivero Ariannys Beatriz Gutierrez Carrillo Frankyanna Del Valle Romero Rivero Jesus Enrique Castillo Rodríguez According to the United States Attorney's Office, the company was a family affair. Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera and Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero were mother and son, respectively, while five of the other accused were Mota Rivero's girlfriend, his children, or their spouses, according to a court document. All of them are accused of conspiracy to commit interstate transportation for the purpose of prostitution and conspiracy to commit interstate and international travel or transportation in aid of racketeering enterprises. Gómez Machuca, Mota Rivero, and Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera also face a separate charge of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, which carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Mota Rivero faces a charge of possession of a firearm by an unauthorized alien. All of the accused are without lawful immigration status. Two of the accused had previously been arrested and incarcerated in Davidson County on charges in a state court. Train of Aragua originated as a prison gang in Venezuela, but has expanded its presence in the Americas in recent years, according to the United States Department of the Treasury. In July 2024, the Treasury, under the Biden administration, sanctioned Tren de Aragua as a transnational criminal organization involved in various illicit activities, including human trafficking and trade, gender-based violence, money laundering, and illicit narcotics trafficking. The announcement by the U.S. Attorney General aligns with the administration's Trump-established law enforcement priorities of violent crimes and immigration issues.Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera, 52, and Mota Rivero, 35, had been charged separately in Nashville with multiple counts of sex trafficking for commercial sex acts. Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera faces nine counts of the offense in Davidson County, while Mota Rivero faces four counts of sex trafficking for commercial sex acts, as well as two counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in two separate cases in Davidson County Circuit Court. The TBI said that they confirmed Mota Rivero was a member of Tren de Aragua. They have remained in Nashville's jails since their arrests. Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera's bail had previously been set at $480,000, and Mota Rivero's at $375,000, but they will not be eligible for release on bail since the federal system does not use cash bail. Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera currently has a deportation order against her by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Evelyn Daiana Carrera, who was 35 years old, passed away last Wednesday after several days in the Central Hospital of Mendoza. This tragic outcome was due to complications that she suffered as a result of surgery. While the investigation into the alleged malpractice that led to her death is ongoing, the Justice has opened a parallel case to investigate a rape that the victim herself reported on a piece of paper before dying. THE CHILLING WRITING LEFT BY EVELYN BEFORE DYING On December 12, her mother visited her in the Intensive Care Unit where she was hospitalized. Since she couldn't speak, Evelyn wrote a heart-wrenching message on a paper napkin: They're raping me, they're raping me. In shock, her family members questioned her about this situation, and she wrote again, "ene fm e," which implied that the perpetrator of the rape was a nurse and that she had been attacked six days earlier, as published in the newspaper El Sol. The mother of Evelyn reported the incident the same day and a case was opened for sexual abuse, under the prosecution of prosecutor Flavio DAmore. The prosecution requested the images from the security cameras in the sector of the assistance center where the victim was interned to try to identify the nurses in charge of the patients in the days before the report. INVESTIGATE IF THERE WAS BAD PRACTICE IN EVELYN'S SURGERY From the death of the complainant, a new file was initiated under the charge of Homicide prosecutor Carlos Torres to clarify if there was or not bad practice during the operation to which the woman had to be subjected for an intestinal affliction, a condition that caused her death weeks later. Evelyn Carrera was a mother of two children, a 15-year-old girl and a 17-year-old boy. IF YOU SUFFERED A SITUATION OF ABUSE OR VIOLATION, YOU CAN ASK FOR HELP In Argentina, you can call the 144 Line to receive assistance in case of gender violence. You can also call Line 137 for attention in case of family and sexual violence. Line 144 is a free and anonymous service. It is available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. It offers information, support, and counseling. You can call in case of physical, psychological, sexual, economic, patrimonial, and symbolic violence. Line 137 is available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. It offers accompaniment from a team formed by psychologists and social workers. You can call in case of family and sexual violence. In case of an emergency, you can call 911.

Agents from the Scientific, Penal, and Criminal Investigations Corps (Cicpc) apprehended Mariángel Victoria González. The 18-year-old girl had allegedly faked being a victim of sexual abuse on Bella Vista Avenue, Alto Los Godos parish, Maturín municipality, Monagas state. What happened? According to the report by Cicpc Director Douglas Rico, González went with her parents and uncles to the police station, where she claimed to have been abused by a bus driver and a fare collector, whom she had taken after leaving Rómulo Gallegos University on her way home. According to her account, during the ride, she observed passengers getting off and began to cough, losing consciousness. Upon regaining consciousness, she found herself on the sidewalk without a shirt. She also mentioned that upon arriving home and taking a shower, she experienced bleeding and pain in her intimate area, which alarmed her parents and uncles about the alleged sexual abuse. A catch that drew attention was the young woman's refusal to undergo a gynecological exam to verify the truth of her accusation. Eight Venezuelans face federal charges, for human trafficking. The U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee says the accused were arrested in Tennessee and other states. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Tennessee announced the formal indictment of eight Venezuelan citizens allegedly linked to a human trafficking operation. The formal indictment alleges that the eight worked together to recruit and bring women from Central and South America to the U.S., specifically to Tennessee and other states, to operate a commercial sex business. Prosecutors claim that the accused targeted young, poor, and vulnerable women from Venezuela and other countries. The formal indictment states that the defendants convinced the women they would have a better life, but once in the U.S., they demanded the exorbitant cost of their travel by forcing them to engage in sex with strangers. I want to reiterate that human trafficking is a real problem here in our community, said federal prosecutor Robert Maguire. Ignoring it won't make it go away. We can't live in the shadows, we have to bring it to light and make those who commit these crimes in the darkness accountable. Officials said this was the result of a years-long investigation into this operation with the help of multiple local, state, and federal agencies. Leaders say the investigation began with the Nashville Metropolitan Police Department and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. The following people were formally charged: Yilibeth Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera (also known as Yibi) charged with conspiracy to commit sex trafficking across international borders, conspiracy to commit travel or transportation in aid of racketeering enterprises, and conspiracy to commit sex trafficking. Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero (also known as Kleiber) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for the purpose of prostitution, conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or to aid organized crime businesses, conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien. Yuribetzi Del Valle Gomez Machuca (A.K.A. La Gorda) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for the purpose of prostitution, conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or to aid organized crime businesses, and conspiracy to commit sex trafficking.Wilmarys Del Valle Manzano Solorzano (A.K.A. La China) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for the purpose of prostitution, and conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or to aid organized crime businesses.Endrik Alexander Morales Rivero (A.K.A Ariannys Beatriz Gutierrez-Carrillo (A.K.A Nani, Nany) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for purposes of prostitution and conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or transportation in aid of organized crime enterprises, Frankyanna Del Valle RomeroRivero (also known as Franya) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for purposes of prostitution and conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or transportation in aid of organized crime enterprises, Jesús Enrique Castillo Rodríguez (also known as Chu Chu) charged with conspiracy to transport individuals across international borders for purposes of prostitution and conspiracy to facilitate travel within and outside the country or transportation in aid of organized crime enterprises, The prosecution alleges that the defendants used hotels in the Nashville area to lure buyers to locations where they forced victims into providing sexual favors in exchange for payment. According to court documents, they used online advertising and messaging services like WhatsApp to determine prices based on certain favors. Prosecutors claim that Yibi and Kleiver used their connections with the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua (TdA) to intimidate victims into continuing to participate in commercial sex acts. We rely on the community to make a difference in the lives of more vulnerable women and girls who have been separated from their families under false pretenses and forced into the worst imaginable hell, said Maguire. Several law enforcement representatives spoke at a press conference on Tuesday, condemning human trafficking and urging community members to remain vigilant. Human trafficking is abhorrent to all of us, said MNPD Chief John Drake. It's a modern form of slavery. I want to be clear that our police department will always prioritize human trafficking investigations in our department, regardless of where a suspect is located. Maguire said they were focused on prosecuting the accused here in Nashville before deportation was mentioned. Specifically, the message that authorities are sending with this indictment is that human trafficking is an abomination, Maguire added. That we will find it wherever it exists and whenever it exists. That we will recover the survivors and put an end to it once and for all. Maguire said the dozens of victims in this case will receive victim support services, likely through local and state organizations. The eight accused are in federal custody awaiting prosecution. They were arrested in multiple states, including Tennessee and Texas. If you or someone you know is a victim of human trafficking, authorities ask you to call 1 (888) 373-7888. The Libertad PNP Destructs Illegal Mining Tunnels In an operation in La Libertad, the Police destroyed 77 illegal mining tunnels and equipment in Huamachuco. In a joint operation, the Peruvian National Police (PNP) and the Public Prosecutor's Office intervened in the La Libertad region to curb illegal mining. In just two days, authorities destroyed 77 tunnels in the Bosque El Polo and Shiracmaca sectors, in the Huamachuco district, Sánchez Carrión province. The PNP Environmental Department Director, General Manuel Lozada, detailed that the intervention consisted of the blasting of tunnels used for the illicit extraction of gold. According to authorities, the seized material exceeds S/ 70 million in value. During the operation, heavy machinery from the Regional Government was used to dismantle camps, remove motors, and eliminate pits used in mineral extraction. Chemical supplies and other tools related to this illegal activity were found. General Lozada warned that illegal mining is linked to crimes such as money laundering and human trafficking, so the PNP is working in coordination with other specialized departments to combat these criminal networks. Authorities reported that these interdiction operations will continue in other provinces affected by illegal mining, such as Santiago de Chuco and Pataz. The fight against this illicit activity seeks to slow down the environmental damage and its connection to other crimes in the region.

In 2024, it was reported that at least 14 children go missing daily in Mexico. The United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child has expressed deep concern over the alarming situation faced by girls, boys, and adolescents in Mexico. The recent report highlights significant increases in homicides, femicides, forced disappearances, forced recruitment, child labor, and sexual violence, among other violations of children's rights.Homicides and Femicides on the RiseAccording to data from the Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (Redim), based on official figures, between January and October 2024, there were 2,049 homicides of minors aged 0 to 17 years in the country. Of these victims, 422 were women and 1,627 were men, representing a 4.9% increase compared to the same period of the previous year. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child has called on the Mexican government to implement urgent measures to prevent these homicides and feminicides, including those perpetrated by police forces. The imperative need for an immediate response is to safeguard the lives and well-being of children in Mexico.Forced Disappearances: A Persistent CrisisForced disappearances of minors continue to be a grave concern. By October 11, 2023, 96,966 people aged 0 to 17 years were reported as missing, unlocated, or located in the country. Of this total, 65,489 (approximately 67.5%) were women. Moreover, on the same date, 9,065 women and 7,797 men in the same age range remained missing or unlocated. The UN Committee has urged Mexico to adopt effective measures to prevent, investigate, and punish all cases of child disappearance, emphasizing the importance of coordinated and effective action to address this crisis.Forced Recruitment: An Alarming RealityAlthough Mexico is not in a declared state of war, there are disturbing reports of the forced recruitment of minors by organized crime groups. These children are used in illicit activities, exposing them to extreme risks and violating their fundamental rights. The Red Cross has highlighted the problem of children being used in conflicts, noting that around 300,000 minors worldwide are forced to participate in armed conflicts, facing kidnappings, physical abuse, and sexual abuse. Although these numbers are global, they reflect a problem that also affects Mexico, especially in regions controlled by organized crime. Child Labor: A Persistent Practice Child labor continues to be a common practice in various regions of Mexico. Children and adolescents are forced to work in precarious conditions, depriving them of their right to education and exposing them to situations of exploitation and abuse. According to data from the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH), despite government efforts, thousands of minors continue to work in sectors such as agriculture, mining, and informal commerce, often in hazardous conditions and without adequate legal protection.Sexual Violence: A Lurking Threat Sexual violence against minors is a pressing problem in Mexico. In 2022, 337 cases of women aged 0-17 years were reported as victims of human trafficking, representing a 28.6% increase compared to 2021. Although from January to October 2023, a 37. A 0.5% compared to the same period of the previous year, with 273 reported cases, the figure remains alarming. Moreover, sexual violence is closely linked to the disappearance of girls and adolescents. A report from various human rights organizations revealed that the lack of coordination, training, and corruption in the prosecutor's offices contribute to the perpetuation of this problem, making it difficult to search for and rescue the victims. Contributing Factors and Recommendations Various factors contribute to the violation of children's rights in Mexico, including poverty, inequality, lack of access to education, and weakness in the application of child protection laws. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child has issued several recommendations to the Mexican government, including:Implement Effective Public Policies Develop and implement comprehensive policies that address the underlying causes of child violence and exploitation.Strengthen the Justice System Train judicial and law enforcement authorities to effectively and sensitively handle cases of child violence and exploitation.Guarantee Universal Education Ensure that all children have access to quality education, thereby reducing their vulnerability to exploitation and abuse.Promote Community Participation Involve communities in protecting children's rights, fostering a culture of reporting and support.The situation of children's rights in Mexico is alarming and requires immediate and coordinated action from the government, civil society, and the international community. It is imperative that effective measures be implemented to protect Mexican children from violence, exploitation, and other violations of their fundamental rights. The Peruvian National Police (PNP) blows up illegal mining tunnels. The PNP destroyed 77 illegal mining tunnels and camps in La Libertad. Operations will continue in Santiago de Chuco and Pataz. Photo and video Canal N The fight against illegal mining in La Libertad continues. In an operation led by the Peruvian National Police (PNP) and the Public Prosecutor's Office, 77 tunnels used for the illegal extraction of gold in the Huamachuco district, Sánchez Carrión province, were destroyed. The intervened sectors were Bosque El Polo and Shiracmaca, where authorities carried out explosions to render the clandestine tunnels useless. According to General Manuel Lozada, director of the PNP's Environmental Directorate, the seized material is worth S/170 million. Demolishing camps and removing illegal machinery In addition to the tunnels, the operations included the destruction of camps, motors, and pits used by the illegal miners With the help of heavy machinery from the Regional Government, structures that allowed the continuation of this illicit activity were removed. General Lozada warned that illegal mining not only affects the environment, but is also related to crimes such as money laundering and human trafficking. Therefore, the PNP is working together with other units to stop these illegal operations. More operations on the way The interventions in La Libertad will continue in other provinces, such as Santiago de Chuco and Pataz, where illegal mining continues to be a problem for local communities. Authorities have reiterated their commitment to fighting this illicit activity and its associated criminal networks.

Prosecutor Alberto Torres charged three men with sexual abuse of a defenseless person and requested a declaration of rebellion from the Penal Guarantees Court. They are the brothers Vicente Cabrera Rejala (29) and José María Cabrera Rejala (33), as well as Aldo Ramírez Ramírez (41), who are fugitives from justice. The cited individuals allegedly forced a man under the influence of alcohol into sexual submission after a beating. The incident occurred on January 31, 2025, around 8:00 p.m., in a secluded location near the Yatai Bridge in the San José neighborhood of Tavapay district, in the south of Alto Paraná, with a victim over the age of 18. According to the investigation, on the indicated date, the alleged perpetrators, along with unidentified subjects, arrived on their motorcycles at a warehouse in the aforementioned neighborhood, where the victim was consuming alcoholic beverages. Subsequently, they invited him to go to another location and continue drinking, but the affected person refused categorically. However, they forcibly lifted him onto one of the bicycles, took him near the mentioned bridge, and after beating him, they subjected him to a group sexual assault before fleeing the scene and leaving him abandoned. Later, the victim was assisted and taken to a care center, where he received medical attention. Subsequently, he filed a complaint with the police authorities of the 39th sub-comisaría jurisdiction. In the context of the investigation into the incident, the suspected perpetrators were identified, who are now charged and being sought by the Police. Prosecutor Alberto Torres requested that the three men, once detained, be sent to prison, considering the gravity of the case.

The Trump administration's external aid freeze reduces medical care and food for thousands of migrants in Tijuana. Following President Donald Trump's executive order that halted billions of dollars in foreign aid, agencies in Tijuana are suspending medical care and psychological programs, food assistance, and other services that helped thousands of migrants and low-income residents. On Friday, a community health clinic and social services called Comunidad AVES closed its doors indefinitely in response to the order, reported shelter leaders to inewsource. A handwritten note on a chalkboard outside read: We will not be providing services at the moment. Also, preparations are being made for other impacts. Food vouchers for a church that housed over a thousand migrants were canceled. A childcare program for children and adolescents was terminated. And a planned project to improve infrastructure at another refugee shelter for women and children was put on hold. Trump's order of January 20 froze US aid payments for 90 days while the administration reviewed the efficiency of the programs and their alignment with Trump's America First foreign policy. In the order, Trump said that foreign aid is not aligned with US interests and in many cases is antithetical to American values. The US government spends only a small fraction of its budget on international aid, approximately $72 billion in 2023, or 1% of the total US expenditure that year. Promoted as a tool to advance US foreign policy worldwide, foreign aid programs have also been subject to criticism and questioning over the value of the spending for US taxpayers The effects of the pause have been felt worldwide and right across the border between the United States and Mexico. We're left alone, said Claudia Portela, who directs two migrant shelters and a soup kitchen under the Salesian Project, a Catholic missionary congregation that has been in Tijuana for nearly 40 years. The Salesian Project attends to more than 1,000 asylum seekers, deportees, and homeless people daily. Portela said that more than half of its services are affected by the freeze on funding. It's unclear when services can be restarted. People will keep coming. Those who are refugees here will stay here. They need to be taken care of, so it's very difficult, Portela said. Most of the more than 30 shelters in Tijuana are privately operated and rely on subsidies and individual donations, which means that financing basic needs is a constant challenge. American aid helped provide services that shelters couldn't offer on their own. AVES Community, a collaboration between Salesianos and the International Organization for Migration, has offered basic health care, therapy, job training, legal assistance, and other services to thousands of migrants and low-income residents in Tijuana since 2023. A few days after Trump's order, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced exemptions to the freeze for vital humanitarian aid, but it's unclear if those permits include services in Tijuana. In 2023, the US granted over $240 million in aid to Mexico, administered through associated organizations, including the International Organization for Migration and the United Nations Children's Fund, or UNICEF. Approximately 12% of that funding, just under $30 million, was allocated to humanitarian aid in Mexico. Most of the funding went towards economic development projects, security, and governance, including improving the justice system, ending human trafficking and child labor, reducing corruption, and promoting job opportunities. A spokesperson for the International Organization for Migration in Mexico refused to comment on the situation in Tijuana. A UNICEF spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees, who also works in Tijuana, said they understand that some exceptions will be made, but they do not have specific information. The administration is also trying to cut funding for the United States Agency for International Development, or USAID, one of the federal agencies through which US aid is distributed. A federal judge blocked plans on Friday to put thousands of USAID workers on leave. In a shelter for women and children near the border, projects to repair the roof and floors were canceled after aid was frozen, according to Judith Cabrera, who co-directs the Border Crisis Center. On a recent rainy afternoon, broken windows allowed air currents to enter the room, puddles formed near an entrance, and chunks of drywall were falling from the ceiling. Inside, children took turns riding a scooter, while others ate pancakes and drew with markers. Cabrera said they are accustomed to working with very little government help from both the United States and Mexico, but the immediate and drastic policy changes by Trump on immigration and the border have taken a toll. data.text: Suspects from the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua were among the eight people charged with federal human trafficking offenses in Tennessee, said the U.S. Department of Justice. Acting Attorney General Robert E. McGuire said on Tuesday that two of the accused used their affiliation with Tren de Aragua to intimidate the victims and force them to continue engaging in commercial sex. All eight accused are Venezuelan citizens, and five of them are women, according to the federal indictment. The human trafficking conspiracy allegedly conspired to identify and recruit young, poor, and vulnerable women from Venezuela and other countries in South and Central America with the intention of transporting them to the United States and profiting from their commercial sex acts, the indictment says. The U.S. Attorney's Office For the Middle Tennessee District, charges were announced at a press conference shortly after the indictment was made public. While arrests focused on dismantling a prostitution ring, at least one of the accused human traffickers was also charged with the illegal possession of a firearm, McGuire said. After the victims arrived in the United States, they were imposed with an inflated debt and required to engage in commercial sex acts for the benefit of the accused, until, and sometimes even after, the debt was paid off, the indictment states. Due to the imposed debt, the victims continued to participate in commercial sex acts out of fear of severe harm they or their families could suffer if they attempted to leave before paying their debts, the indictment states. CNN was unable to locate a defense attorney for the accused and no attorney was listed in court records. The investigation by multiple agencies began as a local inquiry by the Metropolitan Police Department of Nashville and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), according to federal officials. The Tren de Aragua crime gang originated in a Venezuelan prison and has gradually spread both north and south of the Caribbean country in recent years. Recently, it has brought terror not only to Venezuela but also to Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, and Peru. While the gang has focused primarily on human trafficking and other crimes affecting migrants, it has also been linked to extortion, kidnapping, money laundering, and drug smuggling, according to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury. A U.S. government decree Signed on January 20, it specifically named the Aragua Train and the Salvadoran gang MS13 as threats to the stability of international order in the Western Hemisphere, based on their campaigns of violence and terror in the United States and internationally. As CNN previously reported, federal officials dismantled in April 2024 another human trafficking ring linked to the Aragua Train that was based in Louisiana and operated storage houses used for human trafficking in Texas, Virginia, New Jersey, and Florida.

data.text: The defendants are accused of luring dozens of victims to the United States with the promise of a better life before saddling the women with outrageous debts that far exceeded the costs of their travel. Coerced by the debts, the women were forced to have sex with strangers for the benefit of the defendants, said the U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee, Rob McGuire. It is alleged that the illegal sex trafficking operation was active from at least July 2022 to March 2024, according to prosecutors. The eight defendants were in federal custody on Tuesday morning, McGuire said. Two of the defendants were accused of using their ties to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua to intimidate the women, according to the indictment. The federal indictment does not specify whether the two defendants were members of the gang or used the specter of affiliation with the Aragua Train as a tactic of fear, although the TBI had previously identified one as a confirmed member. We will do everything necessary to try to save the lives of the victims we help, McGuire said. He said he could not comment on whether any of the undocumented victims in the US could face deportation, but said it is an interest of our office that any survivor of sex trafficking be able to make their abuser answer to the court. The formal charges against multiple individuals were made public on Tuesday, and officials from the prosecutor's office, the FBI, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, the Nashville Metropolitan Police Department, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the National Security Investigations met in the federal courthouse in downtown Nashville to make the announcement that afternoon. The accused are Yilibeth Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera, Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero, Yuribetzi Del Valle Gomez Machuca, Wilmarys Del Valle Manzano Soloranzo, Endrik Alexander Morales Rivero, Ariannys Beatriz Gutierrez Carrillo, Frankyanna Del Valle Romero Rivero, and Jesus Enrique Castillo Rodríguez. According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, the business was a family affair. Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera and Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero were mother and son, respectively, while five of the other accused were Mota Rivero's girlfriend, his children, or their spouses, as per a court document. All of them are accused of conspiring to transport individuals across state lines for the purpose of prostitution and conspiring to transport individuals across state lines and abroad or to aid in the operation of organized crime enterprises. Gómez Machuca, Mota Rivero, and Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera also face a separate charge of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, which carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. Mota Rivero faces a charge of possession of a firearm by an undocumented person. All of the accused lack legal migratory status. Two of the accused were previously arrested and incarcerated in Davidson County on charges in a state court. Tren de Aragua began as a prison gang in Venezuela but has expanded its presence in the Americas in recent years, according to the U.S. Department of the Treasury. In July 2024, under the Biden administration, the Treasury Department sanctioned Tren de Aragua as a transnational criminal organization involved in various illicit activities, including human trafficking and trade, gender violence, money laundering, and the illicit trafficking of drugs. The announcement by the U.S. Attorney General aligns with the Trump administration's law enforcement priorities of violent crimes and immigration issues.Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera, 52 years old, and Mota Rivero, 35 years old, had each been charged in Nashville with multiple counts of sex trafficking for commercial sex acts. Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera faces nine counts of the offense in Davidson County, while Mota Rivero faces four counts of sex trafficking for commercial sex acts, as well as two counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in two separate cases in Davidson County Circuit Court. TBI confirmed that Mota Rivero was a member of Tren de Aragua. They have been held in Nashville's jails since their arrests. Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera's bond had previously been set at $480,000, and Mota Rivero's at $375,000, but they will not be eligible for release on bond as the federal system does not use cash bonds. Del Carmen RiveroDe Caldera currently has a deportation order against her from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The L. responded to an order from the Penal Court No. 6 of San Martín. His capture was made possible by the same program, which allowed him to be identified during a security check. Maidana had an active arrest order since 2020, issued by the Federal First Instance Court in Criminal and Correctional Matters No. 2 of Lomas de Zamora, for his alleged participation in an extortionate kidnapping committed in the Villa Caraza locality, Lanús district. According to the judicial cause, on November 29, 2020, Maidana and a group of accomplices detained two 14- and 15-year-old adolescents against their will, demanding a ransom of 80,000 pesos and a cell phone for their release. During captivity, the victims were beaten and threatened with knives. One of them was even warned that they would be left naked if they did not deliver what was demanded. The Bonaerense justice had been looking for him since 2020. He was detained last night after passing through the Tribuna Segura control at the Monumental Stadium. The incident originated on the night of November 28, when the young women attended a party in the El Tala neighborhood of Villa Caraza. Shortly afterwards, they headed to the residence of Maidana and his cousin, Ezequiel Navarro, who was also identified as a participant in the kidnapping and has a warrant out for his arrest. One of the teenagers spent the night with Maidana, while the other did so with Navarro. The next day, Maidana accused the teenagers of having stolen his cell phone, which prompted a series of physical assaults. According to the judicial file, the young women were beaten with iron rods, thrown to the ground, and threatened with setting their hair on fire. The mother of Maidana, identified as L.N., was present during the events. The kidnappers took the teenagers to a basement, where they forced them to call their families to demand the ransom money. The victims were also forced to send audio and video calls under threats. Evidence collected in the case led to the issuance of arrest warrants for Maidana and Navarro, identified as the main perpetrators of the kidnapping and the assaults. Four years after the kidnapping, Maidana was arrested while attending the Monumental stadium wearing a River Plate jersey. The Minister of Security of the City of Buenos Aires, Waldo Wolff, commented on his capture, saying "The passion that condemns them," in reference to his detention while attending a match. Following his detention, Maidana was taken to the Comisaría Vecinal 13A of the City Police, where he remains under custody. Judge Anabel Garmendia approved his arrest and ordered his detention at the police station. His cousin, Ezequiel Navarro, remains at large.

Cuba Steps Up Protection for Special Women. The Cuban Women's Federation (FMC) is increasing actions against any type of violence towards girls, young people, and adults on the island through the National Response to Gender-Based Violence Support Project. This was assured by FMC Secretary member Osmayda Hernández at a press conference for the presentation of that program, sponsored by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFP) and the Canadian Embassy in Cuba. The project responds to the national priority of guaranteeing a comprehensive and integrated response to the prevention and effective attention to gender violence, declared the FMC representative. Osmayda Hernández told Prensa Latina that no woman in Cuba is left behind, but the project guarantees attention for more than 30,000 women and girls from 40 Cuban municipalities, and it must eventually be extended to the entire national territory. He also stated that this ensures a comprehensive and integrated response to the prevention and effective attention to gender-based violence, as well as the deconstruction of stereotypes and discriminatory practices that perpetuate it. On her part, the Canadian ambassador to Cuba, Mariancik Tremblay, stated that this project is timely to complement the objectives of the cooperation program between both countries, promoting gender equality and female empowerment. Gender-based violence is a global problem, and that's why we celebrate the priority that the Cuban government gives to preventing it and the support it offers to women, the diplomat said. The UNFPA Country Office Head, Marisol Alfonso, mentioned that one of the organization's greatest commitments to the 2030 Agenda and the main connecting element of the project is the elimination of this type of violence and other harmful practices that affect women, such as child marriage and sex preference at birth. Marisol Alfonso explained that this project is based on strategies that have been implemented for years on the Caribbean island, and at the same time, it offers the opportunity to implement international experiences to establish these services more effectively. To take this model of integrated general service to those territories, where the country works through the FMC, allows them to contextualize and add other initiatives that the country implements today, Alfonso declared. The main lines of work of the organizations involved in the project include the creation of a telephone line for immediate attention of potential victims, the generation of data and statistics through diagnostic studies, and the creation of a continuous and interoperable registry of attention services.

Human trafficking should be considered as modern-day slavery. Human trafficking should be equated with slavery, as it is an international crime against humanity that violates the rights of individuals, including children. Congressman Luis Alberto Chávez García proposed an initiative to reform Article 1 of the Constitution of the United Mexican States. Chávez García recalled that according to the crime incidence statistics of the common jurisdiction of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), as of April 2024, 2,529 people aged 0 to 17 (1,890 women and 639 men) have been victims of human trafficking in Mexico. The entities with the most registered victims of human trafficking among those aged 0 to 17 from January to April 2024 have been the Mexico City (24), Quintana Roo (24), and State of Mexico (22). In Mexico, there are no clear data on the economic gains from human trafficking for various purposes, including sexual exploitation. At a forum held in 2021, the head of the Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) stated that 1,410 bank accounts were blocked for 116 people suspected of human trafficking for sexual exploitation, totaling 144 million 197 thousand 710 pesos, the legislator assured. Human trafficking is a crime that severely violates the rights of girls, boys, and adolescents, which is why it is indispensable to provide the legal protection recommended by the Convention on the Rights of the Child in Article 19, which includes all legislative, administrative, social, and educational measures to protect the child from any form of harm or physical or mental abuse, neglect, or exploitation, including sexual abuse. In addition, it incorporates the Palermo Protocol, ratified by our country on December 25, 2003, which, among other objectives, aims to prevent and combat human trafficking, paying special attention to women and children. The protocol defines human trafficking as the capture, transportation, transfer, reception, or acceptance of people, resorting to threats or the use of force, or other forms of coercion, kidnapping, fraud, deception, abuse of power or a situation of vulnerability, or the provision or receipt of payments or benefits to obtain the consent of a person who has authority over another, for purposes of exploitation. That exploitation will include, at a minimum, the exploitation of alien prostitution or other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labor or services, slavery, or practices analogous to slavery, servitude, or the removal of organs. Therefore, the Convention calls for establishing broad policies, programs, and other measures to prevent and combat human trafficking, as well as to protect victims of human trafficking, especially women and children, from a new risk of victimization. In turn, the General Law to Prevent, Punish, and Eradicate Crimes Related to Human Trafficking and to Protect and Assist Victims of these Crimes expands the concept of human trafficking to include any intentional action or omission to recruit, entice, transport, transfer, retain, deliver, receive, or harbor one or several persons for purposes of exploitation. In the same law, exploitation is understood as slavery, the condition of a serf, alien prostitution, or other forms of sexual exploitation, labor exploitation, forced labor or services, forced begging, the use of persons under 18 years old in criminal activities, illegal adoption, forced or servile marriage, the trafficking of human organs, tissues, and cells, and illicit biomedical experimentation on living human beings. The initiative of legislator Luis Alberto Chávez García proposes reforming the fourth paragraph of Article 1 of the Constitution, which states that slavery and trafficking are prohibited in the United Mexican States. Foreign slaves entering the national territory will, by this single act, gain their freedom and the protection of the laws. The initiative was turned over to the Joint Committees on Constitutional Matters and Citizen Initiatives and Human Rights for analysis and discussion.

Dr. Tejshri Shah, General Director of Médecins Sans Frontières and an expert pediatrician in infectious diseases, warns that it is impossible to contain the Mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo without addressing the needs of displaced people and improving their precarious living conditions. Mpox or simian pox (previously known as monkeypox) is not a new disease in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where it is endemic in several regions. In the last decade, cases have increased, but now, in the Kivus, the virus has mutated, becoming more transmissible among humans. This is alarming, especially in densely populated areas like Goma (with two million inhabitants) and in displacement camps, where hundreds of thousands of people are seeking refuge due to the armed conflict in North Kivu. Although the lethality of this new strain is low, the conditions in Goma and its surroundings do not allow for its spread to be halted. The capacity to treat those at higher risk of complications, such as young children and individuals with advanced HIV, remains very limited. Precarious conditions hinder prevention in displacement camps. How can we expect families living in tiny shelters without water, adequate sanitation facilities, or even soap to implement preventive measures? How can malnourished girls and boys have the necessary strength to avoid complications caused by the disease? How can we expect this variant, primarily transmitted through sexual contact, not to spread in displacement camps, given the dramatic levels of violence and sexual exploitation affecting girls and women living there? We have repeatedly denounced the inhumane living conditions faced by individuals in the camps and the glaring breaches in the humanitarian response. Impact of the M23 Crisis on Living Conditions More than two years after the onset of the M23 crisis and the massive displacement of people it triggered, families living in overcrowded camps still lack the essentials: food, water, basic hygiene items, access to sanitation and medical services. Dr. Tejshri Shah, General Director and pediatrician specializing in infectious diseases, has just returned from North Kivu, and in a session of counseling I attended with survivors of rape, a woman told me that she lives with her seven children under a plastic tarp. Her partner left her after the rape. For women like her, proven and tested solutions to prevent the spread of the epidemic are unimaginably difficult to implement. For the woman Dr. Shah attended to, the solution of using a condom during sex is not a viable option, as she cannot even access a condom. Dr. Shah, and for all the people who have sought refuge in displacement camps, the Mpox epidemic is an additional challenge in the midst of a torrent of problems. And it is not the most urgent one, given the daily struggles they face, including outbreaks of other potentially deadly diseases such as measles or cholera. However, Mpox is there and it must be addressed. To tackle this additional new challenge, we must facilitate the survival of people. This will be achieved with an adapted response to their specific needs and the challenges of real life, adds Dr. Immediate solutions to mitigate the epidemic are necessary. We must listen to people, understand their needs, and provide them with basic supplies for infection control such as water, soap, disinfectant, and access to medical facilities. These are simple but essential things. We cannot rely solely on the arrival of vaccines to resolve the problem. Improving the living conditions of people is also a critical factor in combating these outbreaks, explains Dr. Shah. Along with medical authorities, our teams are doing everything possible to provide care. Raising awareness among people living in these settlements, as we do in other parts of the country affected by the outbreak. Like many others, we hope that vaccines arrive in the country as soon as possible. However, these will not be magic solutions. Government and non-governmental actors must urgently address the underlying response to Mpox, which must be adapted to the needs and realities of the population.Doctors Without Borders (MSF) is an international medical humanitarian organization that provides aid to populations in precarious situations and to victims of natural or human-made disasters and armed conflicts, without any discrimination by race, religion, or political ideology. Currently, MSF has 499 medical and humanitarian action projects in 88 countries, and 7 million partners and collaborators worldwide. In recognition of its humanitarian work, MSF received the 1999 Nobel Peace Prize. For more information, visit the URL.

HELENA, Mont. A man from Montana was sentenced to 100 years in prison with a 50-year suspension and will not be eligible for parole for 25 years for possession of child sexual abuse material. The charges are unrelated to Alicia Navarro, the missing minor from Glendale in 2019. According to Montana's Attorney General, Edmund Davis pleaded guilty to a charge of child sexual abuse in 2024 after material of child sexual abuse was found on his electronic devices in 2023. RELATED The boyfriend of Alicia Navarro faces criminal charges in Montana for crimes related to minors, but unrelated to her disappearance. The devices were found in July 2023, when Montana police executed a search warrant at Davis's residence after it was discovered that Alicia Navarro, who had gone missing from Glendale at 14 years old, was dating him. Navarro opened the door, and the officers saw Davis throw her phone into the trash can in the kitchen. Prosecutors say the images on the phone included images of minors that appeared to be around 13 years old, with two images of children under 5, including images of young children and other images generated by computer or animated content showing children being sexualized. In July 2023, Navarro, who was already 18 years old, presented herself at a local police station in Montana and identified herself as the missing teenager from Arizona. When the police first questioned Navarro in July, she allegedly told them that no one had hurt her. For more Spanish content, visit 12News.com. All the leaders have fallen () are serving their sentence in Challapalca, the police chief stated in an interview with RPP. The Aragua Train has two main characteristics, adaptability and negotiation capacity. In Peru, we mapped them in 2017, and when the migration came in 2018, they began to occupy territories for human trafficking, Ávila added. However, it seems that nothing and no one can stop the Aragua Train in Peru, as the underworld has confirmed that the transnational criminal gang, which has already extended its criminal tentacles to Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Spain, Brazil, Panama, the United States, and Costa Rica, is still alive and maintains control over several illicit businesses in Metropolitan Lima. Prosecutor Mónica Cuñarro requested today the dismissal of Matanza Mayor Fernando Espinoza in the case for alleged sexual abuse against his former private secretary Melody Rakauskas. According to the prosecution's argument in an 80-page document to which Agencia Noticias Argentinas had access, Cuñarro's request is based on the fact that there are no elements of evidence in the case files to support the charges, beyond the statements of the complainant. After this presentation, the judge presiding over the case must decide whether to grant the prosecutor's request. The judge responsible for the case was Luis Schelgel, but he was replaced by Fernando Caunedo. The plaintiff had requested the case to be elevated to oral trial, and in response to that request, the judge asked for Cuñarro's opinion, who recommended the dismissal of Espinoza. Meanwhile, despite the prosecutor's request, Rakauskas' defense team may insist on the case being elevated to trial against the local leader. The former secretary of the Intendant of La Matanza was presented in 2021, when she accused him of having abused her in a meeting that took place outside of work hours. The Chamber of Crime had ratified, in July 2024, the prosecution of the Intendant for the crimes of sexual abuse and disobedience to a judicial order. Therefore, the case was left ready for trial. The accusation of disobedience is based on the fact that, despite having a restriction that prevented him from approaching, Espinoza would have contacted Rakauskas to ask him to cancel the complaint. The community leader has publicly expressed criticism towards his former secretary under the argument that she refused to deliver her cell phone and computer to be analyzed. Espinoza also stated that the complaint is part of a case of espionage against him.
