Every February 12, the International Day Against the Use of Child Soldiers is celebrated, also known as Red Hand Day, a date established by the United Nations (UN) to remember the need to end the dramatic situation faced by nearly 300,000 children and girls in at least a dozen countries in conflict. The UN Report, covering the period from 2017 to 2019, warns of a significant increase in attacks on schools and their military use. In the Central African Republic, at least 3,500 children are linked to armed groups, although the figure could rise to 6,000. UNICEF works to free them and reintegrate them into their communities. It is a difficult task, as groups like the Convention of Patriots for Justice and Peace or the Lord's Resistance Army have a strong presence in Central African Republic villages. That's why the children feel strongly connected to these forces, according to Evelyn Zembea, social worker. Ending it is a complex process that requires a commitment from the entire society. Returning to their lives and recovering their childhood is difficult, because child soldiers see their future cut off. When you are forced to go to war, it takes time to know that something else is possible, says Ismael Beah. I went through that. The worst consequences of using child soldiers Physical consequences can be caused by the battle itself or be a result of the tortures and abuses by their leaders. Many children are mutilated, suffer from malnutrition or even sexually transmitted diseases. In the case of girls, many become pregnant as a result of sexual abuse. Emotional trauma The fact of having witnessed terrible acts of violence or having had to commit them directly can haunt them if they do not receive psychological support. Many times the first act they are forced to commit is to kill their own parents to break the family bond. The difficulty of escaping the spiral of violence and returning home Because they spend the years of their development in the group or armed force, and learn to live in a hierarchical and violent environment. Because they do not know where their family and community are, and when they finally find them, sometimes the family rejects them because of their past, fearing they will be attacked or do not accept the girls when they return with children they have had during their absence. Because they have not been able to go to school, and this greatly reduces their opportunities for a better future. Source: UNICEF.

Raúl Asencio will remain under judicial investigation. According to recent reports, the Provincial Court of Las Palmas has decided to maintain the charge against footballer Raúl Asencio. The judge has rejected the appeal presented by the player, considering that there are sufficient indications of criminality against him. Asencio, who is being investigated for allegedly disseminating a sexual video involving a 16-year-old minor in 2023, will continue to be under legal scrutiny. The magistrate has dismissed the defense's arguments, pointing out that there are rational indications that the player may have committed crimes related to child pornography and invasion of privacy. The central defender of Real Madrid is one of the four players under investigation in this case. The other implicated players are Ferran Ruiz of Girona, Juan Rodríguez of Tarazona, and Andrés García of Alcorcón. Although Asencio's defense argued that the video in question was absent during the investigation, the Provincial Court has ruled that this does not imply that the file never existed. Furthermore, the testimony of one of the investigated parties asserts that Asencio showed him the video, which complicates his legal situation even more. Analysis of mobile phone records has revealed compromising conversations involving both Asencio and the other investigated parties, in which the accuser is treated with disrespect. The accused may face prison sentences of one to five years, depending on various factors such as consent in the recording and dissemination of the video. In the specific case of Asencio, if it is proven that he only disseminated the video without having recorded it, he could face a lesser sentence of one to three years in prison. The Asencio case will continue to develop in the coming months, while the Real Madrid player remains under judicial investigation.

In the tourist Cartagena, of cruise ships, of walled city with houses painted in colors that also wear the black women who sell fruits and fritters, the story of La Madame and her entourage of women seeking dollars from foreigners continues to resonate. Also read The abandoned mansion of Víctor Carranza, who ordered it to be built on the top of a mountain. Although the women selling their bodies no longer roam the popular sector known as the Clock Tower, Cartagena remains for many a city where sex tourism is on the table. Years ago it was an even more open business, that was offered almost to the wind. Liliana Campos Puello, who became known as La Madame, knew it and exploited it. For many years Liliana Campos Puello was one of the madams of prostitution in Cartagena. She was the one who ran the show in Cartagena in the purchase and sale of sex with premium tariff and VIP clients. The parties La Madame organized had all the ingredients for which they were paid very well: women, expensive liquors, exclusive houses, luxurious yachts, and endless nights. Under her hand, Cartagena became, mainly for foreigners, a frenzied party with beautiful women willing to do anything for her - it was a job, a source of employment, and a women-for-hire business. The end of the extravagant life and exotic parties ended in 2018. The justice investigations, in an operation called Vespa, turned her into La Madame. They followed the trail of her exotic parties. Tall men dressed as foreigners looking for women were used to infiltrate her operation. She was charged with three human trafficking crimes, conspiracy to commit a crime, and sexual exploitation. Also read: This is how the man who traveled 45 times to Medellín to commit abuses against minors was arrested in Miami. Liliana Campos Puello was sentenced to eight years. She was in La Picaleña prison in Ibagué, the capital of Tolima. Her husband, Gustavo Ruíz, her father, Carlos Campo, and two nephews also fell under Operation Vespa II. The super parties in Cartagena are over, the flow of foreigners decreased a bit. It was the end of the lucrative business of La Madame, who does not like the nickname they gave her. She spent six years in prison. In May 2023, she was released on probation for good behavior after serving three parts of the sentence. When she left prison, she gave an interview to Julio Sanches Cristo for W Radio and to Nena Arrazola for Los Informantes. She did not speak to the media again. La Madame claimed that in her business, there were no minors. According to her, there was no human trafficking or, much less, sexual slavery, as the headlines in the press had assured. I never locked anyone up. I never forced anyone. They were free women, she replied to Nena Arrazola, with a serenity built that is noticeable, built to a beat. The Madame went further and provided figures, as she said, each of the women who worked for her earned between 12 and 15 million in a week. In a month, they made double the salary of the President of the Republic, and she reiterated that her work was not to exploit the girls but to give them an opportunity. The beginnings of La Madame The story of Liliana Campos, the girl who was born in the humble neighborhood of Blas de Lezo, starts as an undocumented immigrant in the United States in the 80s. She crossed jungles and deserts to achieve the famous American dream. Getting entangled with people she shouldn't have led to more than two years in prison. She returned to Colombia and started selling perfumes, and little by little, she got involved in prostitution, not from the corner, but from an office. She became a sex entrepreneur. In the Crespo neighborhood, in front of the Prosecutor's Office, she had a two-story house where the women who worked for her lived. That's where the women who rotated parties on luxurious yachts, wedding companions, and other high-end parties, which included private chefs, DJs, sound rentals, cars, and boats, that ended with a happy finale, would enter and exit. The numbers were scandalous. A weekend could cost over 50 million pesos, and her clients paid without any problem. Dollars arrived with clients who came from the United States, Europe, Russia, China, and the Middle East, mainly. The Madame offered a showcase of dark-haired, blonde, natural, and operated women. After seeing the catalog, the offer and demand began. It was a market. It was a business. Although she has a few months left to pay her sentence, Liliana Campos walks through Cartagena with her head held high, even though she knows she has a stigma above her that labels her wherever she goes. Mrs. Madame, who now wants to dedicate herself to the clothing business, swears that she won't go back to the business that put her in prison. She assures, as a good local, that the prostitutes are still there, a bit more hidden, but they are there and now managed by other pimps because prostitution, the oldest profession in the world, has no end. Cartagena remains the same city it has always been, nothing has changed, only that now it has one less madame, but many new ones who are in the underground and take more precautions since Liliana Campos Puello was caught.

The Supreme Court confirmed the 8-year prison sentence for police officer César Daniel Carabajal for sexual abuse at a hospital in Río Grande. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation confirmed the 8-year prison sentence for police officer César Daniel Carabajal, found guilty of sexually abusing a young woman with hearing loss at the Río Grande Regional Hospital, while on duty. Judges Horacio Rosatti, Carlos Rosenkrantz, and Ricardo Lorenzetti dismissed the defense's appeal invoking Article 280 of the Civil and Commercial Procedure Code, leaving the 2022 sentence firm. The abuse occurred in two episodes within the hospital. Carabajal inappropriately touched the victim and subjected her to sexual access, using his police position and intimidating her with his official firearm. The victim reported the incident, and her testimony was validated in all judicial instances. In the verdict, Judge Edith Miriam Cristiano emphasized that the victim's statement should be analyzed with special attention, not only from a gender perspective but also considering her disability. The ruling was supported by Judges Cristiano, Carlos Gonzalo Sagatume, María del Carmen Battaini, and Javier Muchnik. The Superior Court of Justice of Tierra del Fuego had already rejected in August 2023 a cassation appeal from the defense. What do you think about this verdict? The Minister of Government (Security) of Bolivia, Eduardo Del Castillo, reported that the Police already have an order of operations to proceed with the capture of former President Evo Morales (2006-2019), whom he is accused of child trafficking for allegedly having impregnated a minor during his tenure. However, Del Castillo indicated that they are waiting for the coca leader to leave his political and trade union stronghold to carry out the operation. Morales is entrenched in the coca region of the Tropic of Cochabamba since the end of September, when it was known that there was an arrest warrant against him that later became ineffective due to a freedom of action. Since then, and in the face of growing rumors of his imminent arrest, the former president has not left the region where he enjoys the custody of his followers. Last year, the Deputy Minister of Interior Affairs and former General Commander of the Police, Jhonny Aguilera, stated that there was a security ring formed by community members to prevent Morales' capture. Mr. Evo Morales can leave the Cochabamba tropics as many times as necessary, Del Castillo stated, implying that there will be no intervention in the Cochabamba tropics. Until October 27, Morales was moving between different localities in the coca-growing region. However, that Sunday when he was being transported to the radio station where he broadcasts his program, he was intercepted by a police operation that fired at the vehicles he was in and injured one of his drivers, in an action that the coca leader characterized as an attempted assassination. The Government admitted to the shootout but attributed it to the fact that the former president's entourage bypassed a routine police checkpoint, ran over an agent, and opened fire on official vehicles. According to Minister Del Castillo, Morales is seeking to generate conflict and injuries if they try to detain him. He is looking for a police officer to lose their life or one of his sympathizers. We are not going to fall into that type of provocation, we already have the operation order and are just waiting for the moment and place to carry out the order issued by the Justice, he noted. The former president was charged with human trafficking for allegedly impregnating a minor in 2016. The supposed victim, who was 15 years old at the time, was part of a youth organization from the party called Generation Evo. According to the prosecutor's documentation, the young woman would have given birth to a girl in 2016, whom she registered as Evo Morales' daughter in a civil registry in the town of Yacuiba, bordering Argentina. The young woman's parents are being investigated for allegedly acting in complicity to obtain political favors. Since the case was exposed, neither Morales nor anyone from his entourage has denied committing the crime, but they have accused the government of being behind the case with the aim of eliminating him from the political scene. Morales was summoned twice to testify on October 10 and January 14, but did not attend. "Even if I were a fool, I would hand myself over," he said days later in his radio program. In response to his absence in January, Judge Nelson Rocabado ordered him to declare himself in rebellion, to be detained, to freeze his accounts, to record his assets, and to issue a new arrest warrant, which is currently in effect.

Anonymous Call Warns of Remains of Missing Woman Mother Tells Diario Extra Agents of the OIJ Found Her in 2 Different Places Selenia Alvarado, the mother of Kembly Dayana Calderón Alvarado, a 39-year-old woman who disappeared on January 27, said that an anonymous call alerted the Judicial Investigation Organization (OIJ) that her daughter was in danger. I didn't know anything about my daughter, they simply called me, came to my house, and told me that an anonymous call had warned them that she was in danger and that was it, she narrated. According to the woman, the last time she saw her was on Monday, January 27, 2025, after spending almost the entire day with her. She would sometimes leave for two to four days and then return, I rather thought she would be somewhere else. On Monday, January 27, she was here the entire day with me, until she washed up and everything, around 8:30 p.m. It was that she left, she said she was going to get something to drink and she never appeared again, she reported. Kembly Dayana has a 12-year-old son, who last year left school, according to the victim's mother. What struck me as odd was that her child was already going to school and was very excited about it, but when the classes started and he didn't appear, it seemed very strange, she added. The facts The Judicial Police reported on Monday that they found human remains in two different locations in Guápiles, which are presumed to be Calderón's. In the afternoon hours of Monday, judicial agents attended the appearance of what seemed to be a leg and an arm, this in the vicinity of Route 32 in Guápiles. They found a leg and two red sandals, as well as the apparent arm, the OIJ reported. Additionally, they added that hours later on the same day, they found other remains in a different location. At night, residents of the Foxhall Las Vueltas ravine reported a strong odor and a black bag containing what appeared to be a person's torso, agents arrived at the scene and lifted the remains, he added. According to the investigative police, these findings are related to Calderón. According to the red sandals, it appears that these remains belong to a woman who disappeared on January 27 (year not specified), this is preliminary, but apparently they belong to this person. In relation to this case, a home was searched last Friday, where bloodstains were found, which are being analyzed, the OIJ added. Randall Zúñiga, director of the judicial police, clarified that this is not a femicide, but a homicide. This involves a patient over the age of 18, who allegedly was a victim of sexual abuse, a fact that was reported to Judicial Unit Nº4 by hospital staff and the perpetrator, another patient. The Diario de Catamarca.com A presumed sexual assault, of which a woman over the age of 18 allegedly was a victim, who was hospitalized in the main hospital of the province. More precisely in the Mental Health area. A patient over the age of 18 reported being a victim of sexual abuse, a fact that was reported to Judicial Unit Nº4, as well as by hospital staff. The incident was known on Thursday, and the accused was another patient hospitalized in the same area. The investigation of the scandalous incident was entrusted to prosecutor Paola González Pintos, who ordered that the victim undergo the sexual abuse protocol. Additionally, a request was made to work on the search for evidence in the place where the alleged incident occurred, which would be a room in the Mental Health area. Victims of family and gender violence can contact the free hotline 144 or 911. The call is anonymous and available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

At the age of 10, I didn't know what I wanted to be when I grew up, but I was certain I didn't want to live the brutal violence that I was experiencing at home alongside my mother. Violence against women is normalized in various settings, including the home, workplace, community, or any other place. I still remember when I was the head of the Commission for the Development of Indigenous Peoples in the Huasteca region, Jesusa pushed her way through the attendees and told me desperately that her alcoholic husband physically abused her and forced her to give him the money she earned from washing other people's clothes. I noticed rage in her face when she told me that the day she went to denounce him to the community delegate, he responded without hesitation, "She's his wife, she has to put up with it." In an era where empathy is a scarce commodity, we must put ourselves in the victims' shoes. In addition to the pain and frustration of acts of violence, there is the indifference or complicity of authorities that only fosters impunity for the aggressors. Last week, for example, we were shocked by a video in which we saw a man, with absolute baseness, stalking a woman and, feeling like the owner of the situation, biting her buttocks. Certainly, that aggressor acted knowing that he would not have any consequences. And so it was initially. The victim filed a complaint with the Regional Prosecutor's Office, but they told her that nothing could be done, since there was neither robbery nor rape. It was thanks to social pressure that the aggressor was linked to a process days later. Another case of impunity is that of Oaxacan activist Sandra Domínguez, who in 2020 exhibited some chats, through which local officials and politicians shared sexual images of indigenous Mije women. Currently, the activist is considered missing and relatives point to Donato Vargas, the state coordinator of Delegados por la Paz, as the suspected perpetrator, who was defended by Governor Salomón Jara and was accused by the activist of participating in the chats. Impunity has reached the highest levels. A few days ago, we learned that Cuauhtémoc Blanco, former governor of Morelos and current federal deputy, was denounced for alleged rape against his half-sister, a relationship he denies. While President Claudia Sheinbaum warned that no one will be covered up, the local congress had already removed the prosecutor of the entity, who had requested Cuauhtémoc Blanco's immunity. Another case, equally grave, is that of Félix Salgado Macedonio, who was accused by Basilia Castañeda and five other women of sexual abuse, without being judged. Now, Salgado Macedonio pretends, without shame, to be the governor of Guerrero in 2027. Salgado Macedonio was protected by former President López Obrador, and now we will see if President Sheinbaum makes her phrases "we are all here" and "it's time for women" valid. The President has to decide whether to stand with the victims or with the aggressors. Having a female leader means nothing if, in the face of demands for justice against sexual violence, she only cares about guaranteeing political protection for her allies. Giving impunity to Cuauhtémoc Blanco and Félix Salgado is a moral defeat for the 4T. Final comment Instead of continuing to deny the accusations in press conferences, Cuauhtémoc Blanco should face the law without immunity, now that immunity no longer exists thanks to López Obrador.

Knowing more The former head of the Miraflores Fire Department Company, Ángel Castro Verástegui, 44, has been denounced by at least six female firefighters for sexual harassment, unwanted touching, and in one case, a suspected sexual assault when they were his subordinates and, in some cases, minors. In a resolution issued on December 16 of last year, the XXIV Departmental Disciplinary Council - Departmental Command Lima South suspended Castro Verástegui temporarily from service as a preventive measure while the internal investigation is being developed to protect the allegedly aggrieved and not expose or re-victimize them, nor hinder the investigations. However, sources from this newspaper question that measures were only taken now, despite previous complaints dating back to 2018. The document, to which El Comercio had access, is based on two cases that allegedly occurred in 2024, when Castro Verástegui was still the Chief of the Miraflores 28 Fire Company (he held the position until December 4th last year). The two accusers, whose names will be kept confidential, accuse him of sexual harassment when they were applicants and were 17 and 15 years old. There are sufficient indications of the commission of the alleged offenses committed, which link the accused as the presumed perpetrator of the same. In the present case, initially, documentary evidence, reports, and other means of proof were offered, notes the resolution signed by the three members of the disciplinary panel (Brig. CBP Jorge Luis Paulet Bobba, Brig. CBP Klaus Talaverano, and Brig. CBP Javier Erken Bosmans), in which it is also specified that the means of proof presented should be expanded and substantiated. For this purpose, hearings have been held with the accusers and the accused, in order for them to present their defenses. The alleged infractions referred to in the resolution are 6 serious and very serious disciplinary offenses included in the Disciplinary Regime Regulation of the CGBVP (E1) Failure to perform the duties of a Volunteer Firefighter as prescribed in Article 16 of the RIF Internal Regulations of Functioning, whose aggravating circumstance will be considered as a serious or very serious offense if as a consequence of this action, any damage was generated to the service or to the image of the CGBVP (E8) Executing acts in CGBVP establishments that offend decency, morality, or good customs. Aggravating Circumstance: If the act implies the violation of another person's intimacy, the offense will be considered Very Grave (E18). Coercing, threatening, or intimidating CGBVP personnel, denigrating, offending, or mocking someone hierarchically inferior to them. (E20) Abuse through proposals, touchings, or analogous acts that threaten the subordinate's sexual liberty hierarchically. (IM4). Force the hierarchically inferior to perform acts alien to the service or contrary to personal or institutional decorum, and (IM10) Abuse of hierarchy denigrating severely the human dignity of the subordinate. Although Castro Verástegui currently holds no position within the institution, the temporary suspension of service prohibits him from participating in any activity of the Volunteer Firefighters General Corps. Three days after the provisional measure, in another resolution of the Departmental Disciplinary Council XXIV, the internal investigation is expanded with the testimonies of four additional alleged victims. In this document, the most serious case is added due to the alleged sexual assault of a minor, which supposedly occurred in the department of Angel Castro Verástegui. In the first of this group of new accusations, a young woman accuses him of violating acts that would attack decency, morality, and good customs (E8), of harassing through proposals, touching, or analogous acts that would threaten the subordinate's sexual freedom (E20), and of forcing a subordinate to perform acts unrelated to their service or contrary to personal or institutional decorum (IM4). Another firefighter reports that the accused had actions and behaviors that made her feel aggrieved, exposed, vulnerable, ashamed, and defenseless, requesting that the relevant actions be taken to safeguard the principles of her integrity and respect within the institution. The third testimony adds that she had previously submitted her complaint to the Instruction Department of the Miraflores company without any action being taken. Finally, the most serious case involves a young woman who allegedly was a victim of sexual abuse by the accused in circumstances of alcohol consumption when they went to a social gathering while she was still a minor. One of the young women, whose name is being kept confidential, told this newspaper that they hope this case will set a precedent so that specific, written protocols can be established to prevent and address sexual harassment. There is no clear protocol for this type of complaint. Being in a hierarchical institution, with a slightly military structure, people of higher rank exercise certain power over us, and it is more difficult for us to be heard. The harassment is often justified as being just jokes. We want an area where this type of complaint can be channeled, she said. According to her account, two years ago, a situation of harassment was reported against one of the applicants by the same accused, but she believes that at the time it was not handled properly. The complaint was not escalated to the departmental level, it was tried to handle everything internally, he was changed to a new position, but they didn't explain why. We only got a lecture from a psychologist to raise awareness, but we felt extremely unprotected, without support, he added.The Comercio contacted Ángel Castro Verástegui on January 9, 2025, to request his defense through an in-person interview or in writing. After two postponements by the accused, on January 27, the meeting finally took place, but Castro did not want to be recorded on video or audio, nor did he want his statements given at that time to be included in this note. Previously, he also did not agree to send his defenses in writing as requested via email.This newspaper notes that in the January 27 meeting, Castro assured that the accusations against him are false and that he would take legal action if they are published. In addition, he showed screenshots of alleged chats with the six complainants, with which he claims to prove that there was communication only for work-related topics. However, he did not want to send us the conversations, which he assures are proof of his innocence, nor be published by this newspaper. Moreover, via email, he stated that the facts he is accused of are false and out of context, and that the complaints are intended to damage his image and his 22-year career in the Peruvian Volunteer Firefighters Corps. Furthermore, this newspaper requested information from the General Command of the Firefighters on specific protocols and directives that prevent or adequately address complaints related to sexual harassment or bullying. The image area sent us the Disciplinary Regulation, published in 2018. The reference to this document's complaints of touching and harassment is the table of sanctions, which indicates that it is an infraction to abuse through propositions, touching, or analogous acts that threaten the sexual freedom of a subordinate hierarchically. Sources from this newspaper indicated that the Departmental Disciplinary Council XXIV held three hearings on the case, one of them to gather Castro's defenses, but he did not attend. The resolution should be given within 15 days. After that, the defendant could appeal. However, last Monday, all members of the Departmental Disciplinary Council who saw the case were changed. The complainants fear that this will influence the final decision. The Minister of Women and Gender Equality, Luz Vidal, referred to the sexual abuse and rape complaint filed against Deputy Jorge Durán (RN) on Tuesday. In this regard, she informed that the National Service for Women and Gender Equality (SernamEG) is taking the necessary actions to address the case. Also read: Deputy Eduardo Durán receives threats From the ministry, the complaint was classified as serious and assured that measures are being implemented to provide support to the complainant, respecting her will at all times. LEGAL MEASURES AND SUPPORT According to La Tercera, Minister Vidal recalled the importance of the Antonia Law, which provides guarantees to victims within the framework of due process and the rule of law. Among these guarantees are the early taking of testimony, the prevention of revictimization, and the protection of the identity of the victims, explained Vidal. In addition, institutions are committed to protecting the complainants and ensuring they have access to psychological and legal support. The ministry also reaffirmed that it will continue to monitor the case and remain attentive to any new measures required to protect the rights of the affected individual.CONFRONTATIONAL POSITIONSAfter the complaint became public, deputy Jorge Durán denied the accusations and claimed that the relationship was consensual. He also asserted that the complaint is an attempt at extortion by his former partner. On the other hand, the complainant addressed the media to reject Durán's statements. She assured that the parliamentarian is lying and detailed the alleged threats she had received from him. The case has generated a strong impact in the political and social sphere, while authorities insist on the importance of ensuring the protection of victims and conducting an impartial and thorough investigation.

A Man Identified for Committing Sexual Abuse Against Young Neighbors' Children in Puertollano Faces Six-Year Prison SentenceA man identified for committing sexual abuse against the minor children of his neighbors in Puertollano, who were 13 and 10 years old at the time of the incidents, has admitted his guilt. As a result, he will face a six-year prison sentence for two counts of sexual abuse.The man has admitted to committing abuse, initially targeting the 10-year-old girl who had a 48% psychological disability at the time of the incidents. During this time, he performed intimate touching on her.The man admitted this before the First Section of the Provincial Court of Ciudad Real after reaching an agreement that reduced the initial request for a one-year prison sentence presented by the Prosecution. Upon accepting the facts, the sentence was finally established at six years. He acknowledged that, after assaulting the girl, he attempted to assault her brother. However, the child managed to escape and immediately alerted his mother, who then proceeded to file the relevant complaint with the National Police's Child Protection Unit. Concha Marín has commented that in the weeks leading up to the incidents, the man managed to gain the trust of both the children and their mother. On several occasions, he offered to pick up or drop off the children from school and also to take them to his home to play.The perpetrator has admitted to the charges. A.C.C. will face a six-year prison sentence for committing two counts of child sexual abuse. In addition, he will be ordered to compensate each of the minors with 8,000 euros for the moral damages caused. After serving his prison sentence, the individual will be prohibited from approaching minors or establishing communication with them for a period of ten years. Additionally, he will be barred from engaging in any work or activities that involve regular and direct contact with minors for a period of 15 years.

On November 26, the Chamber of Deputies approved a set of key reforms to Chile's Migration and Foreigners Law, modifying more than 56 articles of the current legislation. These changes have a significant impact on immigrants' access to employment and labor rights in the country, as well as addressing public safety challenges and regulating migrant flows. The approved reforms in Chile's Migration and Foreigners Law have a profound impact on the country's labor and social landscape. While aiming to improve security conditions and control migrant flows, it is essential that labor and migration policies be developed in a coherent manner to prevent immigrants from being excluded or vulnerable in accessing fundamental rights such as employment and labor stability, notes Pamela Toro, Apparcel Uriarte's director of law. Regarding the new regulations and their impact on the labor world, the professional highlights the following points: Immigration Reforms New Grounds for Deportation and Strengthening of Labor Regulation. One of the most significant modifications in the labor field is the strengthening of the powers of the National Migration Service to revoke migrant permits in cases of convictions for repeated offenses in areas such as disturbing noises, altercations, and street vending. These measures aim to promote harmonious coexistence in neighborhoods and public spaces, which may have a direct impact on those immigrants who are in the informal sectors of the labor market. Although the measure aims to preserve social peace, it is essential that the effects of this regulation do not harm informal workers who rely on these jobs for their livelihood. Impact on Immigrants' Access to Employment The reforms also have implications for immigrants' access to formal employment. Expanding the grounds for deportation to include individuals involved in serious crimes such as domestic violence, sexual exploitation, and the illicit trafficking of migrants aims to improve public safety in the country, but could generate fears in some immigrant communities. It is essential that labor policies be accompanied by strategies that ensure foreign workers have equitable access to formal job opportunities, without being affected by situations of vulnerability or discrimination due to their migratory status. Another important aspect of the reform is the implementation of severe sanctions for individuals, companies, and transportation means that promote or facilitate the irregular entry of immigrants into the country. In this context, companies that hire immigrants without proper documentation may face consequences if they fail to comply with the new regulations. Therefore, employers must be particularly vigilant in meeting the legal requirements to avoid sanctions that could jeopardize the operation of their businesses and affect the labor stability of migrant workers. This does not change the fact that, if the company has hired an informal worker, it must equally pay the corresponding social security contributions, without exception, explains Fernando Carreño, labor lawyer of Apparcel Uriarte.Requirements for naturalization and access to labor rightsThe reforms also include changes to the requirements for naturalization, which now require a ten-year residency period (instead of five) and a knowledge test. This adjustment could delay immigrants' access to full labor rights that are acquired with nationalization, and raises the need for additional measures to ensure that immigrants can enjoy their labor rights in the country while these requirements are met. Given the impact of these reforms on the labor integration of immigrants, the role of the legal area is more relevant than ever. Specialized labor lawyers are crucial to ensure that the rights of migrant workers are respected, especially in a context where regulations can generate uncertainty or confusion. Their work is not only essential to advise immigrants on their labor rights and obligations, but also to ensure that companies comply with the legislation and prevent them from being involved in discriminatory or illegal practices. It is crucial that the reforms to the immigration law not only ensure public safety and order, but also guarantee access to a dignified job, without discrimination, and protect the rights of migrant workers, adds Pamela Toro.

According to official data, since 2015, there has been a decline in the eradication of that illicit crop. Last year, compared to 2014, the reduction was 99.4 percent. The decrease in the surface area coincides with the reduction in the price paid to farmers for Acapulco opium gum, Acapulco, Guerrero, February 12, 2025. In 2024, the sowing of poppy in Guerrero was minimal, proof of this is that the Army destroyed only 42.65 hectares of land cultivated with this plant in 2014, the surface eradicated was 7,529 hectares, and the figure for the last year represents a reduction of 99.4 percent, and reflects that probably the total surface area planted with that illicit plant also decreased in the same proportion. The Secretariat of National Defense (Defense) made public the data on the destruction of illicit plantations in Guerrero, one of the Army's functions. Although official information does not account for the total area planted with coca leaves, only the destroyed area is reported, it is valid to establish a relationship between both, if the personnel, resources, and plans allocated to this task are maintained. A Freedom of Information request by El Sur to the Army reveals that the constant decline in the numbers has been ongoing since 2015, when 4,517,924.1 hectares were destroyed, and in 2016, the area fell to 375,800.2 hectares. This decrease occurred in the context of the decline in the price of opium gum due to the arrival of fentanyl in the US drug market, and the implementation of the Sembrando Vida program, whose main objective was to encourage farmers to stop cultivating illicit crops by promoting legal products. However, it was reported in El Sur on Monday that peasants from the Sierra region have returned to plant this illicit crop due to the surge in the price of poppy gum, also known as opium gum, which is used to produce heroin, and the uncertainty surrounding the continuation of the federal Sembrando Vida program, which could indicate a change in the trend of the last few years. El Sur reported that the price of poppy gum paid to peasants in the Sierra region reached its lowest level in 2024, at 2,000 pesos per kilo, before 2018 when 18,000 pesos were paid per kilo of gum, and in that year it dropped to 3,000. The eradication of plantations is an official statistic indicating a part of the total area planted. The Army was asked for information on the destruction of opium plantations by community and municipality, but replied that it only has information by municipality. From 2014 to 2024, the Army destroyed 93,924 poppy plantations in 14,780.8711 hectares in Guerrero. However, since the second year of this period, a constant decline in the destruction of plantations has been observed.In 2014, 48,108 plantations were eradicated in 7,529.2611 hectares of poppy, of which 1,964.2705 hectares were registered in Heliodoro Castillo. This municipality in the Central region concentrated 26% of the total production, while the second municipality with the highest production was San Miguel Totolapan with 1,442.8995 hectares.In 2015, the eradication fell to 30,295 plantations in 4,517.9241 hectares. The following year, it plummeted to 1,715 poppy plantations in 375.8002 hectares.In 2017, the hectares of poppy destroyed by the Army totaled 497.4801, with 2,285 plantations, and the following year rose to 509.3844 hectares with 3,191 plantations. In 2019, opium eradication efforts fell to 1,817 plantations sown in 303.5113 hectares distributed across various municipalities of the state, in 2020 they decreased to 1,667 plantations in 269.4767 hectares, in 2021 they rose to 1,525 plantations in 288.9036 hectares, in 2022 they increased to 2,572 plantations in 380.8582 hectares and in 2023 they reached only 446 plantations eradicated by the Army. In 2024, 303 opium plantations were eradicated in 42.6527 hectares, which were mainly distributed in the municipalities of Heliodoro Castillo, where 15.5709 hectares were reported, similar to the 16.8832 hectares in San Miguel Totolapan. The drop in opium price and Sembrando Vida El Sur published a report on Monday that quotes Sierra peasants who are in uncertainty about the continuation of the Sembrando Vida program and in some areas at least 40 percent of the peasants returned to planting opium due to the possible closure of borders to fentanil and other synthetic drugs, in contrast to what happened during the government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, when only one out of every 10 peasants continued to cultivate the illicit crop due to the drop in price. Additionally, the price of the kilo of opium gum has improved from 2,000 pesos mid-last year to 6,000 or 8,000 pesos currently. Consulted on the matter, the regional delegate of the Sierra Government, Saúl López Sollano, told El Sur this Tuesday that the poppy has not stopped having a market, not even due to the proliferation of fentanyl, and stated that the farmers of the Sierra have not stopped planting it by tradition, by culture, and even for the ornamentation of their patios. In February 2018, El Sur was the first medium to report on the fall in the price of opium gum, after the Sinaloa Cartel began distributing fentanyl in the United States, considered 50 times more potent than heroin, which is processed with opium gum extracted from the poppy. Fentanyl is one of the reasons for the health crisis in the northern country with thousands of deaths from overdose and one of the many flags of the current President Donald Trump to argue in favor of the militarization of the border and the search for other forms of intervention to stop the trafficking of this synthetic drug from Mexico. In response to the economic crisis caused by the fall in the price of opium poppy, the federal government established the Sembrando Vida program to eradicate the cultivation of that crop and incentivize other legal crops with a monthly payment, and as has been documented in these pages, farmers did indeed stop planting opium poppy when they entered the program. In a workshop conducted by the Grupo de Estudios para el Desarrollo del Sur (GEDESUR) in April 2023, a farmer from Cuatro Cruces, in the municipality of Ajuchitlán del Progreso, shared her testimony of having been a poppy cultivator, "I used to be that, I used to live off it. Maybe it's a sin, but I'm done with it now. Before I didn't know how to harvest a pine tree, pine seeds, and now I know how to plant a pine tree. I've struggled and my little plants have grown." Guerrero, among the first places of opium poppy cultivation UNODC The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, in English) published several joint reports on opium poppy cultivation monitoring, funded by the Mexican government, using a methodology based on satellite photos that allowed for the closest quantification of cultivation, but consistent with the general trends in eradication made by security institutions. The reports documented the evolution of opium poppy cultivation during the government of Enrique Peña Nieto and the first half of the administration of Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In the 2017-2018 report, it is noted that the results of this study and the national eradication data from the government show that the main areas of opium poppy cultivation are located in the state of Guerrero, Nayarit, and the Golden Triangle (Sinaloa, Chihuahua, and Durango). However, reports of a decrease in the area of opium poppy cultivation in the country were already being made, as the area decreased from 30,600 hectares in 2016-2017 to 28,000 hectares in 2017-2018, still higher than the 25,000 hectares reported in 2015-2016. The 2018-2019 report indicates that the national area sown with opium poppy is 21,500 hectares, representing a 23% drop compared to the same period the previous year. The destruction of opium poppy in 2019 was 11,844 hectares, a 50% decrease compared to 2018, and the international agency suggests that the reduction in the area of opium poppy destroyed, as well as the 60% reported decrease in destroyed plantations, may be due to a lower number of operational personnel available for opium poppy destruction activities, this being because the Army, the entity responsible for eradication, contributed a large number of operational personnel to the National Guard to guarantee public safety. In addition, it argues that it is essential to consider the role that new psychoactive substances have played in the criminal markets. Since they usually imply a higher profit margin compared to other substances such as opioids, they would be more attractive to criminal organizations. In its latest report for 2019-2020, published in October 2022, the UNODC reports a one percent decrease in the eradication of plantations with the same argument as new psychoactive substances. It also reports a 12 percent national increase to a total of 241,000 hectares planted, analyses suggest that the pandemic has caused an increase in economic difficulties, which would probably make the cultivation of illicit drugs more attractive to fragile rural communities. data.text: Convicted in Jaén to 30.5 years in prison for raping his two minor granddaughters under 18 for 4 years 21 Hours, 18 Minutes Infobae.comSports Convicted in Jaén to 30.5 years in prison for raping his two minor granddaughters Jaén, 11 Feb (EFE). The Third Section of the Jaén Court has sentenced Pedro G. R., a 64-year-old man, to 30.5 years in prison for raping his two minor granddaughters over a period of four years, starting when they were 6 and 10 years old. According to the ruling sent from the High Court of Justice of Andalusia, the man has been convicted of two continuous sex aggression crimes with intimidation, penetration, and exploitation of kinship, for which he has been sentenced to 15 years in prison. He has also been sentenced to three months in prison for a crime of child abuse and another three months for a crime of possession of child pornography. The sentence also imposes, as an accessory, the prohibition of communicating or approaching within 300 meters of the girls for ten years above the prison sentence once served, as well as ten years of supervised freedom and one year of deprivation of the right to possession and carrying of arms. In terms of civil liability, he must indemnify each of the minors 50,000 euros for the moral damages and harm caused to the two girls. The accused, for whom the Public Prosecutor's Office had requested 36 years of imprisonment, has been acquitted of two continued crimes of threats, of two crimes of psychological injuries, and of the light crime of injuries for which he was accused in the cause. The facts, which were judged last January, date back to May 2018 and extended until January 2023 when the minors were ten and twelve years old. According to the prosecution's account, the accused took advantage of his familial relationship and the numerous occasions he was alone with his granddaughters at home to rape them. To keep the girls silent, the grandfather told them that if they said anything, he would kill them, their mother, and his wife, causing an absolute state of fear in the younger girls, who did not dare to tell anyone until February 1, 2023. The accused has also been convicted of a separate episode of child abuse, where he grabbed one of the girls forcefully by the shoulders and pushed her against a wall in a public street. A mobile phone belonging to the accused was seized and, upon analysis, was found to contain child pornography images of a minor and a video of his four-year-old grandson naked, in which the accused asks the child to dance. During the trial, the defendant claimed innocence, although the verdict considers proven that the defendant repeatedly raped his granddaughters, taking advantage of their family relationship and the numerous times he was alone with them since their parents left them in his care while working. According to the sentence, he used intimidation and threats to overcome the resistance the minors might have presented to the execution of the sexual acts, to the point of threatening to kill their mother and grandmother if they reported anything.

The Metropolitan Police of Santa Marta, under the command of Colonel Jorge Bernal Granada, reported the capture of 49 people during the second weekend of February. According to the authorities, 40 of those detained were caught in the act and 9 were apprehended by court order, for various crimes, as stated in the official report of the National Police. Within the framework of these operations, the authorities seized 2,200 grams of drugs and recovered 10 cell phones that had been stolen in several sectors of the District in previous months. Additionally, the uniformed officers of the Quadrant Surveillance Units issued at least 150 summonses in various urban areas of the city. Also, the police agents managed to seize 3 firearms that did not have the corresponding documentation for their possession, as well as ammunition of different calibers. In other actions against theft, 9 motorcycles were recovered. IN PREVENTIVE MATTERSIn a ceremony held at the facilities of the Metropolitan Police Command of Santa Marta, 57 new police auxiliaries swore to defend the flag and the laws of the Republic. Additionally, they will reinforce the security and citizen coexistence service in the city. During their training, they received training in key topics such as constitutional law, penal regime, police procedures, correct use of firearms, ethics, and values.On the other hand, the Ciénaga National Tourism and Heritage Protection Group in Magdalena carried out different preventive activities against the Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Children, Adolescents, and Girls (ESCNNA), with the aim of guaranteeing the safety and well-being of minors. Finally, the Gaula Police Group conducted preventive campaigns and registration and control plans directed at the commerce sector and the general community in the public market square of Santa Marta. During the activity, security recommendations were offered and the different modalities of extortion and kidnapping were made known.

The Roman Catholic Diocese of Prince George, B.C., says it expects a $3.4 million settlement to provide a degree of restitution to a purported victim of sexual abuse by a schoolteacher for the unjust harm inflicted by their abuser. The settlement between the diocese and St. Thomas More Collegiate, a Catholic school in Burnaby, B.C., was announced in a statement released by lawyer Sandra Kovacs, who represented the anonymous plaintiff in the lawsuit. Also named in the lawsuit was former teacher Alfred Patrick Quigley, whom the anonymous plaintiff alleged was sexually abused by him in the 1990s. Quigley taught at O'Grady Catholic Secondary School in Prince George and it was said that one of the alleged assaults occurred at St. Thomas More Collegiate. The lawsuit accused Quigley of grooming the plaintiff before sexually assaulting him in 1993 and 1994. Quigley denied each of the allegations in his response filed in court, but did not participate in the case as it approached trial and could not be contacted for comment through his former lawyer. The allegations were not proven in court and Quigley, now 75 years old and believed to live in Newfoundland, has not been criminally charged in B.C. Although neither the Diocese nor the School had knowledge of the wrongdoing that occurred in the 1990s, they have acknowledged and accepted vicarious legal responsibility for the actions of their employee in these circumstances, a statement released by the diocese said on Tuesday. We hope and pray that this resolution will allow (the plaintiff) to continue their healing process and that this healing will extend to all victims of abuse. The lawsuit stated that Quigley was unusually friendly and attentive with the plaintiff, and took them to sexually charged movies such as Basic Instinct The lawsuit also alleged that Quigley took the plaintiff under his protection, gave him gifts, took him on nighttime trips, and taught him how to play squash at a facility where they would shower or go to a steam room naked together. Quigley has been named in other lawsuits filed in the B.C. Supreme Court in 2024 that contain similar allegations that have yet to be heard or resolved. Kovacs said that the settlement was reached just before the case was scheduled for a 23-day trial in the B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver, and although it offers his client financial restitution, the lawsuit was also about accountability. This man operated as a master for decades, Kovacs said. What we're seeking is to hold the system accountable. Kovacs said that most of his practice now involves working with survivors of institutional abuse, and cases related to the Catholic Church involve a culture of secrecy. That culture of secrecy and clericalism, the idea that priests and men of the cloth are superior to laity, creates, I believe, a systemic problem that allows this abuse to occur and continue occurring, he said. That's a problem that needs to be addressed functionally at its root in the church, and that still hasn't happened. The diocese and O'Grady Secondary School denied the allegations of sexual preparation and aggression in their response to the lawsuit, and also denied allegations of systemic negligence and deliberate blindness. The plaintiff stated in a statement that he continues to recover from the trauma he suffered, but is now more hopeful than ever that other survivors of abuse will speak as they move towards healing and meaningful justice.

In 2020, Eulalio Lalo Gomes sought the intervention of the then Minister of the Interior, Euclides Acevedo, to achieve the house arrest of Anderson Ríos Vilhalva, detained in the framework of Operation Alba. Leaked conversations reveal that Gomes requested help to influence the judge and the prosecutor in the case, without success in an initial attempt. However, weeks later, Anderson Ríos Vilhalva obtained his release in another case, this time linked to a 2017 human trafficking case. The order for release was signed by Judge Carmen Silva, who also appeared in conversations in other controversial cases, such as the Cachorrão case. The exchanges between Gomes and Acevedo began on September 16, 2020. Gomes inquired about the latest developments in Ríos Vilhalva's situation, who was being held in Coronel Oviedo prison. One day later, on September 17, Gomes sent Acevedo a photograph with the request to review the measures of the case Óscar Duarte and others on criminal association, in which the modification of precautionary measures was requested. On September 18, Gomes informed Acevedo that the judge had rejected the request and mentioned that an attempt had been made to dialogue with Judge Gustavo Amarilla. Acevedo did not respond at that moment. However, on September 21, Acevedo resumed the communication and mentioned that the judge in question had permission until the following Monday. In parallel, Gomes maintained conversations with attorney Myrian Mendoza, in charge of defending Vilhalva. In these messages, Gomes indicated that the first request for review had been rejected due to a confusion and that they had to present a new writ on Tuesday, following Acevedo's recommendations. On September 27, Acevedo wrote to Gomes to remind the lawyer that the document was due to be presented the following Tuesday. On September 30, Gomes indicated that the lawyer had suggested speaking with prosecutor Marcelo Pecci to avoid him opposing the request. Acevedo replied that Sandra was handling the matter. Gomes insisted on the importance of speaking with the prosecutor, calling it special, and Acevedo agreed with the assessment. Finally, the hearing took place on October 1, 2020, without the presence of the prosecutor due to investigative commitments. However, Anderson Ríos Vilhalva's request for freedom was rejected. Despite this setback, on October 24, 2020, Gomes informed Acevedo that they had managed to secure Ríos Vilhalva's release in another case. We got the friend out of Oviedo's, Gomes wrote, to which Acevedo replied Dale pues, my dear brother. This release was made possible through Judge Carmen Silva, who signed the resolution in a human trafficking case in which Ríos Vilhalva was also being prosecuted. The conversations reveal attempts at influencing judicial processes and the intervention of political actors in decisions that should have been resolved within the strictly judicial realm.

Two individuals arrested by the Police are of Guatemalan nationality. They are accused of human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Two Guatemalan immigrants were arrested in Lake Worth Beach, Florida, on charges of human trafficking and sexual exploitation after a victim managed to make a desperate call for help, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in the United States. The call that led to their arrest The 9th of February, around 7:45 a.m., a young woman called the police stating that she was being held against her will and had been a victim of sexual assault. Fearing for her life, she provided limited details about her location, which led the agents to track her call and find a house at the 1400 block of Lake Ave that, according to the authorities, was actively being used as a brothel and was part of a larger human trafficking network. The Yudvin and Glin Zunigalatin brothers face multiple charges, including Human Trafficking, Prostitution Exploitation, Operating a Brothel, and Resisting Arrest. Glin Zunigalatin also faces additional charges of Aggravated Armed Assault and Sexual Assault. Both suspects are being held without bail and have been placed under ICE immigration detention. The police continue to investigate the case, which may be linked to a larger human trafficking ring.

San José, February 12 (Elpaís.cr). At the beginning of February, a video that circulated on social media in Costa Rica shocked the population. In the streets of San José, the capital city, a motorcycle approaches a car and the passenger in the back seat shoots the occupants at point-blank range, killing the two people inside the vehicle. The brutal act, linked to narco-trafficking according to the police authorities, is a reflection of the growing wave of violence that is sweeping the country, traditionally known as the Switzerland of Central America for its political stability and natural beauty, as highlighted by the French newspaper Le Monde on Tuesday, February 11. However, in recent years, Costa Rica has been dragged into cocaine trafficking, transforming from a transit country to a key logistical hub for exporting drugs to Europe. Shift in the Narcotrafficking in Costa RicaCosta Rica, a country without an army and with a long tradition of peace, has historically been a point of transit for narcotrafficking. However, in recent years, its role has evolved. Evelyn Villarreal Fernández, a researcher with the State of the Nation program, a research center created by the country's five universities, explains that the drug arrives by boat or plane from Colombia and other Andean countries, to be subsequently re-exported to Europe. Cocaine is hidden in shipments of emblematic agricultural products of the country, such as pineapples and bananas, Villarreal explained in an interview with the French newspaper Le Monde, which published a comprehensive report on the subject. The report highlights that since 2019, European port authorities have seized 88 tons of cocaine originating from Costa Rica, mainly in the ports of Rotterdam (Netherlands) and Antwerp (Belgium), where shipments of fruit arrive. This drug flow has turned the country into a logistical hub for narcotics trafficking, with local criminal gangs that have established alliances with international organizations, including Mexican cartels, Colombian cartels, and European mafias. The infiltration of cartels in the Tica mountains. In September 2024, the US newspaper The New York Times had already warned about how Costa Rica's lush tropical rainforests were being used by narcotics cartels to map out clandestine routes and evade authorities. The criminal organizations have taken advantage of the lack of equipment and resources of Costa Rica's security forces to operate with impunity. Randall Zúñiga López, general director of the Judicial Investigation Body (OIJ), explained to Le Monde that these new actors have unleashed a wave of violence They wield greater firepower and flood the country with drugs, some of which are sold locally, increasing conflicts between criminal groups. According to authorities, more than 70% of the homicides committed in 2024 are related to score-settling between narco-trafficking organizations. Historic homicide rate Between 2023 and 2024, Costa Rica recorded its highest homicide rate in history, 17 per 100,000 inhabitants, double the rate recorded a decade ago. This increase in violence is directly related to narco-trafficking, which has unleashed a territorial war on the coasts and in San José. In addition to homicides, criminal organizations are involved in other crimes, such as sexual exploitation and the trafficking of species and precious woods. Mauricio Boraschi, assistant prosecutor of the Public Ministry, explained to the French media that international criminals identified two advantages in Costa Rica, both established in the country's Constitution: it has no army and does not extradite traffickers to the United States. These characteristics, combined with the lack of maritime and aerial resources to monitor borders, have facilitated the operation of cartels in Costa Rican territory. Lack of resources One of the biggest challenges Costa Rica faces is the lack of resources to combat drug trafficking. Law enforcement forces do not have the necessary technology, equipment, or personnel to confront the criminal organizations, which operate with sophistication and violence. Additionally, the Government has not prioritized this issue, allowing the problem to worsen. The Le Monde report highlights that, despite the efforts of the authorities, the lack of coordination and resources has limited their ability to face the crisis. The country lacks an integrated strategy to combat narco-trafficking, a French analyst quoted by the newspaper stated. This has allowed criminal organizations to strengthen and expand their operations, not only in drug trafficking, but also in other illicit activities. Costa Rica, internationally renowned for its biodiversity and commitment to sustainability, faces a significant challenge in terms of its international image. The country has been promoted as a safe and attractive tourist destination, but the growing violence related to narco-trafficking could affect its reputation. Tourism is one of the main sources of income for the country, and any negative impact on its image could have severe economic consequences, warned a tourism expert consulted by Le Monde. Threat to the future The situation in Costa Rica is a reminder of how organized crime can infiltrate and transform even the most stable countries. Although the country has managed to maintain a solid democracy and a high level of human development compared to its neighbors, the growing influence of criminal organizations represents a significant threat to its security and future. To face this challenge, it is essential for the Costa Rican government to prioritize the fight against organized crime, invest in resources and technology for law enforcement, and strengthen international cooperation. Furthermore, it is necessary to address the underlying causes of violence, such as inequality and lack of opportunities, which can make some citizens more vulnerable to recruitment by criminal organizations. Costa Rica is at a crossroads. If urgent and effective measures are not taken, the country risks not only losing its reputation as the Switzerland of Central America, but also the security and peace that have cost so much to build. The time to act is now, before violence and narco-trafficking continue to erode the foundations of this nation.

The Supreme Court upheld a conviction against a police officer who sexually abused a young woman while on duty at a hospital. During the trial, the convicted defendant claimed there was consent, but the argument was rejected at all levels. RIO GRANDE (Judicial and our editorial staff). The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation upheld the conviction of eight years in prison for a police officer for having raped a young woman who suffers from hearing loss and has difficulty speaking. The justices of the country's highest court, Horacio Rosatti, Carlos Rosenkrantz, and Ricardo Lorenzetti dismissed the defense's argument by invoking Article 280 of the Civil and Commercial Procedural Code. It all happened in the bathroom of the Regional Hospital Río Grande, Tierra del Fuego, while the accused was performing tasks related to his public service duties. The indictment charges him with having sexually abused and in two occasions, through indecent touching, as well as through carnal access. In the trial, the accused did not deny the facts, but spoke of consent and asked for acquittal. This is the case of the Recurso de hecho deduced by the defense in the Carabajal, César Daniel and another sURLabuso sexual simple in concurso real, where Fernando Carabajal was convicted in 2022 for simple sexual abuse in concurso real with double aggravation of sexual abuse with carnal access. The indictment charges him with having sexually abused and in two occasions, through indecent touching, as well as through carnal access. In the trial, the accused did not deny the facts, but spoke of consent and asked for acquittal. Through appeals, the case reached the Superior Tribunal of Justice of Tierra del Fuego, which on August 25, 2023, rejected the cassation appeal of the defense. Background of the caseOn Monday, October 3, 2022, the Court sentenced César Daniel Carabajal to 8 years in prison for, in a first incident, touching B's intimate areas, kissing her, touching her breasts, and sucking her nipples, and in a second occasion, touching her intimate areas and penetrating her vagina with his penis, all without her consent, taking advantage of B's disability, her position as a police officer, and intimidating her by holding his hand towards his regulation firearm. The judges of the Court classified the behaviors as simple sexual abuse in concurrent real action with sexual abuse with carnal access, both aggravated by being committed by police personnel in the exercise of their functions. The resolution includes the reasoned opinions of judges Edith Miriam Cristiano and Carlos Gonzalo Sagatume, to which judge María del Carmen Battaini and judge Javier Muchnik adhered, making the decision unanimous. Judge Ernesto Löffler does not sign the ruling as he is on leave on the day of the Acordada. In her vote, Judge Cristiano expressed: I consider the sentence imposed by the Criminal Trial Court of the Northern District Judicial Court to be well-founded, as the conduct attributed to Carabajal against B has been sufficiently proven, beyond any reasonable doubt. Ultimately, I do not observe any lack of motivation or arbitrariness in the arguments that support the sentence. The Magistrate observed that it is evident that the controversy lies exclusively in the consent that B may or may not have given, as the defendant's hypothesis claims that the named person's behavior on that day led Carabajal to believe that both were maintaining intimacy by mutual agreement. However, the victim reported the incident, confirming that she was abused by force and her account was consistent throughout all instances of the investigation. In the ruling, Judge Cristiano notes that the experts reported not observing any element during the expert activity that would lead them to consider the account as not credible. She also emphasized that the victim maintained, in essence, the same version of events in front of all her interlocutors from the complaint to the oral debate and that her account even coincides with the accused's version. Additionally, taking into account that the victim suffers from bilateral neurosensorial profound hearing loss, which represents a permanent partial (45%) inability to perform her usual tasks, Judge Cristiano held that her statement should be analyzed with special attention when she is a woman, as it must be judged with a gender perspective, and in this case also with a disability perspective.

Sexual abuse in Santiago has a 13-year-old who gave birth after being pregnant by a 62-year-old man. The girl said that her aunt's partner was abusing her with the complicity of her family. The minor indicated that the attacks occurred three times a week. A grave case of child sexual abuse occurred in Santiago del Estero, where it was known that last weekend, a 13-year-old girl entered the hospital pregnant and about to give birth. After giving birth, the little girl reported that her aunt's partner was abusing her and that her family was complicit in what was happening. The case was made public on Saturday and according to police sources, on that day a minor of legal age entered the Colonia Dora Hospital and, after being examined by a doctor, was sent to the Añatuya Zonal Hospital, where it was discovered that she was in labor. The girl had a 2.9-kilogram baby who was born at term and in good health. The police interviewed the minor's aunt after the incident, who is currently implicated in the case, and explained that she has been living with her since she was 2 years old. The aunt stated that she was unaware that her niece was pregnant. The minor provided more details, stating that her aunt forced her to be locked in with her partner, a man identified as R.C., who abused her. She said that this happened three times a week. The prosecutor in charge of the case, Alejandra Sobreso, ordered the case to be investigated as repeated sexual abuse with carnal access. She also ordered a police report, interviews with the obstetrician and the minor's aunt, a medical report, and a pre-psychological interview. The Liberal reported that the accused are a 62-year-old municipal employee and his 26-year-old partner, who, upon learning of the charges, sent a message to a relative denying the facts. The police arrived at their home in the Las Trincheras neighborhood and both were taken to the Icaño local police station. Previous incident A similar episode occurred in January of last year in the city of Saladillo, when it was reported that a 13-year-old girl gave birth to a baby at the Alejandro Posadas zonal hospital. Following the incident, the prosecution was investigating the mother and her partner. Horror in France, a woman left her 13-year-old daughter to starve to death as a form of revenge against her ex.

The World Day Against the Use of Child Soldiers, also known as the Day of the Red Hands, is commemorated on February 12th of each year. Its objective is to raise awareness about the use of children and girls in armed conflicts and to promote actions for their protection and reintegration into society.Origin of the Day of the Red HandsThe Day of the Red Hands was born as an initiative of various international organizations to bring to light the terrible reality that thousands of minors live in the world. The date of February 12th was chosen because on that date in 2002, the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child relating to the participation of children in armed conflicts, promoted by the UN, came into force. The use of the image of red hands symbolizes the rejection of child recruitment and the demand that all countries comply with international treaties to protect childhood. What does it mean to be a child soldier? A child soldier is any minor under the age of 18 who is recruited or used by state armed forces or non-state armed groups, whether as a fighter, spy, messenger, ammunition loader, cook, or even in some cases, victims of sexual exploitation. Recruitment can be forced through kidnappings or voluntary, due to poverty, lack of opportunities, or social pressure in conflict zones. Current situation Despite international efforts, thousands of children and girls continue to be recruited in conflict-affected countries, such as in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. According to UN data, at least 50,000 children have been used in armed conflicts over the past two decades. What is being done to help? There are several programs and international agreements to eradicate the use of child soldiers. The UN and UNICEF work on the rehabilitation and reintegration of children who have been victims of forced recruitment. The Paris Agreement (2007) A commitment signed by over 100 countries to end the use of children in war. Awareness campaigns such as Red Hands Day On this day, activities are held in schools, public events, and demonstrations to demand an end to child recruitment. How can we help? To help in the fight against the use of child soldiers, we can take several actions Inform ourselves and disseminate the reality that millions of children and girls live in armed conflicts, so that more people become aware. Support organizations that work on protecting children in war zones, such as UNICEF, Save the Children, or Amnesty International Demand governments and international organizations to strengthen laws and measures against child recruitment. Participate in campaigns like the Red Hands campaign, which aims to raise awareness about the issue and push for solutions. Promote education and development in vulnerable communities to reduce the conditions that lead many children to be recruited.
