The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) decided to open a disciplinary incident for verification of compliance with the conditional regime against retired Colonel Jorge Enrique Galarcio Medina of the Army. This measure responds to alleged facts of sexual exploitation of a 14-year-old minor, a situation that could compromise his benefits within the transitional justice system. The disciplinary incident was opened after the remission of a file from ordinary justice that points to Galarcio Medina for being linked to a case of pimping with a 14-year-old minor. Decision ARA035 of 2025, issued by the Chamber for Recognition of Truth and Responsibility of the JEP, details that the facts occurred between April and June 2019. However, the document clarifies that there is no exact date for the events involving the former military officer. Now you can follow us on Facebook and our WhatsApp Channel. According to the authorities, Galarcio Medina had previously appeared before the JEP on two prior occasions for his alleged participation in extrajudicial executions that occurred in the Meta region, although in those processes he did not acknowledge any responsibility. Nevertheless, the situation took an unexpected turn when, in November 2020, it was known that Galarcio had been captured under the alias JorgeMega, accused of leading a sex trafficking ring for children. The Prosecution has evidence that Galarcio used social media, such as Facebook and WhatsApp, to coordinate sexual activities with minors.  Jesus Áviles Infobae Colombia According to the documentation provided by the Prosecution, the former official also faces charges for the crime of using social media to offer sexual activities with minors. This criminal process is being carried out in the 29th Criminal Court of the Circuit with Functions of Knowledge in Bogotá, and preliminary and preparatory hearings began in 2021. In the findings of the accuser's office, it is stated that the retired colonel of the Army would be at the head of a network of child sexual exploitation that operated through Facebook and WhatsApp. According to the evidence collected, the Prosecution obtained nearly 100 anonymous messages, which were stored on a compact disc (CD) and delivered to investigators. These messages, detailing the illegal activities, served as crucial evidence to reach Galarcio Medina. Despite being initially detained in 2020 with a preventive detention measure, Galarcio Medina was released on November 22, 2022, due to the expiration of judicial terms, which has raised questions about the duration of the process and the accused's legal guarantees. Near 100 anonymous messages were found, serving as evidence in the case. Image reference Infobae The JEP has emphasized in Auto ARA035 that the objective of the compliance verification incident is to determine whether the former military personnel violated the agreed-upon conditions for their permanence in the transitional justice system, particularly regarding the prohibition of committing crimes after December 1, 2016, the date the Final Peace Agreement was signed. In this context, if it is confirmed that Galarcio Medina has engaged in new criminal activities, he could lose the benefits granted to him by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, and even be excluded from it. The disciplinary incident will open a stage in which the parties involved, including the defendant's defense, the Public Ministry, and the victims, will have five days to submit new evidence or make observations. Subsequently, the judge's office of Magistrate Alejandro Ramelli Arteaga will decide whether Galarcio Medina has infringed the conditional regime. The JEP is evaluating whether Galarcio violated the conditions agreed upon for his stay in the transitional justice system credit Lina GascaThe complexity of this case highlights concern for impunity and the vulnerability of victims within the Colombian justice system, especially in contexts where authority figures, such as military members, may be involved in crimes of such magnitude.

Legal Reversal Orders Arrest of Evo for His Defense, It's Illegal The legal defense of Evo Morales suffered a judicial setback. This follows yesterday's developments in the crowded case of human trafficking filed against him, when the 5th Anti-Corruption and Violence Against Women Investigating Court in Tarija issued an order for his apprehension. Thus, the arrest and transfer mandate, coded as N 010UR, signed on February 11 by Judge Nelson Alberto Rosales Rocabado, orders the Special Force for the Fight Against Crime (FELCC) to apprehend the former president. Morales, who has been sheltered by his loyalists in Lauca Ñ for more than 100 days, is under the Justice's microscope for the alleged commission of the crime of human trafficking, as a result of a complaint that reports he maintained a relationship with a minor while he was president. ANOTHER BLOW TO THE EVISMO MOVEMENT And it is that the First Chamber of the Tarija Departmental Justice Tribunal (TDJ) rejected and declared the appeal presented by the former president's legal team inadmissible. This, after on January 17, and for the second time, Morales did not appear to appear in court in Tarija. From Sucre, the State Prosecutor General, Roger Mariaca, explained that the Justice did not grant the appeal formulated by Evo's defense. He added that after this appeal demand was resolved, and in view of the existing declaration of rebellion issued on January 17, what remains is to execute the arrest warrant. We are waiting for this to be determined by the judicial authority and for the Bolivian Police to start working, who are responsible for executing the said warrant, Mariaca pointed out. With this new ruling, Morales now has three arrest warrants. The first one is scheduled for October 16, 2024, the second for January 17, 2025, and the third for February 11.DEFENSE OF EVO In response, lawyer Cecilia Urquieta, part of the former president's legal team, stated that the process is in an incidental stage and that the arrest order is illegal. To this, it is added that Morales was not notified of the ruling. It has been requested that the incidents we have raised be taken into account. We are in an incidental stage because that arrest order and all those irregular and illegal actions that have been carried out, have not been officially notified to Mr. Evo Morales in Cochabamba, he maintained. The jurist demanded the presence of international observers to follow the case. From the ranks of evism, his loyalists described the action as part of a political persecution. Senator Leonardo Loza, one of the first to express himself, indicated that this ruling responds to political and electoral decisions. He assured that they do not fear the arrest of the former president. Any process, sooner or later, fabricated, organized, digitized, and managed politically by this government, will eventually fall, he emphasized. On the other hand, the deputy affiliated with the coca leader, Romina Gómez, classified the order as illegal and political. Earlier, the legal defense of the coca leader pointed to the government of Luis Arce as executing a black plan against him, which was strengthened since September 26, 2024, and resulted in 11 processes and complaints. In contrast, the vice president of the Creemos bench, Efraín Suárez, assured that imprisoning Morales is something just since he committed many crimes, not only against minors, but also electoral crimes. For the rector of the Autonomous University Gabriel René Moreno (UAGRM), Vicente Cuéllar, the judicial determination should not surprise, since justice must fulfill its role However, he assured that the former president enjoys protection from the Justice System and the Government.

BOLIVIA Justice Orders Arrest of Former President Evo Morales for Aggravated Human Trafficking The judicial situation of Bolivia's former president, Evo Morales, has significantly escalated in recent weeks. The Tarija Departmental Court of Justice has taken a major step by rejecting the appeal presented by Morales' defense, thereby validating the arrest order that weighs against him. Judge Alberto Rocabado, in issuing the resolution, points to a grave accusation of aggravated human trafficking and statutory rape with a minor. The origin of this case dates back to 2016, when it is alleged that Morales, as president, had a relationship with a minor with whom he later had a child. This situation has led the Court to declare him in contempt after failing to attend two scheduled hearings in a recent period. The defiance, as clarified in the ruling, is a response to the defendant's behavior for failing to comply with judicial procedures without a legitimate justification. Moreover, tensions have increased with statements from the Minister of Government, Eduardo del Castillo, who asserts that the Police have a strategy to proceed with the capture of Morales and will wait patiently for the accused to show their presence outside of Chapare, their known political stronghold.Evo Morales, surrounded by a politicized environment, defends himself by accusing the current government, led by Luis Arce, of executing a political persecution in order to prevent his participation in the August elections. Despite the accusations, Morales maintains that without a victim, there is no crime, referring to the alleged victim in his case. A complex and costly backdrop for the Movement for Socialism (MAS), the party to which both leaders belong, presents internal tensions that reveal fundamental differences in the country's political and administrative direction. Morales faces severe restrictions on his activities, with a ban on leaving the country and measures that limit his assets. Meanwhile, his supporters continue to organize to prevent his apprehension, protecting his figure and future political prospects, and the Convulsive Electoral Horizon of Bolivia foresees prolonged tensions for the Movement for Socialism and the country as a whole.

data.text: Agents from the Violence Against Women Section of the Judicial Investigation Body (OIJ) carried out an operation in various points of San José to dismantle a criminal gang dedicated to human trafficking for sexual exploitation. According to Randall Zúñiga, OIJ director, the operation includes six raids in sectors such as Barrio Escalante, Curridabat, Pavas, Rohrmoser, and Ciudadela 25 de Julio. Zúñiga stated that in total, nine people involved in the criminal organization are being sought for arrest, including the organization's leader, who is already apprehended. The leader, Morales, a 35-year-old man, has already been detained. The director of the OIJ also mentioned that efforts are being made to apprehend the woman of this person, 31 years old. The criminal organization, according to the investigations, was dedicated to recruiting women under the pretext of offering therapeutic massages, but once the victims arrived at the locations, they were forced to offer explicit sexual services to clients. The leader and his partner allegedly established an entire criminal organization that recruits women to appear to provide some type of therapeutic massage. However, once the people arrive, it is clearly no longer just a therapeutic massage, but also an explicit sexual service offered to clients as such, explained Zúñiga. Additionally, the OIJ director stated that the women involved in this crime were forced to perform these acts under threat of fines or penalties if they refused. The people being treated here, the women, are being forced to carry out these types of actions, under the threat of paying a fine or some type of compensation for not carrying out these actions, Zúñiga added. This operation is part of the OIJ's efforts to eradicate human trafficking in Costa Rica and combat this serious social problem. Zúñiga reaffirmed the institution's commitment to protecting women and fighting against sexual exploitation. With this, the commitment to all women in the country is reaffirmed to try to eradicate this serious problem, concluded the OIJ director. The operation continues in progress, and more arrests are expected in the coming hours.

The Supreme Court reduces Ángel Boza's sentence by one year, a member of La Manada, under the "only yes means yes" law. Two of the five Sevillian members of the WhatsApp group La Manada convicted of a continued crime of group rape during the 2016 Sanfermines, José Ángel Prenda and Jesús Escudero, have requested the Second Section of the Navarra Audiencia to reduce their sentences under the Integral Guarantee of Sexual Freedom Law, known as the "only yes means yes" law, which has led to over a thousand sentence reductions due to the unification of sexual abuse and assault crimes into a single type and the legislative maximum that in case of a collision between two penal norms of different temporal validity, the most favorable sentence for the defendant must be applied. Let us recall that initially, the young Sevillians from the WhatsApp group La Manada, who were processed for this case, were sentenced by the Navarra Court to nine years in prison each for a sex abuse crime, but later the Supreme Court (TS) revoked the initial sentence and sentenced all of them to 15 years in prison for a continued rape crime against the victim of the facts. Subsequently, the Navarra Court initially dismissed the request of the convicted Ángel Boza to reduce the prison sentence from 13 years and nine months to the convicted Ángel Boza, thanks to the Law 10/2019 of Integral Guarantee of Sexual Freedom, known as the "only yes means yes" law, but later, the Superior Justice Court of Navarra agreed to the defense's request, reducing the prison sentence to 14 years.

Guatemala City, Feb 12 (AGN). At the Campo de Marte, Vice President Karin Herrera presented the National Plan for the Prevention of Sexual Violence Crimes, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking, as well as the work of mobile units for the Prevention of Sexual Violence Crimes, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking (Univet) 2025. Reaffirming her commitment to eradicating these problems, the Vice President stated: It is a way to protect the lives of Guatemalan women and men. Each victim is a person with dreams and rights, and it is our duty as a state to ensure they receive justice and support. We know that eradicating these crimes is a massive challenge that requires the will and commitment of As part of this initiative, the Secretariat against Sexual Violence, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking (SVET) developed a strategic plan with the aim of coordinating institutional efforts in the prevention, protection of victims, and punishment of these crimes. The National Plan for the Prevention of Sexual Violence, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking prioritizes among its axes the following: 222 municipalities, 15 of greater incidence 30 community facilitators 22 departmental facilitators In addition, it aims to train and inform over 296,753 children, girls, and adolescents 161,865 adult women 80,932 adults in mixed groups 1,800 educational centers With this, the plan aims to reach around 539,550 people in the 22 departments of the Republic of Guatemala by 2025, with a focus on minors. Continuing to take a firm step in the fight against Sexual Violence, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking, we present two key initiatives. The National Prevention Plan for VET crimes will focus on training and awareness-raising. @SVET (secretariasvet) February 12, 2024 Univet As for the Univet, SVET aims to reach 97 prioritized municipalities and 20 departments this year, with 9 units across the country, of which 6 are in border areas. Through these units, the entity brings information and reporting services for sexual violence, exploitation, and human trafficking crimes to vulnerable communities. The objectives set out aim to train and inform approximately 113,850 people in 20 departments of the Republic of Guatemala. Divided into 62,618 children, adolescents, and girls, 34,155 adult women, and 17,077 adults in mixed groups. Refer to more than 100 vulnerable individuals for their protection. Reach 450 families with the school for families program. In total, SVET plans to reach 653,400 people through the National Plan for the Prevention of Sexual Violence, Exploitation, and Human Trafficking Crimes and Univet this year. The implementation of these measures aims to ensure that no case of violence is forgotten and that each victim receives the support and justice they deserve.

Organized Crime Ring Forced Young Women to Engage in Sex for $10,000It is estimated that at each massage parlor, there were 16 sexual encounters per day. Christian Montero, 12/2012The organized crime ring operating massage parlors in San José forced women to engage in sexual encounters for $10,000. Located in high-value areas of San José, six massage parlors concealed the illicit business of sex services. One of them, for example, was located in the Escalante neighborhood, behind the Santa Teresita church and surrounded by restaurants and other businesses. Agents from the specialized section on gender violence, human trafficking, and illicit migrant trafficking, along with the Prosecution, raided the six massage parlors in the afternoon on Wednesday. In the 25 de julio city in Hatillo, they raided the home of the crime ring's leader, Morales, a 32-year-old man, and in Escalante, they detained a 29-year-old woman named Ureña, who was the administrator of the last-mentioned location. According to the investigation, the criminal organization generated weekly earnings of 6 million colones. Each woman forced into sex work received a payment of 10,000 colones per encounter. It is estimated that 16 sexual encounters occurred at each location per day. The couple leading the group advertised massage parlors on the Telegram messaging app under the name Confort. Through catalogs, they offered young women access to the locations, and victims were recruited for dates. Following the raids, five women with the last names Godínez, aged 29, Vargas, 19, Barboza, 28, Picado, 39, and Ugalde, 31, were detained. The accused were seized with 1 million colones in cash, 12 cellphones, four vehicles, three computers, two tablets, and documentation related to the investigation. Additionally, 15 women were rescued, who were being forced to provide sex services and are now considered victims.

US actor Kevin Spacey faces another sex abuse lawsuit in the UK, more than 18 months after he was acquitted of all charges in a high-profile criminal trial. The 65-year-old was sued civilly in London's High Court on Wednesday, according to court records. The AFP agency reported that the lawsuit was brought by a former actor, according to information from his law firm. The lawsuit also names the London theater Old Vic, where Spacey worked as artistic director around 2003. Spacey, who faces another lawsuit in London over alleged sex abuse, was unavailable for comment. During his criminal trial, Spacey, who has always denied allegations of sexual misconduct, said that three of the complainants in the criminal case had also filed civil lawsuits against him. I assume full responsibility for my past behavior and actions, but I will not take on or assume responsibility for or apologize to anyone who has fabricated things about me or exaggerated stories about me, he said in a televised interview last year. It was not possible to speak with the Old Vic immediately to make a statement. A spokesperson for the law firm representing the plaintiff confirmed that a lawsuit had been filed. Spacey, an Oscar winner for American Beauty and The Usual Suspects, was one of Hollywood's biggest stars before being accused of sexual assault for the first time in 2017, after which he was removed from the TV drama House of Cards. In 2023, he was tried at Southwark Crown Court in London, accused of sexually assaulting four men in the UK between 2004 and 2013, and was acquitted on his 64th birthday.

Caracas, February 12, 2025. The FBI and federal authorities dismantled a criminal organization dedicated to human trafficking in central Tennessee, allegedly led by members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Eight people were arrested and face charges for sexually exploiting women brought from Venezuela and other Latin American countries under false promises of employment and better opportunities. On February 11, the Acting Attorney General, Robert E. McGuire, and the Nashville Police Chief, John Drake, confirmed the arrests at a press conference. The victims, according to the indictment, were forced to work under exploitation conditions through debts exceeding the cost of their travel. The operation was part of a joint investigation between the FBI, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), and the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department. According to the federal indictment, the defendants recruited vulnerable women from Venezuela, Colombia, and other countries, promising them help to migrate to the US. However, upon arrival, they were subjected to sexual exploitation. The victims were coerced and forced to engage in sex with strangers for the benefit of the accused, federal prosecutor McGuire stated. According to local media outlet The Tennessean, two of the detained individuals are linked to the Aragua Train gang, known for human trafficking, extortion, and narcotics trafficking. They used their affiliation with the gang to intimidate the victims and execute the illegal smuggling of individuals for a profit. The Aragua Train gang, originating from a Venezuelan prison, has expanded its operations to several countries in Latin America and, most recently, the US. In July 2024, the US Department of the Treasury The gang was cataloged as a transnational criminal organization, highlighting its role in illicit activities such as human trafficking and money laundering. According to prosecutors, the network operated between July 2022 and March 2024, recruiting vulnerable young women in several countries. Once in the U.S., the victims were subjected to excessive debts and forced into commercial sex acts. In some cases, they were even exploited after being paid. The identities of the detained, all Venezuelans, include five women. Charges include conspiracy for interstate transportation for prostitution purposes and facilitating organized crime businesses. Some face additional charges for sexual trafficking, which could result in a life sentence. Prosecutor McGuire did not clarify if undocumented victims could be deported, but emphasized the importance of them being able to testify without fear of reprisal.

Federal Police officers arrested a father and his son in the locality of Gregorio de Laferrere and González Catán, who are accused of sexually abusing a minor. The case originated when the victim, upon reaching adulthood, filed a criminal complaint in which she claimed to have been outraged during her childhood by who was her stepfather at the time. The incidents occurred in the family home located in the locality of Gregorio de Laferrere between 2010 and 2012, and at times when the victim was 5 and 6 years old. According to the testimony, the abuses occurred while the victim was in the care of her mother's partner, who subjected the girl to various sexual practices and threatened her with death, forcing her to remain silent. In this way, he managed to remain unpunished. Over time, between 2016 and 2017, she and her mother moved to another residence, where she was once again a victim of sexual abuse, but this time by the primary aggressor's son, who was her mother's partner. By the end of January, after the corresponding complaint had been filed, the Specialized Unit for Instruction and Judgment in Family Violence and Gender Violence and Sexual Integrity Crimes N1 locally ordered the relevant investigation to be carried out to make the arrests of those involved effective. Both detainees were placed at the disposal of the intervening magistrate for the crime of Gravely Degrading Sexual Abuse committed against a minor under 18, taking advantage of the situation of cohabitation and having been committed by the person in charge of the guard, in ideal concurrence with aggravated corruption of a minor.

Amnesty International (AI) denounced on Wednesday that criminal gangs in Haiti are recruiting, attacking, and raping minors, as part of a crisis that is becoming increasingly grave. According to a report from this organization, more than one million children and girls live in areas controlled by criminal gangs or under their influence. The criminal gangs have caused widespread anguish in Haiti, as they threaten, beat, rape, and kill children and girls, stated Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of the organization. Sexual exploitation of girls The members of the criminal gangs have kidnapped, raped, and sexually assaulted girls during attacks on neighborhoods or after taking control of areas, according to AI. The organization noted in its report that attacks on girls who go out onto the street are common, and they also deliberately attack them in their homes. Similarly, members of the criminal gangs sexually exploited girls in relationships and for commercial sex, Amnesty International added, documenting the cases of 18 minors who were raped and subjected to other forms of sexual violence by the out-of-law groups. Ten of them suffered gang rape, the report added, indicating that some became pregnant and several resorted to unsafe methods to attempt to interrupt the pregnancy because abortion is illegal in Haiti. Survivors face different obstacles to accessing justice, amidst the impunity that plagues Haiti, where 5,626 people died in 2024 as a result of the actions of criminal gangs (1,000 more than the previous year), 2,213 were injured, and 1,494 were kidnapped. Many of the minors interviewed, the report added, did not intend to report the aggressions suffered to the authorities due to the absence of police forces in areas controlled by criminal gangs. A girl who was kidnapped and raped by several members of a criminal gang in 2023 and who suffered another sexual aggression by a member of a criminal gang in 2024 told AI: "There is no police. The only authority in the area are the gang members."

data.text: Since his return to the White House, Donald Trump has intensified massive deportations using ICE as a tool of repression. RAYA spoke with Professor and researcher Justin Akers Chacón, who analyzes the evolution of this armed agency, the process of criminalizing migrants, and the resistance strategies adopted by the affected communities. By Enrique Gamboa, Journalist, Revista RAYASince he returned to the White House, Donald Trump launched a national immigration control operation to expel undocumented migrants from the United States, mainly of Latin American, Arab, and Muslim origin. At the forefront of this persecution is the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE, for its English acronym), an armed agency created in 2003 as a response to the September 11 attacks against the Twin Towers in New York. Their work consists of carrying out immigration control through raids and arrests against these communities. ICE manages a budget of around $9 billion and has over 20,000 employees, of which 8,000 are dedicated to deportation operations. As of February 7, more than 8,000 people have been deported from the country, according to figures from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). One of the agency's missions is to deport convicted immigrants, however, it can also arrest any undocumented migrant. In fact, White House spokesperson Karoline Leavitt stated that the Trump administration considers all undocumented immigrants to be criminals. The drug traffickers, the rapists, the murderers, and individuals who have committed heinous acts within our country should be the top priority of ICE, but that doesn't mean that other undocumented criminals who have entered our nation's borders are off the table. Although the growing persecution of immigrants is filling the headlines of Latin American news, this policy has been pushed, in a radical way, since the administration of Bill Clinton, through those of George Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump, and Joe Biden. It is expected that in Trump's second term, measures will be hardened even further. On the history of repression against migrants in the United States, there have been texts explaining its forms and consequences. One of those books is called "No One Is Illegal," written by Mike Davis and Justin Akers Chacón, which covers episodes of racism and state violence, from conquest to the present. In the section on Trump and the failure of neoliberal immigration reform, the authors warn about the radical anti-immigrant measures that began in Donald Trump's first government and continued during the Biden administration. According to Davis and Akers, at that time, changes were made to the known immigration regulations, known as guidance memos, which expanded the powers of ICE to arrest and deport undocumented individuals. Additionally, they were given authorization to act on their own initiative, without restrictions or supervision.RAYA spoke with A at the beginning of the 1990s, Akers Chacón moved to southern California where she pursued her university studies in Chicana/o Studies, focused on the historical and cultural studies of Mexicans and Latin Americans in the history of the United States. There, she witnessed the construction of the border wall being built to divide the United States from Mexico. The strategy called Operation Gatekeeper, driven by Bill Clinton that radicalized border persecution, was designed to force people to cross the border through deadly terrain. This operation, which Justin Akers Chacón says did not stop migration, but made it deadlier, was the starting point for joining activism and supporting the causes of undocumented people, who represent 5% of the workforce in the United States. His interest in immigration policies did not stop there, so he became a researcher, writer, and professor of migration phenomena at San Diego City College, where he teaches the Chicana and Chicano Studies class. What is the main risk faced by immigrants in the United States Inside the country, the greatest risk they face today are the ICE raids and attacks against Mexican and Latin American communities. Trump has given orders for the ICE to have a more visible presence inside the country, especially in states and cities with policies protecting undocumented migrants, known as sanctuary cities. He also revoked an order that prohibited the ICE from making arrests at schools, hospitals, and churches. During the Biden administration, ICE actions were more restricted and less visible to the public, although the rate of detention and deportation was high. Biden spent his last year approving a more restrictive border policy and Kamala Harris campaigned to restrict immigration. They were trying to show that they could be just as tough on immigrants and refugees as Trump. This only legitimized Trump's false claims of a border crisis and that migrants and refugees are a threat. It has created an atmosphere where he is waging war against migrants and refugees. Apart from a greater application of the law, this climate creates the risk that fascist individuals and groups will attack migrants and support far-right politicians in pushing for more restrictive and punitive policies and laws. How migrants in the United States are organizing to face the measures of the government of Donald Trump In the last week, we have seen protests across the country, mainly in migrant communities, where their families and supporters have taken to the streets. In some cases, businesses have closed in support of the protests. In San Diego (California), more than 5,000 people marched through the city center this week against ICE, Trump, and deportations. There are several types of organizations that are forming in response to what is happening. One of them is the national or ethnic association that organizes community and cultural activities, but they can also become organizing networks Other organizations are human rights organizations that pressure politicians to apply legal reforms. There are also left-wing political groups and small socialist organizations that support and align with immigrants from a class struggle and defense perspective. In some communities, these groups organize vigilance against ICE actions and rapid response protest networks. What tools do immigrants have to defend themselves against the policies of the United States government At this point, there are very few tools available. There are human rights groups and migrant and refugee rights groups that are filing lawsuits to try to get federal judges to suspend the executive orders issued by Trump. Apart from that, there are community organizations within migrant communities to monitor the ICE and respond to raids with public protests. Community members are being educated on their rights and how to respond to ICE agents if they appear at their homes, workplaces, or in public areas. This is the most violent immigration policy of Donald Trump's compared to his first term. While raids and deportations terrorize and displace immigrant communities, the situation has changed since his last administration. In 2017, Trump began dismantling the asylum-based immigration policy through the Remain in Mexico policy. Those who continued to seek asylum were arrested en masse, charged with illegal entry, and sent to makeshift prisons and concentration camps. In this process, families were separated, and thousands of children were detained in deplorable conditions, with untrained personnel and little supervision, resulting in numerous incidents of abuse, neglect, and sexual violence. In his first term, Trump attempted to expand and strengthen the border wall, but faced significant opposition from some unions that threatened to hold massive strikes and protests in major cities across the country. So far, we are not seeing the same level of opposition in his second administration, which means things could get worse. What are the main differences between Trump's first and second terms in terms of immigration policy? Trump's second administration is unfolding in very different circumstances. Politics in the United States have shifted to the right within both parties, and both Democrats and Republicans have adopted harsher anti-immigration stances. I would say, based on polls and other evidence, that this political shift is happening much faster among the ruling class than among the general population. With such a terrain, and with less formal opposition, Trump and the far-right majority of the Republican Congress have had more room for action and tools to cause more harm. How far can Trump's persecution of immigrants go? The goal of this new wave of attacks is not to expel all immigrants, but to target and deport only a small percentage to instill fear in the rest. It is a state strategy to have greater control over a significant portion of the country's workforce. There are states where the situation is more complicated for immigrants. The intensified attack on migrants operates at the federal, state, and municipal levels. Therefore, there is a geographical variation in terms of repression. Things are worse in the Midwest and Southern states of the United States, where the far right and the Trump wing of the Republican Party dominate. There needs to be a legal context placed on a 1996 law approved under Bill Clinton's administration, which allowed municipal governments to work with federal immigration agents to pursue, detain, and arrest suspected undocumented immigrants. This policy, known as 287G, is in effect in 135 cities across 21 states, primarily in the Midwest and South. Thanks to this policy, there has been a wave of punitive state laws passed in recent years, leaving immigrants in some areas even more exposed and repressed. Texas and Florida have two of the most anti-immigrant state governments. However, from a federal level, the Trump administration has shifted the majority of ICE activities to liberal states and cities as a form of political retaliation. This assault on migrants can be compared to another period in history. In terms of scale, yes. There were two previous periods against immigrants in which large-scale deportations were carried out. One was at the beginning of the Great Depression in 1929, where the US government deported up to two million Mexicans over the following decade to blame immigrants for the economic crisis. After that, the United States deported more than two million Mexican citizens, between 1953 and 1955, as part of Operation Wetback, a Cold War repression that used police, the military, and immigration agencies to repress unionism led by the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO). The CIO began to organize Mexican working-class populations, blacks, and other racially segregated groups in the labor movement and against racial segregation policies and practices. The State used selective roundups and deportations to counter and undermine the efforts. However, the largest scale of repression against immigrants has been institutionalized since 1996. The federal policy approved at that time, again under the Democrat Bill Clinton, greatly expanded the scope of the State to deport undocumented immigrants. Since then, the average number of deportations has increased significantly, from 300,000 to more than 2 million deportations each year. Which communities are most affected by Trump's new immigration policy ICE command centers are established in the 50 states of the country, but operations are concentrated in the industrial and agricultural regions of the southern region, where larger populations of Mexican, Latin American, and African working-class immigrants are concentrated. This reflects the racist nature of immigration law enforcement. The creation of racial profiles has been legalized by previous Supreme Court rulings, allowing ICE agents to direct the majority of their repressive operations against Mexican and Latin American communities. Although up to a third of undocumented individuals are Europeans, Canadians, Australians, the practice and enforcement of immigration law are primarily directed towards these specific groups crossing the border from the south. Latin American governments can take joint measures to protect the migrant population. I believe there are limitations to what Latin American governments can do directly. The US government has dedicated years to building an international infrastructure and regional integration for immigration law enforcement. The U.S. ICE and U.S. Border Patrol now operate on an international level, with associated operations in many countries, including Mexico and parts of Central America. The United States allocates resources, primarily arms, surveillance technology, and training, with the aim of militarizing immigration law enforcement along corridors from South America to the U.S. border. It was inspiring to see Colombian President Gustavo Petro and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confront Trump regarding the treatment of deported and returned migrants, and even present countermeasures to Trump's tariff threat. However, due to economic risks, they could only react to Trump and attempt to reduce the damage of the deportation process, but would not risk going further. What are the main human rights being violated for migrants? Important human rights are being violated For example, death from exposure when forced to cross the border through a deadly terrain. There are many documented cases of Border Patrol and ICE agents committing acts of violence and sexual abuse against migrants in custody. There have been reported murders and aggressions, as well as family separations, prolonged detention, lack of due process, forced labor, super-exploitation, and re-institutionalization of racial segregation in residential, educational, and economic spheres, among the ways in which migrants are affected.What does the United States lose with the departure of undocumented migrants? The United States is experiencing a substantial shortage of labor and the exploitation of undocumented labor is a source of great profits for many sectors of the capitalist economy. At the same time, the anti-immigration policy provides a different type of benefit, especially for Trump and the far-right Republicans now in power. Building anti-immigration narratives allows them to create scapegoats for an economy that is failing the majority of the working class. Blaming immigrants diverts attention from rampant capitalist greed and corruption, growing social inequality, the endless increase in the imperial war budget, and a social welfare system that is underfunded.

data.text: The Trump administration appears to be considering a plan to send immigrants facing deportation to a recently closed federal prison plagued by rampant sexual abuse known as the "membership of rape," according to an email sent by federal correctional officials from the Union of Prisons. Approximately 20 miles east of Oakland, the federal correctional institution in Dublin closed last year after more than a half-dozen correctional officers and the former warden were accused or convicted of sexually abusing inmates. Currently, the federal prison's website shows that there are no inmates in the facility, although the long-term fate of the complex has never been clear. But Thursday, the Federal Correctional Officers' Council of the American Federation of Government Employees 33, which represents federal correctional officers, sent a request for information to the correctional system, requesting data related to the closures of facilities. Some paragraphs in the four-page request, union leaders expressed concerns about the future of the facility. FCI Dublin had at least one completed assessment on July 22, 2024, which we believe was considered a structural assessment, the letter said. The union has learned that this assessment has been provided to ICE for what appears to be the potential for ICE to seize the facility. The move comes days after the Federal Bureau of Prisons confirmed that it houses migrant detainees in some facilities, an admission that provoked concerns from union officials who say it seems the bureau is preparing to house migrants on a massive scale. My fear is that the Office will become an ice rink, but that's not what we do, said to The Instances John Kostelnik, western regional vice president for the corrections workers union. Our main focus must be and has always been to keep the community safe from convicted murderers and rapists, and our private sector is doing a tremendous job on that, even in the midst of a private disaster. But now we have an additional mission thrust upon us, he said, that could paralyze our ability to do what we're supposed to do. Although the Bureau of Prisons confirmed in an email that it is helping the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement with detained housing, prison spokespeople refused to provide information on the authorized status of the detainees or where they will be housed. A spokesperson for the prisons cited security reasons for declining comments, while another directed all immigration-related questions to ice. In an email on Wednesday afternoon, ICE said that its enhanced enforcement operations have made enough arrests to require increased detention capacity, although the agency did not provide information on what that meant. While we cannot confirm individual pre-decisional conversations, the statement said, we can confirm that ICE is exploring all options to meet its current and future detention requirements. In recent weeks, the Trump administration has begun to ramp up immigration enforcement operations nationwide, promising to deport millions and millions of people back to their countries of origin. According to the Associated Press, ICE has the budget to detain only 41,000 people. Typically, those detained are held in ICE processing centers, private prison facilities, and local jails that contract with federal immigration officers. However, with the administration's more ambitious deportation goals, officials have begun exploring untested alternatives. This month, the US military started transporting detained migrants on flights to the US Navy Base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele has offered to have US officials send migrants as well as US citizens to his country's notoriously tough prisons. The first indications that the White House planned to keep detained migrants in US federal prisons arrived at the end of last month. On January 26, the leadership of the Union wrote to Senator Alex Padilla's office, warning the state's senior senator that Trump officials had begun directing the Bureau of Prisons to leave space for more inmates in facilities across the country. Currently, the Trump administration is having the BOP conduct a bed space audit and ask facilities to consolidate inmates to make space (free up units), the letter said. This last time, said Kostelnik, was during Trump's first term. BOP officials were forced to make space for 1,600 immigrants, including many asylum seekers, in federal prisons in Oregon, California, Arizona, and Texas. By August 2018, two months after federal officials publicly confirmed the controversial housing scheme, the American Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit alleging that it was a violation of the migrants' due process rights under the 5th Amendment. In October, news reports indicated that the administration had returned to using federal prisons to house migrant detainees. However, according to Kostelnik, those few months proved chaotic for the detainees and the private prison, which were ill-equipped to safeguard the migrants, many of whom had different medical needs and cultural backgrounds than the typical office prison inmates. Communication sometimes became a challenge, as many detainees did not speak English, nor any other language spoken by the private prison staff. I fear that this will arrive soon, he wrote in the January email to Padilla's office, and all facilities in CA are currently moving on this request, and they are even taking our bus crews and specialized equipment prepared for similar missions. The first federal prison in California for detained migrants from the House of Representatives appears to have been the Metropolitan Detention Center in downtown Los Angeles. According to two officials familiar with the situation, national security investigations appeared on a weekend with a group of around nine African migrants. The officials requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Initially, the private prison was unsure whether to accept the detainees or how to keep them better separated from other prisoners. Finally, they placed the men in their own unit within the facility, creating additional work for the private, who said an official had no guidance on how to handle migrants differently from typical federal prisoners. The official also stated that, although the number of migrants housed in the Los Angeles block has not increased, he expected it to because his superiors had begun discussing how to adjust private schedules to handle more weekend intakes. It is unclear how many other facilities have been tasked with housing migrants, but last week, the Associated Press reported that a federal prison in Miami and a federal prison in Atlanta were also being used for that purpose, and internal BOP emails may show that more facilities are being used. In the past few days, federal prison officials have begun asking workers to consider taking temporary jobs elsewhere to help manage the influx of ice detainees. On Monday, a captain at FCI Sheridan, a medium-security facility in Oregon, sent an email to private staff there to gather volunteers willing to work across the country at FCI Berlin, a medium-security facility in rural New Hampshire, which is expected to receive at least 500 migrants on ice. The private staff will work correctional service posts in support of the BOP's mission to temporarily house ice detainees, explained Captain Joseph Cerone, according to a copy of the email obtained by The Instances. Since we anticipate more than 500 detainees will be headed to Berlin, in addition to custody assistance, they will probably need help with health and psychology services. The email did not specify when the immigrants are expected to arrive. The influx of detainees could strain the federal prison system, which is already facing problems. Perhaps most notable in FCI Dublin, which was one of several facilities, the Office of Closure or Deactivation targeted it last year. But it may not be the only one slated to be used for ice. On Wednesday, Kostelnik told The Instances that he had just learned that immigration officials are scheduled to visit a federal facility in Morgantown, which was also targeted for closure, for an evaluation very similar to the one in Dublin. For a private system already tense and stretched, Kostelnik told The Instances, seeing the facilities where they have worked for so long taken and handed over to another agency is extremely demoralizing.

A woman from the Dominican Republic, María Estela Fajardo Liriano, was turned over by the Haitian Judicial Police (SMPJ) to the Specialized Land Border Security Corps (CESFRONT) and the General Directorate of Migration, accused of kidnapping minors and sexual exploitation. The arrested woman, Fajardo Liriano, is reportedly the owner of a club in the Tabarre commune, Haiti, called La Patrona, which was apprehended in Port-au-Prince on Monday, February 3 of the current year, at the request of the authorities of the Dominican Republic. Fajardo's detention occurred in relation to the disappearance of a minor. She also faces charges for alleged transnational delinquency, kidnapping of minors, and sexual exploitation. During her interrogation, the woman denied all accusations made by the authorities of the Dominican Republic. The delivery of María Estela Fajardo Liriano was carried out on the binational bridge between Dajabón and Juana Méndez, it was directed to the reception center of the DGM, and in the coming hours, under the protocols of the place, it will be sent to Santo Domingo. With information from Maria Sigoyen

Convicted to nine years in prison, the tourist guide judged for sexual assault on students The court highlights his identical pattern of gaining the victims' trust and attacking their sexual freedom  Published in 7 minutes of reading The National Court has sentenced the Seville-born tourist guide Manuel Gerardo B.V. to nine years in prison for sexual assault committed against three young American students as the responsible person for the company Discover Excursions, when the same students studied at the universities of Salamanca and Valencia and participated in the trips promoted by the aforementioned company to Morocco and Portugal in 2013 and 2017, according to the sentence issued by the court last Monday, January 10. In its sentence, distributed by the National Court itself, the magistrates of the First Section of the Penal Chamber impose on Manuel Gerardo B.V. A sentence of six years in prison for a crime of aggression with the mitigating factor of undue delays in relation to the initial complainant of the case, the Moroccan victim, and two sentences of one and a half years in prison for two sexual aggression crimes regarding the two remaining complainants, for the events that occurred in Lagos (Portugal). Additionally, the court imposes a seven and a half year ban on working as a tourist guide and condemns him to compensate 40,000 euros to the first Moroccan victim and 1,500 euros to each of the other two victims, despite acknowledging that it is not possible to automatically translate moral harm into money and that the only thing we can do is value the importance of the harm in consideration of the victims' circumstances. The court sentences him to seven and a half years of supervised freedom after serving his sentence, six years of prohibition from approaching or communicating with the first victim, and one year of the same measure with respect to each of the remaining two victims. The sentence closely matches the prosecution's request, which had demanded nine years in prison for the accused for a suspected sex crime, rape, and two supposed sex abuse crimes, currently three different sex crimes as well as six years of prohibition from approaching or communicating with the first victim, one year of the same prohibition with respect to each of the two subsequent victims, eight years of disqualification from the profession of tour guide, and 40,000 euros in compensation to the first victim and 1,500 euros to each of the remaining two victims. The private prosecution, on its side, was requesting a total of 23 years in prison, as well as a compensation of 600,000 euros for the first young woman and 150,000 euros each for the two following ones, while the defense had asked for their acquittal, as he had always denied any wrongdoing. PROVEN FACTS The convicting sentence, subject to appeal, declares proven that within the framework of the trip promoted by the Discover Excursions company in November 2013 to Morocco, on the last night before returning to Spain, on November 2, in a hotel in Tangier, the defendant approached the initial complainant of the case, an American student then affiliated with the University of Salamanca, and her roommates, when the latter were on the hotel's bar terrace. The accused, according to the sentence, proposed that they take champagne in their room, to which they agreed and, once in the room shared by the young women, the defendant, while they were drinking champagne, proposed playing truth or dare and challenged them to remove their t-shirts, which they refused, but he removed his clothes except for his underwear. Then, according to the sentence, the victim began to feel very tired and fell asleep and, upon waking up, she found herself alone in the room, and she went to the bathroom, where she saw her friends in the shower in their t-shirts with the defendant in his underwear. Once the three of them came out of the bathroom, she entered and sat on the toilet, according to the narrative of the proven facts, which adds that then, the accused entered the bathroom in a surprising manner, introducing his penis into the girl's mouth, who then fell to the ground, becoming unconscious, something that the accused denied. . ALSO IN PORTUGAL The sentence addresses the facts related to the other two victims, American students from Florida State University in Valencia, on the night of May 28, 2017, the last day of the trip to Lagos promoted by the defendant's company at the time. According to the proven facts narrative, the accused gave these young women drink tickets at a bar, inviting them to attend a party in his hotel room, which they accepted under the belief that more people would be attending, although upon arriving at the room in the early morning hours, they realized there were no other guests. In the room, according to the proven facts narrative, the accused asked if he could make them more comfortable, removing his pants and remaining in his underwear. Later, according to the sentencing, he asked them about their sexual experiences, proposed playing truth or dare, and at a certain point, after they refused his sexual proposals, he told them to take off their pants, to which they refused, asking him as a challenge, if they kissed their tour guide. Both kissed him on the cheek and, upon his insistence, gave him a superficial kiss on the lips, the sentence notes that the young women also refused the more sexual dance he asked them to do, after which the defendant, with the intention of satisfying his sexual desires, grabbed one's right hand and the other's left hand, immobilizing them in a corner of the room. They wanted to try to escape one of the victims, saying they wanted to leave, but the victim responded, according to the account of proven facts, that he did not do so because he had been intimidated, after one of the girls had kissed him and another had placed her hand on his genitals, after which both were finally able to leave the room.For the sentencing, the court takes the testimony as true and credible from the first complainant, persistent in the fundamental, as it did not appreciate that with this testimony, she would gain an advantage or be driven by hatred or resentment. It is true that the complaint was formulated a long time after, practically five years. The fact that it took years to report the incidents does not detract from her credibility, not all women react in the same way to an attack on their sexual freedom and in this case, the victim recounts in an absolutely coherent manner why she reported it years later, pointing out that she did so upon learning of other women who have been victims, in her opinion, of the same perpetrator. Her statement is also corroborated by peripheral evidence, such as the testimony of the victims of the incidents that occurred in Portugal and that of the police officers investigating the incidents. The court thus identifies the identical pattern reported by the victims in this procedure and those with whom the police officers have contact. It involves, explains, foreign female students, American, who embark on a trip where the accused serves as their guide, who gains their trust by showing kindness, good manners, confidence in what he does, and knowledge of the cities, after which the aggression against the victims occurs in the last moment, the last day of the trip, so that they have fewer possibilities of reacting. In the execution of the facts, the judgment continues, the author follows the same pattern. He approaches the young women, all of them very young, in a friendly manner, proposes that they have a drink and play the same game, in order to finally attack their sexual freedom, concludes.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI, for its acronym in English) and federal authorities dismantled a criminal network dedicated to human trafficking in central Tennessee, allegedly led by members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Eight individuals were arrested and charged with sexually exploiting women brought from Venezuela and other countries in Latin America under false promises of job opportunities and a better life. Eight People Detained for Sex Trafficking in Tennessee On Tuesday, February 11, the acting Attorney General, Robert E. McGuire, and the police chief, John Drake, confirmed the arrests of the eight people at a press conference. It was reported that the victims were forced to work in conditions of sexual exploitation through debts imposed that far exceeded the costs of their travel. The operation was the result of a joint investigation between the FBI, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) and the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department. According to the federal indictment, as reported by CNN, the suspects recruited vulnerable women from Venezuela, Colombia and other countries, offering them help to migrate to the United States. However, once in the country, the victims were subjected to conditions of sexual exploitation. The victims were extorted and forced to have sex with strangers for the benefit of the accused, said interim federal prosecutor Rob McGuire during the press conference. Association with the Aragua Train Network. According to local news source The Tennessean, two of the accused are directly linked to the Venezuelan gang, the Aragua Train Network, a transnational criminal organization known for its involvement in human trafficking, extortion, narcotics trafficking, and other violent crimes. According to the indictment, these individuals, who executed the modality known as coyote to smuggle people across the US border illegally for a fee, used their affiliation with the gang to intimidate and control the victims. The Aragua Train Network, originating from a Venezuelan prison, has expanded its influence in several Latin American countries and, more recently, in the US. In July 2024, the US Department of the Treasury sanctioned the gang as a transnational criminal organization, highlighting its involvement in illicit activities such as human trafficking and money laundering. The modus operandi of the criminal organization in Tennessee. According to the prosecutors, the network was active between July 2022 and March 2024. The accused identified and recruited young women in vulnerable situations in Venezuela and other countries in South and Central America. Once in the US, they were imposed with inflated debts and forced to engage in commercial sex acts until they were paid off. In some cases, the victims continued to be exploited even after paying off the debts. The head of the metropolitan police stated that the investigation began with a local complaint and subsequently became a federal operation with the collaboration of the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the TBI. In April 2024, according to CNN, another federal operation dismantled a similar network in Louisiana, linked to the Aragua Train. Authorities discovered that the organization operated storage houses used for human trafficking in Texas, Virginia, New Jersey, and Florida. Identity of the Detainees and Charges Against ThemAccording to local media outlet The Tennessean, the accused, all Venezuelan nationals, of which five out of the eight are women, were identified as Yilibeth Del Carmen Rivero De Caldera, Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero, Yuribetzi Del Valle Gómez Machuca, Wilmarys Del Valle Manzano Soloranzo, Endrik Alexander Morales Rivero, Ariannys Beatriz Gutiérrez Carrillo, Frankyanna Del Valle Romero Rivero, and Jesús Enrique Castillo Rodríguez.According to the formal accusation, the presented charges include conspiracy to commit interstate transportation for prostitution purposes and conspiracy to facilitate organized crime businesses. Some of the detainees face additional charges, such as conspiracy to engage in human sex trafficking, which could lead to a life sentence. Mota Rivero faces an additional charge of illegal possession of a firearm. The prosecutor McGuire did not confirm if any of the undocumented victims could face deportation proceedings, but assured that the priority is for the survivors to be able to testify against their aggressors without fear of reprisals.

Prosecutor Ana María Caro requested the DNA sample of a fifth suspect to be analyzed for his alleged participation in the murder of 15-year-old Natalia Melmann, which occurred in Miramar in February 2001. The suspect is a 60-year-old former police officer, currently residing in the city of Trenque Lauquen, Buenos Aires Province. The proceedings were finally carried out at the Expert Advisory Board of this city, given that the Scientific Police could not intervene as some of the implicated individuals were members of the force. The body of 15-year-old Natalia was found under a pile of leaves in the Florentino Ameghino nursery, in Miramar. The autopsy revealed that the girl was asphyxiated with the cord of her shoes, although a superficial examination showed bruises, burns, fractures, and a blow to the skull. The necropsy indicated that there were genetic traces of five different individuals, confirming that she was raped by various men. Ricardo Anselmini, Ricardo Suárez, and Oscar Echenique were sentenced to life imprisonment in September 2002 for the crimes of kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse with carnal access by multiple people, and criminally caused homicide. In the meantime, former convict Gustavo Gallo Fernández was sentenced to 25 years for his participation in the kidnapping, although the sentence was reduced to ten years. Ricardo Panadero had been acquitted twice due to lack of evidence, however, the Provincial Penal Appeals Court decided in 2019 to annul the verdict and announced that the fourth policeman of the Bonaerense must be judged for his participation in the crime. Finally, on November 13, 2019, Chamber III of the Bonaerense Court of Cassation overturned that dismissal and ordered a new trial to take place, which was conducted in 2023, where the fourth police officer was found guilty of the crimes of aggravated illegal deprivation of liberty, aggravated sexual abuse, and double aggravation of homicide, due to the premeditated concurrence of two or more people and committed to ensure impunity, and received a life sentence.

Another step in the formation of those who lead the Missionary Justice Created February 13, 2025 The specialized course in child protection, developed on the eLearning eLod campus of the International Centre for Missing Exploited Children (ICMEC), remains available in the framework of an international cooperation initiative. This training program emerged from a meeting held on November 7, past between the President of the Superior Court of Justice, Rosanna Pía Venchiarutti Sartori, the Attorney General, Carlos Giménez, and representatives of the National Center for Missing Exploited Children (NCMEC), the principal non-governmental organization for child protection in the United States. In that meeting, guidelines were established for a common agenda that will enable Missionary Justice operators to strengthen their knowledge and tools to address crimes against children. The course has a total duration of 38 hours and is composed of six levels of training. The modules are designed in the format of short video clips and are delivered by international experts from Canada, Spain, Germany, Argentina, and the United States, among other countries. The contents include:Childhood Human Rights Introduction. Victim-centered approaches. Use of technology in the fight against child sexual crimes. Healthcare response to human trafficking. Development of medical protocols for addressing child sexual violence. Access and Registration ModeThe course is available for free through the ICMEC Spanish platform, accessible from computers and mobile devices. To register, interested parties must complete the Institution field with Judicial Power of Misiones Province and grant the necessary permissions to share their registration. With this initiative, the Judicial Power of Misiones reaffirms its commitment to protecting childhood, incorporating innovative tools and promoting continuous training for its members on high-complexity issues. Although the training is primarily aimed at members of the Penal Court, it is also open to all judges and judicial officials interested in expanding their knowledge on this highly relevant topic.

Prosecutor Mónica Cuñarro requested a dismissal due to lack of evidence against Matanza Intendant Fernando Espinoza, who is charged in the case for alleged sexual abuse of his former private secretary Melody Rakauskas. Cuñarro's position was made in response to a request made by the judge in the case, Fernando Caunedo, following a complaint presentation to elevate the process to oral trial. According to Cuñarro's argument, there are no elements of evidence in the case files that support the accusation, beyond the statements of the accuser. The argument was made in an 80-page written submission. Despite the reasoning, Rakauskas's defense lawyers insisted on the accusation and reiterated the request to elevate the case to oral trial against the intendant. The community chief has publicly criticized his former secretary, citing that she refused to hand over her cell phone and computer to be analyzed. Espinoza also argued that the complaint is part of a case of espionage against him. However, those were not the only objections to the accuser. According to what was made public, Rakauskas had previously reported her mother for physical abuse and violence, attempting to get her mother to pay compensation. She also reported her 87-year-old grandfather for allegedly trying to kill her and seeking compensation. There were requests for psychiatric evaluations of Rakauskas.

On February 11, 2025, the National Police confirmed the extradition of an Ecuadorian wanted for the crime of human trafficking. The subject was identified as Stalin Rafael Zambrano and had a red Interpol arrest warrant and notification. The suspect was arrested in the United States and coordinated with the authorities of that country for his return to Ecuador. The extradition was carried out on February 10 and Zambrano was handed over to the Police at the José Joaquín de Olmedo International Airport in Guayaquil. According to the Ministry of the Interior, the subject has an ongoing process at the Los Ríos Judicial Penal Unit. He hid himself almost 10 years in the United States. According to Captain Paúl Alejandro García, of the General Directorate of Investigations of the Police, the subject hid himself almost 10 years in US territory. This after being part of a human trafficking gang that operated in Ecuador and Peru. Specifically, in that neighboring country, a 15-year-old victim was rescued who was being sexually exploited. The minor was rescued in a nightclub in Lima. After knowing the case, the police units were activated and found the criminal organization of Stalin Rafael Zambrano. However, the subject was able to leave Ecuador and settled in Houston, since August 2013. Despite changing his identity, due to his irregular migratory status, he was detained and spent the last two years in prison. According to García, the criminal organization linked to Zambrano had its base in the San Camilo sector, in Quevedo, in the Los Ríos province. In that place, women were recruited with deceit and various economic offers. They especially sought out vulnerable minors. For this crime, the subject could face a sentence of up to 10 years. Other extradition cases in Ecuador In the past January, Ecuador registered three other cases of extradition of subjects with outstanding accounts with justice. The first case was the return of the main suspect in the femicide of Diana Carolina, which occurred in Quito in July 2023. The suspect was captured in Chile. Then, a similar case was confirmed, when Interpol extradited from Germany to Ecuador the third most wanted for the crime of femicide. The crime took place in October 2019 in Guayaquil. After five years of evading justice, a Red Notice from Interpol and an arrest warrant were made effective against him. Finally, before January ended, the case of Nain Massuh, better known as alias El Turco was reported. This individual was linked to the Encuentro case and mentioned in the Metástasis case.
