Seven people have been charged over an alleged scheme of fraudulent compensation claims for sexual abuse that supposedly netted over $1 billion. New South Wales police alleged that the claimants approached former juvenile offenders, prisoners, and public school students, encouraging them to lodge fraudulent compensation claims for historical child sexual abuse while in care. The claims were made against the NSW Department of Communities and Justice and the NSW Department of Education. Police said the claimants had trained potential claimants on how to lodge fraudulent claims through various Sydney law firms. According to reports, the earnings were known as "Bum Money" within prison circles. Police suspected that a significant portion of the $1.3 billion claims were fraudulent. A superintendent of detectives, Gordon Arbinja, told journalists on Thursday that the charges were only the tip of the iceberg and we have a very, very big problem here. A third of the inmates at Cooma Correctional Centre have lodged claims, which I am going to investigate, he said, adding that several law firms were being investigated. On Wednesday, detectives executed a search warrant in Girraween and arrested a 55-year-old man who was charged with 21 offences, including nine counts of dishonestly obtaining a financial advantage through deception. He was refused bail to appear in the native court of Parramatta on Thursday, where police will allege he was a claims farmer in the scheme. Arbinja alleged that the man had lodged claims for compensation on behalf of others and had 100 claims pending worth $220,000 as part of a very lucrative business. Some statements would have been rejected because there was a low threshold, but there is still some threshold, said the detective. The police were not trying to raise the threshold and strengthen the process. NSW Police support legitimate victims, they said. They must be compensated, and that's why the system was introduced in the first place. The problem is that the system is porous, and the system must be strengthened. Five other people were arrested and charged with publishing false or misleading material to gain an advantage. This includes a 53-year-old woman from Granville, a 32-year-old man from Pendle Hill, a 52-year-old woman from Horsley, a 35-year-old woman from Pendle Hill, and a 42-year-old man who was detained at Gladesville Police Station. A 23-year-old man from Mermaid Seaside in Queensland also received a future court attendance notice for the same charge. Arbinja claimed that the 23-year-old player's father had also been involved as part of a group of victim advocates and had been under police investigation since last February, but now he has passed away. The police will argue in court that the seven people accused of earning $3.75 million in fraudulent compensation claims, but the scheme was discovered before payments were made. Arbinja claimed that the 55-year-old man had earned hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not a million dollars, through the scheme and was the head of the syndicate, just like the other 23-year-old man from Mermaid Seaside. The police also executed a search warrant on a law firm in Sydney, taking documents they said were relevant to the investigation. They said the investigations continue and more arrests are expected.

The National Court has sentenced Manuel Gerardo Blanco Vela, a native of Seville, to nine years in prison for sexual assault crimes committed against three young American students as the responsible party of the company Discover Excursions, when the students were studying at the universities of Salamanca and Valencia and participating in the trips promoted by the company to Morocco and Portugal in 2013 and 2017, according to the sentence issued by the court last Monday, January 10. In its ruling, the magistrates of the First Section of the Penal Chamber of the National Court impose a six-year prison sentence on the defendant, identified as Manuel Blanco Vela, for a crime of assault with the mitigating factor of undue delays in relation to the initial denouncer of the case, the Moroccan victim, and two prison sentences of one and a half years for two sexual assault crimes with regard to the remaining two denouncers, for the events that occurred in Lagos (Portugal). Furthermore, it imposes a ban on him from working as a tour guide for seven and a half years and sentences him to compensate the girl who suffered the sexual assault in Morocco with 40.00 euros and 1,500 euros to each of the other two victims, despite acknowledging that it is not possible to automatically translate moral damage into money and that the only thing we can do is assess the importance of the damage based on the circumstances of the victims and try to convert that estimate into a concrete monetary amount. The sentence thus largely corresponds to the Public Prosecutor's Office's request, which had demanded nine years of imprisonment for the defendant for a presumed sex crime, rape, and two alleged sex abuse crimes, currently three sex crimes of different typification as well as six years of prohibition from approaching the first victim or communicating with her, one year of the same prohibition with regard to each of the two subsequent victims, and eight years of disqualification for the profession of tour guide, and that he indemnify with 40,000 euros to the first victim and with 1,500 euros to each of the two remaining ones. The private accusation, on the other hand, requested a total of 23 years of imprisonment, as well as a compensation of 600,000 euros for the first young woman and 150,000 euros each of the two following ones while the defense had asked for his acquittal.

Beirut Efforts to end child marriage in Iraq face a grave threat, as the Iraqi Parliament's Council of Representatives has passed amendments to the Personal Status Law of Iraq, sparking major concern over the risk of allowing child marriage of girls. These legal amendments would grant Iraqi religious authorities greater control over family matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and child care, by allowing Islamic clergy to rule on them in accordance with their interpretations of Islamic law. This includes allowing marriage of minors based on the specific religious sect under which the marriage contract is conducted, meaning that the minimum age for marriage could be lowered below 18 years and vary between different religious confessions. If this continues, it would represent a profound violation of human rights and could undermine the legal protections for women and girls, in direct contravention of Iraq's international human rights commitments, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which Iraq is a signatory. It is essential to note that these changes have yet to be implemented in Iraq's Personal Status Law. The amendment approved by the Iraqi Council of Representatives on January 21 only granted religious authorities the capacity to interpret and potentially modify the law, but the modifications have not been implemented. On February 4, the Federal Supreme Court of Iraq suspended the application of the contentious bill after several parliament members filed a complaint alleging that the voting process was illegal. This presents a crucial opportunity to continue the defense, and the persistent efforts of civil society organizations are already having a positive impact. Now is a critical moment for us to unite in action to help safeguard and strengthen the rights of women and girls in Iraq, and to prevent their fundamental human rights from continuing to erode. Child marriage increases the risk of girls suffering harm. If the amendment is applied, it could put an end to the ban on marriage of minors under 18 years that has existed in Iraq since 1959, although this included a provision that allowed a child to marry with a judge's consent. In 2022, the United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) reported that 28% of girls in Iraq married before the age of 18, and 7% did so before the age of 15. The author, Dima Dabbous. Marriage rates for minors vary across Iraqi regions, with the highest prevalence found in Missan (43.5%), Nayaf (37.2%), and Karbala (36.8%). Legalizing child marriage under any pretext sets a dangerous precedent. It is not a cultural or religious necessity, but a harmful practice that perpetuates cycles of poverty, illiteracy, and gender-based violence. Marrying girls at a young age exposes them to a higher risk of exploitation and is associated with higher rates of early and forced pregnancy, physical and sexual abuse, psychological trauma, and limited access to education, employment, and economic independence. Women and girls need greater protection in personal status laws. Personal status laws govern some of the most intimate aspects of family relationships, including marriage, divorce, child custody, inheritance, and property. In many countries, these laws are deeply rooted in discriminatory traditions that prioritize the rights of men and boys over those of women and girls. As a result, women and girls in Iraq, and in many other countries, continue to face significant challenges due to the sex-based discrimination embedded in personal status laws. You can read the English version of this article here. Reforming this type of legislation has proven to be one of the most difficult areas of legal change to address, as laws governing family relationships are deeply intertwined with religious, traditional, and cultural beliefs. The weakening of legal protections for women and girls in Iraq reflects a disturbing global trend. Across the globe, efforts to roll back laws that protect the rights of women and girls are gaining momentum, putting millions at risk of child marriage and forced marriage, sexual and gender-based violence, and forced pregnancies due to restricted access to reproductive healthcare. Collaborating to protect the legal rights of women and girls Proposed amendments to Iraq's Personal Status Law threaten to normalize harmful practices such as child marriage, which could undermine decades of progressive reforms that established greater safeguards for women and girls and helped unify the country's family law provisions. As highlighted by the United Nations in Iraq in its statement published in response to the recent events, legal reforms must be justified in light of Iraq's international commitments on human rights, particularly in relation to the protection of the rights and well-being of women and children, so as to meet the aspirations of the Iraqi people and preserve the country's historical achievements. Advocates for women's rights have joined forces to oppose the detrimental legal reforms that threaten the rights of women and girls in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Local advocates in Iraq are collaborating with leading women's rights organizations in MENA as part of the Hurra Coalition, which seeks to reform family laws at the national and regional levels in line with international human rights norms. Through evidence-based defense and survivor-centered approaches, members of the Hurra Coalition are building a regional movement to protect the rights of girls within families, their safety, and autonomy over their future. This includes demanding comprehensive reforms to family law that defend and promote equality, guarantee safety and access to justice for all, without discrimination. We urge the global community to support the human rights of Iraqi women and girls by expanding defense and promoting their protection. Governments, lawmakers, and global institutions must remain steadfast in defending the legal rights of women and girls to protect them from harm in Iraq and worldwide. Dr. Dima Dabbous is the regional representative for Equality Now (Equality Now) in the Middle East and North Africa. Equality Now is an international human rights organization dedicated to protecting and promoting the rights of all women and girls worldwide.

The violence against migrant children and adolescents on the southern border remains a humanitarian crisis that is being invisible. Sexual abuse, trafficking, and child exploitation are realities that authorities have yet to curb. Aquínoticias Staff On the southern border of Mexico, migrant children face a crisis of violence and abandonment. The president of the organization Por la Superación de la Mujer, Elsa Simón Ortega, revealed that they have attended at least 10 cases of child violence against migrants, although the real number could be much higher due to fear of reporting. Despite the existence of the Law for the Protection of Children, Adolescents, and Youth since 2012, the situation has not improved, and the suffering of these minors remains a silent cry that authorities do not hear. The testimonies collected by the organization are heart-wrenching. Four-year-old girls have been victims of sexual abuse. Children and adolescents are forced into labor and sexual exploitation. In the border city cruises, it is common to see infants cleaning windows or begging for alms, a clear evidence of the extreme vulnerability in which they are found. The most alarming thing is that the majority of the aggressions come from close relatives, making it even more difficult to denounce and protect minors. Despite the efforts of the association to provide legal support and bring perpetrators to justice, the lack of action by institutions such as the municipal and state DIF perpetuates this cycle of impunity. Migrant children not only face the dangers of forced transit, but also the abandonment of a system that should protect them. With information from Diario del Sur.

data.text: Teresa DomínguezURLIgnacio Cabanes València 13 FEB 2025 1038 Updated 13 FEB 2025 1117 Like in all previous occasions when the National Police have struck the El Faku gang, of Salva and of Erik, all of them pseudonyms of the main leaders, in this latest police operation, announced exclusively by LevanteEMV on Wednesday, the victims of their extortion with a sexual background number in the dozens and are spread across half of Spain. So far, more than 50 people have been detained in this large-scale operation, according to various sources, which began at dawn on Tuesday in numerous homes in Valencia where the majority of the arrests took place in Pobla de Vallbona and, above all, in Benissa. There, in a chalet in one of the multiple urbanizations of that municipality in the Marina Alta, is where the supposedly directed network of sextortion, allegedly led by Facundo B. S. At 24 years old and going by the name El Faku, Ismael B. O., alias Salva, and Massinissa F. M., Erik, had set up this time their headquarters in the form of a call center from where they made dozens of calls to cybersex workers until one of them fell into the provocation and ended up paying the revolutionary tax in exchange for not spreading their perversion or not physically attacking them. Both Faku and Salva, through whose mediation the former Levante UD footballer Toño was detained during the dismantling of the same network in 2019 (the player was fully exonerated), were detained in Benissa, as they personally supervised the work of those who answered the call center. The highest rung But, on this occasion, the specialists from the Kidnappings and Extortions unit of the UDEV central office in Madrid, who have been leading the investigation, and those from Cybercrime at the València Superior Police Headquarters, have taken a step further and have reached, according to sources of utmost reliability, the highest level of the plot, which manages and launders the hundreds of thousands of euros that they have been obtaining from their victims over the past few years. According to those sources, dozens of bank accounts have been frozen, not just those that mules opened so that the pimps could deposit the various amounts they were demanding from their clients under very serious threats, but above all, those of the actual masterminds behind the plot, which has been operating for more than six years. In that sense, the investigators would have managed to immobilize a significant asset with the assets acquired in the process of money laundering and with money stored in those accounts, as well as cryptocurrency credentials. In principle, the detainees will be handed over to the judge handling the case next Friday morning, the presiding judge of the Instruction Court number 20 of Valencia since its inception. The most media-visible of the detainees is undoubtedly the Uruguayan Facundo B. S. H., alias El Faku, detained for the first time at 21 years old and who three years later has risen to become one of the leaders of the part of the organization dedicated to setting up false prostitution contact scams and subsequent threats to sex workers who have fallen victim to calls on phones that search through pages that promote sexual exploitation. As reported by the National Police in a statement following the detention of Facundo B. S. H. In the spring of 2021, in a town in Jaén where he was hiding, within the operation Girasol, exclusively advanced by LevanteEMV, the alleged offender was known as the Messi of work (they called work his business and the method they used in sex trafficking, the same as any other similar scheme) on his Instagram account, where he defined himself with the term I'm a criminal (in English). With more than 20 police and judicial complaints against him and an undeniable criminal record, for now, this confessed criminal is back behind bars.

Dr. Tejshri Shah, General Director of Médecins Sans Frontières and a pediatrician expert in infectious diseases, warns that it is impossible to contain the Mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo without addressing the needs of displaced people and improving their precarious living conditions. Mpox or simian smallpox (previously known as monkeypox) is not a new disease in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where it is endemic in several regions. In the last decade, cases have increased, but now, in the Kivus, the virus has mutated, becoming more transmissible between humans. This is alarming, especially in densely populated areas like Goma (with two million inhabitants) and in refugee camps, where hundreds of thousands of people are seeking refuge due to the armed conflict in North Kivu. Although the lethality of this new strain is low, the conditions in Goma and its surroundings do not allow for its spread to be halted. The ability to treat those at higher risk of complications, such as young children and individuals with advanced HIV, remains very limited. Precarious conditions hinder prevention efforts in refugee camps. How can we expect families living in tiny shelters, without water, adequate sanitation facilities, or even soap, to implement preventive measures. Malnourished girls and boys, how can they have the necessary strength to avoid complications caused by the disease. How can we expect this variant, which is primarily transmitted through sexual contact, not to spread in refugee camps, given the dramatic levels of violence and sexual exploitation affecting girls and women living there. We have repeatedly denounced the inhumane living conditions faced by people in the camps and the glaring gaps in humanitarian response. Impact of the M23 Crisis on Living ConditionsMore than two years after the start of the M23 crisis and the massive displacement of people it triggered, families living in overcrowded camps still lack the essentials: food, water, basic hygiene items, access to sanitation and medical services. Dr. Tejshri Shah, General Director and pediatrician specializing in infectious diseases, has just returned from North Kivu, and during a counseling session I attended with survivors of rape, a woman told me that she lives with her seven children under a plastic tarp. Her partner left her after the rape. For women like her, proven and tested solutions to prevent the spread of the epidemic are unimaginably difficult to implement. The woman Dr. Shah met expressed her despair: "I don't know how to protect my children from diseases. We don't have soap, we don't have water, and we don't have a place to go to the bathroom." Dr. Shah, and for all individuals who have sought refuge in displacement camps, the Mpox epidemic is yet another challenge amidst a torrent of problems. And it's not the most urgent one, given the daily struggles they face, including outbreaks of potentially deadly diseases like measles or cholera. However, Mpox is here and we must address it. To tackle this new additional challenge, we must facilitate the survival of people. This will be achieved with an adapted response to their specific needs and the real-life challenges they face, adds Dr. Immediate solutions to mitigate the epidemic are necessary. We must listen to people, understand their needs, and provide them with basic supplies to control infection such as water, soap, disinfectant, and access to medical facilities. These are simple but essential things. We cannot rely solely on the arrival of vaccines to resolve the problem. Improving the living conditions of people is also a critical factor in combating these outbreaks, explains Dr. Shah. Along with medical authorities, our teams do their best to provide care. We raise awareness among people living in these settlements, just as we do in other parts of the country affected by the outbreak. Like many others, we hope that vaccines arrive in the country as soon as possible. However, these will not be magic solutions. Government and non-governmental actors must urgently address the underlying response to Mpox, which must adapt to the needs and realities of the population.Doctors Without Borders (MSF) is an international medical humanitarian organization that provides aid to populations in precarious situations and to victims of natural or human-made disasters and armed conflicts, without any discrimination based on race, religion, or political ideology. Currently, MSF has 499 medical and humanitarian action projects in 88 countries, and with 7 million partners and collaborators worldwide. In recognition of its humanitarian work, MSF received the 1999 Nobel Peace Prize. For more information, visit URL

The justice system of his country issued a capture order against him in the framework of the case for alleged sexual abuse, and the government of Luis Arce supported the measure. After the First Penal Chamber of the Tarija Justice Court rejected Morales' appeal, Judge Nelson Rocabado ordered the Special Force Against Crime to detain the former head of state and coca leader. In this context, Minister of Government Carlos Eduardo del Castillo stated on Monday that the order of operations to carry out the apprehension is already ready, but they are waiting for the precise moment and place to execute it without generating confrontations and avoiding the loss of human lives. The Tarija Prosecutor's Office investigating the case has Morales in its sights for rape and human trafficking, of course. The former MAS leader is accused of having had sexual relations with Cindy Saraí in 2016 when she was a minor, from which a daughter was born. In this scenario, Morales was supposed to appear for a statement on January 17, but as he missed his second court date, the Justice declared him in default and confirmed the arrest order that had been issued in October 2024. Additionally, he ordered the freezing of his bank accounts and assets. Ten days later, on January 27, the Tarija Court rejected the defense's appeal, thus aggravating Morales' judicial situation. The State Attorney General, Roger Mariaca, reaffirmed that the arrest order must be executed by the police. Mariaca also determined that a prosecutor can intervene in case an entry is required. In response to the judicial orders, Morales is holed up in the Chapare, Cochabamba department (center), his political stronghold, where he has the backing of hundreds of cocaleros who have warned of a possible social convulsion in case of his detention. Evo Morales denounces persecution by the Bolivian Justice and Government. The new media operation by the government to detain me within the framework of their "Plan Negro" (lawfare) aims to cover up the now-unavoidable scandal of corruption over contracts to give away lithium to foreign companies, Morales expressed on his social networks. That strategy consisted of inventing an accusation for a presumed crime just to detain me, destroy me politically and morally, and take me out of the electoral race, by manipulating a prosecutor and using a judge appointed by the illegitimately self-extended members of the Judiciary Council. The Black Plan by Arce also included, with the complicity of the TCP and the TSE, the theft of the MAS acronym and the designation of leaders by hand, without the vote of the militants, he affirmed. Two de facto magistrates of the Constitutional Tribunal, Gonzalo Hurtado and Iván Espada, protected by the regime, issued unconstitutional sentences that aim to disqualify me as a presidential candidate, concluded Morales in his post on X. Cousin, help me, cried a 21-year-old young man who was standing at the door of his house, located in a municipality of the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (GMA), when two armed men approached him to take him away. Alerted by her nephew's cries, his aunt peered out onto the street and saw how they forced him into a vehicle. This happened at 2:30 pm on a day in September 2023, and since then, he has not been found. A total of 1,248 people have experienced a similar situation to the young man's since 1998 in Jalisco, who were deprived of their liberty in their home, workplace, or neighborhood by a varying number of people, almost five on average, and in the events, there were arms, punches, threats, or some other form of coercion. Almost all of them disappeared starting from 2020 and up to December 2024, according to an investigation conducted jointly with Dr. Jorge Ramírez Plascencia, a scholar from the University of Guadalajara (UdG). To obtain the data, the summary of facts contained in 8,072 reports of missing persons with a search warrant in the possession of the Jalisco State Commission for the Search of Persons (Cobupej) was consulted. The majority of the more than 1,200 victims remain missing, as only 212 have been located, although 84 of them were found dead. Despite the large number of people who disappeared with violence, not all of them are included. The analyzed reports are characterized because there was at least one witness to the deprivation of liberty who reported what happened so that the victim's family could file an official report with Cobupej, providing data on the violent mechanism that caused the disappearance and requesting the issuance of a search warrant. However, in the universe of more than 8,000 reports with an official search warrant, cases were also found in which there is no information on how the disappearance occurred, as there were no witnesses. Additionally, the number of missing person notices analyzed represents only 24.35 percent of the 33,145 official cases of disappearances and locations contained in the Jalisco State Registry of Missing Persons (REPD) as of December 31, 2024. WHO ARE THE VICTIMS The identified victims are mostly males among the 1,248 referred, 1,117 are men and 131 are women. The median age of that universe is 30 years for both sexes and the most repeated is 25 years, that is, it is a population that is mostly young. The greatest impact of violent disappearances is observed among people aged 20 to 39 years. Violent disappearances were concentrated mainly in municipalities of the ZMG, as they accumulated 76.06 percent, but in 72 of the 125 demarcations of Jalisco, at least one absence of this type was registered. The North Highlands region of Jalisco also had a high incidence, and in it, the municipalities of Lagos de Moreno, Encarnación de Díaz, and San Juan de los Lagos stood out. Tepatitlán de Morelos, Atotonilco el Alto, San Miguel el Alto, and Arandas, all from the North Highlands, also stood out. It is practically a geographic corridor of violent disappearances that begins in the capital of Jalisco and ends in municipalities bordering Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, and Zacatecas. The analyzed reports cover a temporal arc from 1998 to 2024. However, from 2021, despite partial confinement due to the Covid-19 pandemic, reports skyrocketed. That year, there were 197 disappearances of this type, and since then, they have continued to increase until 2023, when they reached their maximum peak. On average, in the referred period, one violent disappearance occurred every 1.40 days, however, in 70 days, there were at least three violent disappearances. The last quarter of 2024 showed a decline in the number of reports and reached levels not seen since 2018 or even 2016. September had 10, October 10, November 8, and December 2 more. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE VICTIMS Of the 1,248 identified cases, only 212 people were located, that is, 17 percent. The low location rate is more notable in male victims than in female victims, as only 15.48 percent of men were found, while in women the indicator is 30.53 percent. The majority of people disappeared in violent events focused on a single person for whom a search warrant was issued, although in 162 cases the deprivation of liberty involved more than one victim, generally family members and friends. Although there are 1,087 reported incidents, there is only a record of one victim. In some cases, there are descriptions of multiple disappearances, but it is not specified if there are official reports or complaints filed with the authorities regarding the remaining missing people. For example, on January 5, 2022, several armed individuals broke into a residence in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga and forcibly took a young man and his father away. They also detained two men who were with them. Official records exist for the first two individuals, but not for the rest. This investigation identified cases of two individuals who were each subjected to two separate incidents of kidnapping by armed subjects at different times. The research also found a decrease in the number of missing persons cases in recent years. In 2020, 27.8% of the missing persons were located, whereas in 2024, only 16.6% were found. THE MECHANICS OF VIOLENT ABSENCE One of the patterns found in violent disappearances identified was that in the majority of cases, it involved acts where several individuals with firearms were involved. Based on these data, there were almost five armed individuals on average in the reports analyzed. References were also found to the possible participation of police corporation elements together with armed groups, as there were mentions of the presence of patrols, plates, uniforms, or expressions indicating that the aggressors belonged, for example, to the State Prosecutor's Office.Firearms are the articulating and driving element of the violence deployed by the individuals who participated in almost all identified disappearances, as in 663 reports, their presence was indicated in the events (generally a combination of short and long arms). In addition, most of the disappearances occurred in the private residence of the victims, just a few meters away from their home or in the neighborhood where they resided. There were violent break-ins in the homes. In the process of the disappearance of one or several people using this modus operandi, it was also identified that often other family members present were targets of physical or verbal aggression, and even the theft of their belongings. From the 1,248 reports analyzed, in 161 it was mentioned that the victim and/or a family member was beaten during the deprivation of liberty, sometimes with the same firearms (with the pistol or rifle grip), others with blunt objects (sticks, baseball bats, hammers), and in most cases, with kicks and punches. Moreover, in 82 reports, it was indicated that firearms were used. There were shots in the air, attacks on the homes where the victims resided, and direct shots at the victims. THE UNDERWORLDThe leads found in the reviewed cases of violent disappearances point to underworld connections directly related to organized crime, but also to private individuals. One of the most frequent motives has to do with the illegal drug market; those responsible for the disappearances were looking for people who allegedly possessed them, sold them, and consumed them. More than 50 reports contain indications of this nature.In the documented cases, disappearances linked to fuel theft and resale, or general theft of goods for the forced commercialization of certain cigarette brands, and the operation of illegal slot machines (also known as "maquinitas") in convenience stores in the ZMG area were also found. Another reason for the absences was the possible forced recruitment by disappearing entire teams of workers, but there were also others due to forced informants, mistaken victims, substitute victims, human trafficking, vicarious violence, family or neighborhood conflicts, road accidents, and disappearances to avoid the absence of a family member. This type of absence grew during Alfaro's sexenio. In Jalisco's previous state administration (2018-2024), violence as a means to disappear people intensified. Of the 1,248 identified cases, 1,096, i.e., 87.82%, occurred during the period from December 2018 to December 2024, when Enrique Alfaro Ramírez governed. While over a thousand Jaliscienses were forcibly taken from their home, workplace, or vehicle, Alfaro Ramírez dismissed the crisis by stating that most of the disappeared people left voluntarily. Even reaffirmed that stance in its last Security Report, submitted on November 4, 2024, when it said that 75 percent were not victims of a crime. In this year (2024), we have seen many cases of denunciations for disappearance that generate a march, two marches, or three marches, attacks, accusations, and then the disappeared person turns out to have left of their own free will. If we do not understand this, I insist, if we do not have a clear diagnosis, we are going to make mistakes always in the prescription, he said when talking about disappearances. Despite speeches like the previous one, the data analyzed in this research show a different reality in which violence in disappearances is not an isolated fact, but a constant in Jalisco. Lauro Rodríguez Affected youth The median age of the victims detected in this research is 30 years for both sexes, and the most repeated is 25 years.

The AIC handed over a wanted delinquent to US authorities at the II RENÉ ARELLANO International Bridge. Elements of the Criminal Investigation Agency of the State Attorney General's Office (FGE) of Coahuila, in coordination with the National Migration Institute, carried out a controlled delivery at the II International Bridge in Piedras Negras, of a North American man being sought by US authorities. According to information provided by the FGE, the detained person is identified as James N, who was being sought for several pending crimes of child abuse in his country, which was handed over to U.S. Marshal elements at the checkpoint of the aforementioned border crossing. The State of Coahuila authorities announced through a statement that, based on an investigation and coordination with other security agencies, it was the AIC of the FGE of Coahuila that located the now-detained individual in the city of Saltillo. Given the detainee's North American origin, it was the personnel of the National Migration Institute (INM) who, under their authority, carried out the controlled deportation at the International Bridge II, which connects the border cities of Piedras Negras, Coahuila and Eagle Pass, Texas, thereby interrupting vehicular traffic for a few minutes.

The request came from lawyer María Fernanda Petersen, representing the victims, as the sole accuser in the debate, since the prosecution has withdrawn from the case. This is the first trial for a criminal offense that takes place with this characteristic in the city of Bahía Blanca. Pinta's defense, led by lawyer Maximiliano De Mira, requested the acquittal of his client. Judge Daniela Fabiana Castaño, who presides over the debate as the representative of the Criminal Court Nº 3, will announce the verdict on Thursday of the following week at 12. The incidents attributed to the athlete and former municipal official would have taken place between 2011 and 2016, to the detriment of at least two students from the kayaking school in that city, when they were 14 years old and 16 years old, respectively. Madeline Soto Case Madeline Soto Why the videos found on Stephan Sterns' phone could lose their validity in the trial Univision, ORLANDO, Florida. The trial against Stephan Sterns, accused of child sexual abuse and murder of minor Madeline Soto, was rescheduled for the month of May 2025 due to a series of legal factors that have prolonged the process. The case remains stagnant as several delays have occurred in previous hearings leading up to the trial. Sterns, who faces over 60 charges related to child sexual abuse and pornography, was arrested in February 2024 following the disappearance of Madeline, a 13-year-old girl who was found dead days later. During the investigation, police discovered over 1,500 images and videos depicting Soto's sexual abuse, material allegedly collected over several years. These findings are crucial for Sterns' charges of sexual abuse and child pornography, but they are also the reason why the trial has suffered several delays. This Wednesday, the last pre-trial hearing before the sexual offense trial, which was scheduled for February 24, 2025, took place. Judge Keith Carsten agreed to the defense's request to postpone the trial until spring, as Sterns' legal team has not had access to the key evidence in the case. The prosecution, represented by State Assistant Attorney Danielle Pinnell, explained that the defense has yet to review sensitive material, including images and videos found during the investigation. Due to the delicate nature of the evidence, these can only be viewed in the prosecutor's office, resulting in additional waiting time. Furthermore, Sterns' defense has submitted three motions to suppress evidence obtained in the case. The main objection stems from the police not following the proper procedures when seizing Sterns' mobile phone, which could compromise the validity of the evidence obtained. Alesha Smith, Sterns' attorney, stated that she could not schedule a hearing to resolve these motions until she presented a fourth motion requesting the court to seal the courtroom. This series of additional procedures has contributed further to the prolongation of the case. New trial dates set for sexual abuse charges against Stephen Sterns The trial for the sexual abuse charges is scheduled to begin on May 5, 2025, while the murder trial, which Sterns faces for the death of Madeline Soto, will take place on September 22. In the event of being found guilty of murder, the suspect could face the death penalty. Madeline Soto went missing on February 26, 2024, when her mother, Jennifer Soto, went to pick her up from school and was informed that she never made it to class that day. Four days later, her body was found in a rural area of Osceola County, in an area where Sterns had been seen changing a tire. According to the investigation, the girl was murdered before school hours and her body was later moved. The preliminary report from the medical examiner determined that the cause of death was strangulation, with signs of damage to the hyoid bone, indicating a homicide. Sterns was the boyfriend of Madeline's mother and lived with them in the same house. Police reports indicate that it was not unusual for him to sleep in the same bed as the minor, even when her mother was not present. Since his arrest in February 2024, Sterns has waived his presence at all previous court hearings before the trial. The Sterns and their lawyers have requested to withdraw the death penalty as a possible sentence, as well as other requests such as allowing him to be unshackled during the trial and to use a real pen in court.

Nashville News It is alleged that these individuals recruited young and vulnerable women from Central and South America to force them to work in a commercial sex business in the United States, primarily in Tennessee. The accused promised the victims a better life, but upon arrival in the U.S., they revealed that they had to pay off their debts through sex with strangers. Federal Prosecutor Robert Maguire emphasized the gravity of the human trafficking problem in the community and the need to combat it. The investigation, which spanned several years, was led by the Nashville Metropolitan Police Department and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. The accused individuals are Yilibeth del Carmen Rivero Caldera (alias Yibi), Kleiver Daniel Mota Rivero (alias Kleiber), Yuribetzi del Valle Gómez Machuca (alias La Gorda), Wilmarys del Valle Manzano Solórzano (alias La China), Endrik Alexander Morales Rivero (alias Endri), Ariannys Beatriz Gutiérrez Carrillo (alias Nani, Nany), Frankyanna del Valle Romero Rivero (alias Franya), and Jesús Enrique Castillo Rodríguez (alias Chu Chu). The accused individuals used hotels in Nashville and online platforms to lure their victims and offer sexual favors. It has been reported that some of the accused were linked to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, which helped them intimidate their victims. The eight accused individuals are currently under federal custody awaiting trial after being arrested in multiple states, including Tennessee and Texas. The former National Party legislator committed 22 sex crimes against minors. The 4th Turn Penal Appeals Court overturned this Wednesday the judge's order, Marcela Vargas, who last week ordered the total house arrest and electronic ankle bracelet for the former National Party senator, Gustavo Penadés, and the History professor, Sebastián Mauvezín, who are accused of sex crimes linked to minors. Penadés and Mauvezín had been charged on October 10, 2023. In the case of the former nationalist legislator for 22 sex crimes against minors, and the teacher for seven crimes of contributing to the sexual exploitation of minors. Both were complying with the preventive detention measure awaiting trial. On Wednesday, February 5, the Justice ordered both to comply with total house arrest and electronic ankle bracelet. The Sexual Crimes Prosecutor, Alicia Ghione, had requested an extension of the preventive detention measure until June 10, 2025, arguing that the anticipated statement of one of the victims was still pending, which had been proposed last year but the victim felt fear and did not want to testify. Additionally, two forensic tests were still pending by the Technical Forensic Institute (ITF) of the Judicial Power due to the emotional trauma the victims had undergone, the cross-matching of data from their cellular phones, and the expansion and analysis of the financial information of Penadés and Mauvezín. The Prosecution appealed Vargas' ruling, and the Appellate Court gave Ghione the right, revoking the disposition. Minutes before 5 pm, Penadés was notified of the judicial resolution, as recorded by photographer Dante Fernández of the Foco Uy News Agency.

Incidents Detained in Alcalá del Río for Exploiting Resourceless Immigrants The Civil Guard has proceeded to the detention of two individuals and the investigation of a third as suspected perpetrators of a crime against the rights of foreign workers, as well as the investigation of the owner of an agricultural exploitation for having declared as a witness and lied in their testimony. The actions form part of a series of joint activities framed within the plan against human trafficking and labor exploitation. The investigation by Team Roca 10 began last May 2023, when agricultural sector representatives from Andalusia of a union, brought to the attention of the Civil Guard that several people had worked in an agricultural exploitation in the locality of Alcalá del Río (Seville) without receiving any economic remuneration. In order to verify the facts, the agents interviewed the victims, who were all Senegalese nationals and residents in a migrant reception center managed by the Spanish Refugee Aid Commission (CEAR). Following the necessary investigations, the Civil Guard learned that in January 2024, the victims had been recruited by a Nicaraguan couple to work in the harvesting of field fruits in several agricultural exploitations in the province of Seville. This couple, who were functioning as traffickers and were also in an irregular situation in the country, took advantage of the victims' vulnerability due to being in Spain without legal authorization and without permission to work, in order to impose labor conditions that violated the rights recognized by legal dispositions and collective agreements. The suspects forced them to perform long working hours, without rest and in abusive conditions, for which they received salaries far below the stipulated amount, resulting in an economic debt of over 7,000 euros with their workers. The victims stated that they accepted the working conditions imposed on them due to their situation of need to send money to their relatives residing in Senegal and economically dependent on them. In the same operation, a businessman from the agricultural sector, of Spanish nationality and residing in the locality of Brenes, has been investigated. Supposedly, being aware of the victims' situation of need and knowing that they did not have work authorization in Spain as they were in an irregular situation, he hired them through Nicaraguan intermediaries to work in several agricultural exploitations. Similarly, the entrepreneur failed to comply with the obligation to register his workers with the Social Security system, thereby obtaining greater economic benefits by saving on the payment of these contributions, which resulted in a serious detriment to the rights of his workers, such as not being able to enjoy medical assistance, right to sickness benefits, work accident and occupational disease benefits, etc. It is worth noting that one of the victims suffered a work accident that made it impossible for them to continue with their working hours. The accused, who denied them medical assistance, urged them to continue working under the threat that they would not be paid for the day worked. The victim was only assisted with the injuries suffered when his colleagues ended their work shift and the traffickers took him to a reception center where he resides, and it was the workers from the aforementioned center who took him to the nearest emergency service. The investigation was initiated by the ROCA Unit of the Civil Guard in La Rinconada, the Woman and Minor Unit (EMUME) of the Sevilla Command, and Labor Inspection. The detainees, along with the proceedings, have been placed at the disposal of the Sevilla court on duty.

data.text: The Murders of Street-Working Women Testimonies. Since 2019, Carmen, Fernanda, Katherine, Lucía, Liliana, Marcela, Paulina, and Roxi have been living in fear of being extorted, violently attacked, murdered, or disappeared by the Aragua Train, the Venezuelan megaband that has expanded throughout South America. The fear experienced by these women is fueled by the fact that they serve as the city's criminal thermometer, being the first to feel the effects of the predatory criminal economies that have driven the expansion of the Aragua Train in Lima.For Lara Loaiza Paulina, 15 years of working as a sex worker on the streets of Lima have been a means of supporting her family, as she has no other means of sustenance. When you have children, you have to look for whatever it takes so that they can eat, Paulina says. During all these years working as a sex worker, she has lived through countless acts of violence firsthand and has witnessed the abuses suffered by other sex workers. Paulina thought she had seen it all, until in September 2022, some criminals murdered one of her colleagues on one of the main streets in the center of Lima. They killed her because she refused to pay and for denouncing that they were charging a quota, meaning a type of extortion that criminal groups charge sex workers in exchange for allowing them to work on the streets. Paulina feared falling under the radar of the criminals and them starting to charge her a quota, so for the two months that followed the murder of her colleague, she did not return to work. However, her fear became a reality in November, when she began receiving different WhatsApp messages. The alleged authors, members of the Aragua Train, a Venezuelan megaband that has expanded across South America since 2019 and has become the main criminal threat in Lima, left a clear warning. They contacted me, stating they were the Aragua Train and that if we didn't pay protection money, they would kill us, remember. They were charging 400 soles (around US$100) as an enrollment fee to continue working in the area they had been operating in for years. Apart from the initial fee, I had to transfer 150 soles (US$40) each week to an account, and send a photo of the payment receipt with my name. Fearing for my life and that of my children, Paulina began paying the protection money. You work or not, you have to gather your money, because if you don't pay them, they'll kill you, she adds. YOU CAN SEE PNP Rescues 7 Women Victims of Sexual Exploitation in Los Olivos Trafficking Ring Was a Faction of the Aragua Train However, soon it began to have difficulties in collecting the full amount of money. The days when there were not enough clients, it was impossible for her to gather the entire payment. In some cases, she had even had to stop eating in order to be able to pay the quota. But when she couldn't gather the full amount, Paulina sent the little she managed to get to the criminals. Still, these men threatened her for not paying the full quota. If you don't like the rules, leave the area better so you don't get killed, one of the messages sentenced. Although Paulina had a lot of fear of suffering reprisals, denouncing the situation was not an option for her. In Peru, sex work is not penalized, but neither is there a specific framework for its regulation, and sex workers like her have been left unprotected against all types of violence. Additionally, the security forces, which had been the main aggressors of sex workers in Lima, generally discriminate against them and do not usually help them in situations like this. One goes to report and they tell you "No, no, I don't believe, I don't believe they're going to kill you." And when they kill you, they say "Why didn't you report? Why didn't you warn?" And when you call them, they don't show up, explain. Sex workers in Lima have systematically faced extortions, beatings, rapes, and even murders and disappearances. All this violence at the hands of their families, clients, security forces, and local mafias. But despite the abuse and mistreatment having been a constant in their lives, the different factions of the Aragua Train have taken the violence to unprecedented levels. YOU CAN SEE Father Rescues Daughter from Los Hijos de Dios del Tren de Aragua in Moquegua was a Victim of Human Trafficking The Street is Tough Before the Arrival of the Tren de Aragua in 2019, among the main perpetrators of violence against sex workers were the local mafias led by mamis and papis, known as pimps, who, on occasion, extorted money from small groups of sex workers. The mamis and papis also managed local human trafficking networks for sexual exploitation. There have always been mafias, explains Ángela Villón, leader of Miluska Vida y Dignidad (MVD), a sex workers' association in Lima. They would cut off your clothes and tell you that if you don't pay the next time, we'll do the same thing to you, but on your skin. It's a terrifying thing, but they wouldn't kill you. But, in addition to the mothers and fathers, for decades, the main aggressors of sex workers in Lima were members of the Peruvian National Police (PNP) and the Municipal Serenazgo, a institution in charge of urban security. Taking advantage of the legal loopholes in Peru regarding sex work, members of the PNP and the serenazgos conducted operations against sex workers and arbitrarily detained them, according to a dozen sex workers who spoke with InSight Crime. They claim to have received blows, mistreatment, extortion, and even sexual abuse during these operations. Another sex worker leader, Leida Portal, who heads the organization Rosa Mujeres de Lucha, dedicated to advocating for sex workers, was a victim of three police officers who burst into her workplace, beat her, stole her money, and took her to the police station, where they subjected her to further abuse and discrimination. However, things began to deteriorate for sex workers with the arrival of Venezuelan organized crime groups in 2019. A decade ago, thousands of Venezuelans fled their country to escape the economic and political crisis. One of the first destinations for migrants was Peru, where currently reside 1.6 million Venezuelans, according to data from the humanitarian coordination platform R4V. In 2018, when the Venezuelan migration flow reached unprecedented levels, the Aragua Train began to expand across South America, using migrant trafficking to establish themselves outside of Venezuela. To take root in Peru's capital, a notorious faction of the group known as Los Gallegos began to displace small Peruvian organized crime groups. Among their primary objectives were the networks extorting sex workers in Lima. According to sex workers and members of the PNP who spoke with InSight Crime, the arrival and expansion of Los Gallegos in the area was announced on the night of Thursday, January 9, 2020, when three men murdered Isaac Hilario Huamanyalli, known as Cholo Isaac. Cholo Isaac allegedly controlled the collection of quotas in the Lince district, a hotspot for sex work in central Lima. The murder of Cholo Isaac was one of the key moves that highlighted the expansion of the Tren de Aragua faction in the city. But it was not the only signal. According to sex workers who spoke with InSight Crime, one of the Peruvian madams also opened the door to Los Gallegos. A girl teamed up with a Venezuelan man. He taught her how to collect quotas, and the Venezuelan mafia took the girl away, and he kept everything for himself, asserts Roxi, a Venezuelan sex worker who has been working in Lima for three years. The Aragua Train factions displaced other Peruvian mom and pop networks and usurped their throne in the quota collection business. With local competition out of the game, Venezuelan criminal groups extended their tentacles over sex workers. The Gallegos began extorting Venezuelan sex workers and then focused on Peruvian, Colombian, and Ecuadorian sex workers. What they did at that time was kidnap sex workers and kept them two, three days in a place where they didn't let them sleep, all the time telling them how they were going to kill them, precise Ángela. With the arrival of the COVID-19 pandemic, sex workers who couldn't go out to the streets in Lima migrated to messaging apps like WhatsApp to coordinate with each other and schedule meetings with their clients. The Gallegos knew how to take advantage of this, not only did they retain the cell phones of sex workers, but they also collected numbers of others through group chats that they were part of and thus caught new victims in their extortion web. When we were still in the midst of the pandemic, they sent us the first message where they introduced themselves, recalls Ángela. They were communicating that from that moment on, we had to pay the quotas to them. Pay or die. Today, six years after the arrival of the Aragua Train in Peru, all the women who engage in sex work on the streets of Lima must pay a quota to this gang, or to one of its associated factions, such as the Gallegos, the Sons of God, or the Alayón Dynasty. What interests them is their money. Either you pay or they kill you, says Liliana, a Venezuelan sex worker. Extortion is everywhere. Some, like Paulina and Liliana, receive threatening messages from criminal groups on their phones and the groups they use to communicate with other sex workers. Others are cornered in the streets and even in their own homes. They're closing in on all fronts, and eventually, you're sucked into this cycle of criminalization, notes Lucía, a Peruvian sex worker who works through online ads. If you don't pay, you don't work, adds Lucía. Criminal groups constantly monitor sex workers who advertise online, using their contact numbers to extort "cupo" fees. They send you threatening messages on WhatsApp as soon as they see your ad, Lucía says. The text messages ultimately lead to bank account numbers where they demand a specific amount of money be deposited. First, they must pay the permit, or the registration, as the extortionists call it, to be able to work in areas under the group's control. The price depends on the faction and the area, which can range from 200 to 400 soles (US$50-100). Then, like Paulina, they must make a weekly payment that ranges from 150 to 250 soles (US$40-66), although it can sometimes reach 500 (US$130). The collections are not the same for all. The Venezuelans, who were the first to be extorted, must pay more simply because they are Venezuelans. And if they delay with the payment, their debt accumulates. Despite the threatening messages almost always coming from men, the women who are part of the Tren de Aragua, or in some cases, victims of human trafficking, are the ones who collect the quotas on the streets. According to the testimonies of sex workers and leaders, these women pass through the areas where sex work is concentrated every day to collect the quotas. Some, despite being associated with the criminal group, are also targets. One of them was assassinated by the group after becoming known in the area, according to sex workers who spoke with InSight Crime. They charged her and the same criminals killed her, Katherine asserts, another woman who spoke with InSight Crime. She charged all Peruvian women, but as she became ambitious, she joined up with stronger people. However, with the mafia, no one plays, because the mafia bores you and kills you. If any woman refuses to pay or does not have permission from the group to work in the area, they threaten her, beat her, and even kill her. The violence is not random. It is a written warning with blood for other sex workers who refuse to pay and will suffer the same fate. Members of criminal groups kidnapped Lucia in 2023. She had agreed to meet a client at a house, but upon arriving at the location, she realized the situation was not what she had expected. Inside the residence, she found a man armed, who told her she was not on his list of authorized women to work and abused her while threatening her with the gun. Although she managed to escape, Lucía fears being attacked again. The families of sex workers are also in the crosshairs. In August 2023, Katherine's husband was having lunch with his family in the capital. Unaware that armed men were following him, he stepped out onto the street to hail a taxi, but moments later the men shot him and killed him. It was because he didn't pay the fee, Katherine says.

According to judicial documents, they met several times at the Mall before the minor visited Gómez's house, where the abuse occurred. Initially, the minor claimed they had a relationship only once, but Gómez stated it was two occasions. On October 28, 2022, Gómez admitted to knowing the minor through Facebook and that she contacted him first. She admitted that she told him she was a minor and acknowledged that the relationship was inappropriate.

The Constitutional Committees, Gobernación and Justice and Political Matters, as well as the Committee on Gender Equality and Against Human Trafficking of the Tlaxcala Congress, presided over by lawmakers Jaciel González Herrera and Lorena Ruiz García respectively, unanimously approved the resolution of the initiatives proposing constitutional reforms to ensure substantive equality for women, eradicate gender violence, and eliminate the pay gap. The reforms harmonize the State Constitution with the federal constitutional reform published on November 15, 2024, driven by President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, which recognizes historical inequality and establishes mechanisms for its elimination. The initiatives were presented by Deputy María Ana Bertha Mastranzo Corona, Deputy Lorena Ruíz García, and the women from the collectives Mujeres Libres and 501 Capítulo Tlaxcala. In their proposals, they stand out for recognizing the right of women to a life free of violence in the local Constitution, incorporating a gender perspective in the administration of justice and public security, as well as the creation of a Special Prosecutor's Office for Crimes of Gender Violence. The deputies reaffirmed their commitment to building a more just and equitable Tlaxcala, where equality of rights between women and men is a reality. With the approval of this resolution, the initiatives advance in the corresponding legislative process. Follow the latest information on the social media of URBANO Noticias Puebla and Tlaxcala.

24 years after the crime of Natalia Melmann, the 24-year-old girl who was murdered in Miramar in February 2001, prosecutor Ana María Caro, who is investigating the case, requested that DNA of a fifth suspect be analyzed. The suspect is a 60-year-old former police officer currently residing in the city of Trenque Lauquen in Buenos Aires Province. His identity has not been disclosed yet. The analysis was conducted at the Expert Advice office in that city due to the fact that the Scientific Police cannot intervene since some of the implicated individuals were part of the force. The prosecution's goal is to match the suspect's DNA with the genetic material found on the victim's body. On February 4, 24 years had passed since the brutal murder of Natalia Melmann. On the same date in 2001, the 15-year-old girl was returning home from dancing in the town of Miramar. It was around 7 in the morning when a group of police officers intercepted her, beat her, and forced her to get into a patrol car. After that, they took her to a house in the Copacabana neighborhood, on the outskirts of the city, where they tortured her, raped her, and hanged her with the cord of her own shoe. For four days, there were no news of Natalia. Her family and friends searched for her alongside the security forces, unaware that the police had participated in the atrocious act that was about to shock the entire country. Her body was found on February 8, buried under a pile of dry leaves in the Florentino Ameghino nursery. It is presumed that they discarded it in that place on the same day of the crime. Natalia had bruises on her thighs, cigarette burns on her left hand, a broken septum, and a strong blow to the skull. Later, the autopsy revealed the presence of five different genetic profiles. In September 2002, officers Oscar Echenique (61), Ricardo Anselmini (53), and Ricardo Suárez (58) were sentenced to life in prison. Gustavo Fernández, also known as El Gallo, was also sentenced. Fernández received a 25-year prison sentence for being considered the person who handed over Melmann to his killers, but was acquitted of charges of co-authoring the homicide. However, his sentence was later reduced to 10 years. In the case of Ricardo Panadero, he was acquitted twice due to lack of evidence. Nevertheless, in 2019, the Provincial Penal Cassation Court revoked the decision and held that the fourth member of the Bonaerense Police must face a trial for his participation in the crime. Finally, on November 13, 2019, Chamber III of the Bonaerense Cassation Court annulled his overruling and ordered a new trial to be held. This took place in 2023, and as a result, Panadero was found guilty of aggravated illegal deprivation of liberty, aggravated sexual abuse, and double homicide aggravated by the premeditated intervention of several people and committed to ensure impunity. The sentence handed down was life imprisonment.

At the request of lawyer assistant Lucila Maggiora, a male, identified by the initials J.A.P, accused of holding his ex-partner captive, injuring her, and sexually abusing her, will continue to be detained under house arrest. J.A.P is accused of the crimes of threats, aggravated light injuries due to the relationship, and having mediated gender violence, in ideal concurrence with illegal deprivation of liberty, aggravated. These in turn concur with the figure of sexual abuse with carnal access as an author (Articles 54, 92 in conjunction with Articles 89 and 80, paragraphs 1 and 11, 119, third paragraph, 142, paragraph 1, and 45 of the Penal Code). During the hearing held, the representative of the prosecution requested that the precautionary measure currently close to expiring be extended. The required period was two months, starting from February 22, and for the purpose of reaching the hearing to control the accusation, where it will be possible to discuss and verify if the procedural risks that the prosecution intends to cautelar, continue in force. He added that in the hearing to formulate charges held on May 22, 2024, the accused was detained in preventive prison for a period of 10 days. Then, his detention was converted into a home detention, valid until the current date. Maggiora added that the request to extend the measure, is to mitigate the risk of interference so that both the victim and the witnesses can testify in a possible trial. Judge Ignacio Pombo granted the prosecution's request and ordered house arrest for the defendant for the required period. According to the theory of the case being investigated by the Public Prosecutor's Office, the incident occurred on May 21, 2024, around 3:00 pm in the city of Junín de los Andes. The defendant approached his ex-partner, who was walking in a public area. He grabbed her by the arm and hair and took her to the residence of a family member. Once there, he forced her to enter the interior and locked the door with a key, preventing her from leaving. He then assaulted and sexually abused her.In the hearing to formalize charges, defense attorney Lucila Maggiora explained that the victim reported other incidents of violence, and that the defendant had a suspended trial on probation for three incidents of threats with weapons, which he had violated.

In Viedma, a man was charged with simple sexual abuse after kissing a 9-year-old girl on the mouth inside the supermarket where he works. According to a report from the Río Negro Public Prosecutor's Office, the man allegedly took advantage of the girl being momentarily alone to approach and kiss her without her consent, while her mother was a few meters away, unaware of the situation. The prosecution supported the accusation with various evidence, the complaint filed by the girl's mother, the testimony given by the victim and her brother in Camera Gesell, and the security camera footage from the supermarket, which recorded the moment of the incident. Despite the opposition from the defense, which presented a different version of events, the Guarantee Judge ruled that the accusation was filed and extended the precautionary measures imposed on the accused. These include the prohibition of approaching the victim, her family, and the witnesses who testified in the case.

A 34-year-old man was arrested in the Rivera department in recent hours as a suspect in sexual abuse against his 13-year-old daughter. According to a report by the Telemundo news channel, the complaint was filed by a 30-year-old woman, the mother of the victim and the accused's partner, who said she learned of the situation while investigating a punishment imposed on the younger child. The woman reported that one day, when her husband was leaving for work, he instructed her not to let the girl use her cell phone because he had put her in time-out. Since the man did not provide explanations, she asked her daughter about the reasons for the prohibition. According to the woman, that morning the man saw the girl was connected to WhatsApp and sent her a message telling her to send a photo of herself and her cousin naked. When the girl refused to comply with the request, her father took away her cell phone and prohibited its use. The woman was alarmed, and she spoke with her daughter, asking if similar situations had occurred before. According to the aforementioned report, the victim stated that on other occasions, the father had touched her intimate areas, and he had also rubbed his penis against her legs. Following the complaint filed by the wife of the detained man, the police are investigating whether he had similar conduct towards the other children he has in common with the woman, three minors aged 11, 9, and 4 years. For the time being, a precautionary measure was ordered, requiring the accused to leave the home and prohibiting all types of contact with the family for a period of 180 days. It was also resolved that the four minors of legal age undergo psychological evaluations and medical forensic examinations.

Edgar met Edgar on LinkedIn. He worked for a Canadian software company, she was from Singapore and worked for a large consulting firm. They were just friends, but they chatted online all the time. One day, Rita offered to teach him how to operate with cryptocurrencies. With her help, he made a lot of money. So he increased the stakes. However, when Edgar tried to collect his winnings, he discovered that the cryptocurrency trading website was fake, and he had lost $78,000. Moreover, Rita was a Filipino victim of human trafficking who was being held captive in a Myanmar prison complex. In their own way, both Edgar and Rita were victims of the "pig butchering" scam, the most lucrative global sector that steals more than $500 billion from victims worldwide every year. We are facing the most significant change in decades in the realm of transnational organized crime. The term "chinese shazhupan", pig slaughter or killing pigs, belongs to the underworld slang. First, the scammers construct a pen, made with false profiles on social media. Then, they choose the pig, i.e., they identify the target, they bait them, passing weeks or months generating trust, they stab them with a knife, tempting them to invest, and then they skin them to take advantage of everything from them... from them, their family, and their friends. The sector is growing rapidly. In Singapore, scams have become the most common crime. According to the United Nations, the sector employed almost 250,000 people in Cambodia and Myanmar in 2023, and another estimate puts the number of workers worldwide at 1.5 million. In a podcast by The Economist, cases are analyzed of a man from Minnesota who lost $92 million and a rural bank in Kansas that went bankrupt when its CEO diverted $47 million to invest in cryptocurrencies, guided online by a fake woman named Bella. A part-time pastor also stole from his church. Online scams are now comparable in size and scope to the illegal drug trade. However, in many ways, they are even worse. One reason is that everyone becomes a potential target simply by living their life. Among the identified victims in The Economist's podcast is a neuroscientist and also relatives of FBI agents whose work is to combat scams. Instruction manuals offer people like Rita step-by-step instructions to manipulate victims by exploiting their emotions. It is an error to think that the sentimental factor is the only hook. Scammers target all human vulnerabilities: fear, loneliness, greed, sadness, and boredom. Another reason why scams are worse than drugs is that they often operate outside the reach of the law. In the physical world, those who engage in pig slaughter operate from complexes that house production lines of scammers and are a hybrid between a prisoner camp and a colonial business district of another era, with supermarkets, brothels, and gaming rooms, as well as torture chambers for unruly employees. A part of the profits is used to buy protection from politicians and officials. In the Philippines, a Chinese citizen named Alice Guo became the mayor of a small, declining city and built a complex of over thirty buildings dedicated to scams. More than $400 million passed through their bank accounts between 2019 and 2024. In Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar, cybercrime has become a pillar of the economy. It is likely that state scammers will be harder to combat than narco-states. Digital scams are more difficult to curb than drug transactions, and some countries provide cover for them. The use of AI will increase their chances and scammers are equally elusive in the digital world. Chinese organized crime syndicates that run them are not hierarchical mafias. Rather, they are a submerged collaborative economy. A group can specialize in setting up scams, another in advising them to invest in cryptocurrencies, and a third in laundering the stolen money. Digital fracking of human vulnerability is highly modifiable. The last reason why scams are worse than drugs is that they are very innovative. The scammers use advanced malicious software to obtain confidential data from the victims' devices. Cybermarkets trade tools and services, including web domains, artificial intelligence (AI) software, and torture instruments. Cryptocurrencies allow criminals to quickly and anonymously move money in the real world. Regardless of their merits, the deregulation of cryptocurrencies taking place in the United States will give them new opportunities. AI will turbocharge all those innovations. Currently, it only takes 15 seconds of someone's voice to produce a clone that criminals use to impersonate identities. An Arup employee in Hong Kong was tricked into paying $25 million via a video call with deepfakes of their colleagues, including the finance director. Combining the AI's voice and facial changes with translation services and the vast amounts of stolen data sold on black markets, scammers will be able to target more victims in more places. Criminals will also be able to use analysis tools to identify affluent, lonely, or troubled individuals in large datasets, making them promising targets. Online scams will be even harder to suppress than drug trafficking, and unlike the latter, there is no option for legalization, regulation, or treatment. Education may be of some help. In Singapore, warnings appear on public transportation and during digital transactions. However, law enforcement action must also change. To combat scammers, authorities must create their own networks. Today, many police forces with vast resources dedicated to combating drug trafficking view scams as an inconvenience and victims as naive. Instead, they need to work with banks, cryptocurrency wallets, internet service providers, telecommunications companies, social media platforms, and e-commerce companies. Singapore has created a nerve center where police, banks, and e-commerce companies can track and freeze money instantly when scammers move the loot between accounts. Countries also need to look beyond their borders. Criminals move money and people across many jurisdictions, so the global law enforcement machinery is unable to keep up with them. Many leaders of groups involved in scams are from mainland China, and the Communist Party of China arrests hundreds of thousands of suspected scammers every year. No country understands better the scale and sophistication of these criminal groups. In a time when the US and China are at odds, scams are an area where they could and should collaborate for the greater good. 2025 The Economist Newspaper Limited. All rights reserved

Graduate Program on Mechanisms and Tools for the Prevention, Attention, and Combat of Child Labor Approximately 2,000 people participate in this activity in person and virtually. Press ReleaseURLGutiérrez The rector Oswaldo Chacón Rojas, inaugurated the activities of the Graduate Program on Mechanisms and Tools for the Prevention, Attention, and Combat of Child Labor, Forced Labor, and Human Trafficking with a focus on Public Policies. The program is organized by the Intersecretarial Commission for the Prevention and Eradication of Child Labor (CITI), the State Secretariat of Labor and Social Security of Chiapas, the State Human Rights Commission, and the Institute of Legal Research of UNACH. With the presence of the State Coordinator of INEGI, Francisco Velázquez Sotelo, and the Specialized Visitor for Attention to Matters of Girls, Boys, and Adolescents of the CEDH, César Andrey Molina Velasco, the rector Oswaldo Chacón Rojas stated that being part of a project that addresses a topic related to humanism is something that characterizes the University. The diploma is built with the work and commitment of the university's teachers, with their research lines, but above all with society, so the academic offer of this nature must be expanded, with the purpose of addressing the majority of the problems that affect society, he pointed out. Accompanied by the General Secretary, María del Carmen Vázquez Velasco, he stated that the IIJ represents the values of what we want to promote from UNACH, such as overcoming, the elevation of the standards of quality of academic work and research, as well as close linkages with the major social, economic, and political problems of our society. Regarding this, the Undersecretary of the National Employment Service, Mauricio Ibarrola Obregón, referred that this diploma program invites participants to strengthen their capacities to design, apply, and evaluate effective public policies for the protection of human rights, especially those concerning people with greater vulnerability. Before Deputy Andrea Negrón Sánchez, President of the Congress State Labor Commission, stated that through the joint efforts of the government and academic sectors, a positive impact can be generated in the formulation, implementation, and evaluation of strategies against child labor. In this regard, Jorge Humberto Pascacio Bringas, Director of the Institute of Legal Research, emphasized that it is of utmost importance to address this social phenomenon from academia, which is why this second edition of the diploma has a focus on public policies. The diploma, which involves around two thousand people, both in person and virtually, aims to address the numbers issued by international and national organizations on Child Labor. In 2018, UNICEF estimated that more than 151 million children were victims of child labor, while slightly over 72 million were affected by slavery, trafficking, forced labor, or recruitment for armed conflicts.

In Fort Smith, the Arkansas State Police (ASP) and the Arkansas Human Trafficking Council conducted a human trafficking operation, rescuing over 40 victims. Colonel Mike Hagar highlighted the collaboration of several organizations in this effort. The investigation remains active, and no further details are currently available.
